is there any additional human-caused climate change at all? is this 3.5% co2 that humans are responsible for really relevant? how much is the climate affected by the varying intensity of the sun's radiation? what is the effect of the greenhouse gas water vapour? what other influences are there on the climate? is a possible increase in the temperature of the earth the result of an increase in the concentration of co2 or is it the other way around? we don't know all that for sure yet. many models suggest a man-made greenhouse effect. but they're still guilty of the final proof. as i said, ladies and gentlemen, we must therefore be careful and reduce co2 emissions as much as possible. but at the same time we must urgently invest more in climate research and give our support to those researchers who are not in the mainstream. we need a broad spectrum of opinion to be able to make the right decisions in the interests of the people as soon as possible and on the basis of solid data. because if we have solid data, we will be able to convince other countries to join us on this path.

it confers new rights on european citizens, in particular by giving them the opportunity to take initiatives towards the institutions, and in particular towards the commission. this treaty confirms that we are no longer an economic union but a political union in the making: we are first and foremost a union based on common values. in this respect, the constitution is an essential step in the integration process. after the european parliament, the citizens will have a say: directly, by means of referendums, in the countries where referendums will be held, or indirectly, by means of parliamentary ratification. the council undertook to make every effort to ensure that this constitution is adopted in all the member states. it is now up to each member state, each government and each parliament to take this step so that the constitution can come into force, and i would add, come into force on the date indicated. we share a great responsibility in this respect, the european parliament, governments and national parliaments. we must rise to this challenge together. vice-president of the commission. mr president, the constitution before us today would not have been possible without the european parliament. this house has played a crucial role in strengthening the foundations of our common enterprise, not least through the substantial contributions made by members of this parliament during the european convention. it would also not have been possible without that european convention, which provided such a dynamic, open and innovative means of negotiation. the involvement of the european parliament in this unprecedented process culminates today with an excellent and well-written report, which sends a clear message on the benefits of the constitution and the need for its ratification. i wholeheartedly congratulate parliament, and in particular the committee on constitutional affairs and the two rapporteurs, richard corbett and íñigo méndez de vigo. the commission fully supports your resolution. we firmly believe that the constitution allows the union to make significant improvements. in simple terms, for the first time the powers, competences, rights and duties of the union are set out in a single constitution. the constitution consolidates and simplifies half a century of treaty changes, allowing us to move from 12 basic treaty acts to a single text. it makes the union more open and simpler to understand. the constitution modernises the institutional structure. it increases the powers of the european parliament and provides for citizens actively to participate in the decision-making process through a petition with one million signatures. we will have more democracy. the constitution sets out, in 54 concise articles, the fundamental rights we will guarantee to our citizens. for the first time the union will accede to the european convention on human rights, so there will be more rights for our citizens. these three simple concepts – more rights, more democracy and more openness – explain why this constitution should be ratified. we would certainly have wished to be more ambitious in certain policy areas, but the final result is the best possible compromise in the current political situation. i also accept that people have fears and criticisms regarding this constitution. it is not a perfect text and we should not hide from responding to these concerns. our latest eurobarometer survey shows that 68% of our citizens support the idea and principle of having a european constitution. other opinion polls show that many feel they are inadequately informed about the content of the constitution. your report has made a good start by rejecting some of the misconceptions and scare stories about the constitution. it provides a range of good reasons for the euro-specialists to be voting yes, but these are not always the reasons that will persuade a single mother in gdansk, or a shipyard worker in spain to do so. the ratification of the constitution is an opportunity to debate the kind of europe we want. i welcome this opportunity to remind ourselves of what europe has achieved and what europe stands for, as has so elegantly been explained by others. in the mid-1980s, the vision of creating a genuine single market seemed a bridge too far. and yet it happened, bringing in its wake an economic dynamism from which we still benefit. to cite one simple example, the fact that we do not have to go through customs at borders has dramatically reduced costs and delivery times. in a single step we removed the need for 60 million vat documents per year. today, the younger generation treat as a right the idea of a zone of free movement, in the same way that they expect the union to ensure a clean environment and cross-border cooperation on public health. today, in 12 countries of the eu, we have a piece of europe in our pockets, with the euro being taken for granted across the union and with new member states joining the queue to introduce it. finally, first through membership of greece, spain and portugal and now with the 10 new member states, we have helped guarantee and consolidate democracy and the rule of law across the whole continent. we must now turn to the ratification of the constitution. while we respect our different constitutional roles in relation to the national ratification processes, we cannot tolerate the debate being confused by myths or misconceptions about the content of the constitution. all of us have a duty to make available clear and reliable information on what the constitution does and the benefits it can bring. in so doing we must compare the results of the constitution with the current situation. lithuania and hungary have already ratified the constitution. i would, in particular, like to pay tribute to lithuania and the speaker of the lithuanian parliament, who is here in the chamber today. (applause) we must now start to show what concrete impact the constitution can have on the daily lives of the people we represent. indeed, there is no shortage of good examples in this respect. as i said earlier, the inclusion of the charter of fundamental rights is far from a symbolic innovation. citizens will have a catalogue of rights and principles whose respect by the public authorities – be they european or national – they will be entitled to invoke before the courts. the possibility of concrete participation in the functioning of the union is extended far beyond the election of the members of the european parliament. the citizens' initiative will, for the first time, make european citizens protagonists in the legislative process. modernisation of the area of freedom, security and justice will allow the union to respond to the growing demand for more effective european action in the fields of border controls, asylum and immigration. the same is true for judicial and police cooperation. the constitution lays the foundations for a single area of liberties and guarantees. the new provisions on public health will provide higher quality standards with regard to safety. the union will be able to intervene in a more effective way to prevent and fight cross-border health threats such as avian flu or bse. today, we cannot avoid thinking about the tragic events in southeast asia. the union is already playing a key role in providing humanitarian aid and contributing to the political, economic and social reconstruction of that region. the new provisions on civil protection, which entrust the union with the task of promoting consistency in international civil protection work, will allow us to make our international action even more effective in the future. we have, of course, already put in place a number of initiatives aimed at informing the public about the content of the constitution. the commission has produced written and audio-visual material, developed a website, promoted and financed information relays, and sponsored seminars and other public initiatives. the european council has supported our efforts, calling on the member states to the possibility of putting in place joint communication initiatives with us that can maximise the impact of our initiatives. i refer, in particular, to the possibility of organising media events at both european and national level during a 'european week', around 9 may 2005. in the meantime the commission will not refrain from developing other ideas that can assist the member states in drawing up and implementing their national communication strategies. i can also assure you that the commissioners themselves will be active in the debate on the constitution and the future of europe. securing the ratification of the constitutional treaty is the main concern for the member states and for the european institutions. however, while we do not intend to anticipate application of the constitution, we must also devote some effort to ensuring a smooth entry into force of the constitution once the ratification procedures have been successfully finalised. that is why we need to open discussions on preparing for implementation of the current provisions. the commission has been engaged in this process from the start. we are proud of the text of the constitution and will do our utmost to ensure that it sees the light of day. i remain committed to dialogue with the european parliament. our work will not stop today. in fact it is only just starting. i look forward to debating at least when it comes to decisions - and because the clearer allocation makes the procedures more understandable. the insufficient but substantial expansion of majority voting has strengthened the efficiency of the european union, as reflected in other areas, such as the abolition of the pillar structure and the introduction of a single legal personality, and in particular in the substantial progress made in the field of foreign, security and defence policy. we have a europe based on values. the charter of fundamental rights, which i understand is very much based on the christian view of man, is - question no 35 by mr staes (h-0510/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: does development cooperation depend on chance? by the campaign are you leaving the decision to chance? europe not! the commission is telling europeans that europe is putting a lot of money into development cooperation. the declaration by commissioner ferrero-waldner on this campaign shows that the world is to be a better place, obviously first and foremost for europeans, and that development cooperation is to lead first and foremost to stability in 'near neighbours'. the fight against poverty is subordinated to this objective. can the commission state whether this approach, which seems to be aimed primarily at improving the security of europe rather than providing sustainable solutions for the development of the third world, is consistent with the development agenda of the developing countries and with article 177 of the treaty, and with the objectives of the united nations millennium project?
commission. thank you for acknowledging that this campaign is going to the right development goals. it underlines the key sectors of the external assistance policy, as defined in the development policy communication and in the development goals. there are seven elements to the seven priorities of the european commission intervention. one is prosperity, achieved by trade and the private sector. second, security, which is being achieved via justice and regional cooperation. third is freedom, achieved by human rights and good governance. fourth is food: food security and rural development. fifth, water: the water initiative protecting sustainable development. sixth, education: education systems and access to schools. lastly, the europeaid message – 'partnerships improving lives worldwide' – evokes the how and why of external assistance. with regard to scope, the campaign is reaching out to over 150 countries worldwide. it is establishing long-term partnerships, and its approach is to focus on ownership of projects in partner countries. priority areas results are also to be focused upon: there must be a demonstrable impact on people's lives. this campaign has really gone to the heart of what we want to do and comes under the umbrella of the overall goals.

vice-president of the commission. the issue of illegal immigration is one of the commission's priorities. as you have said, while we are preparing common european policies and solutions, we must also be concerned about the daily drama of people in desperation. the commission can and must act, and will act, to ensure that the fundamental rights of people entering european territory are respected, including, of course, those who enter illegally: the right to respect for human life and dignity is not a matter of legal differences. that said, strategic policies must be accelerated. we cannot take advantage of a delay to continue to allow an illegal influx, we must immediately respect the fundamental rights of people and at the same time prepare common policies for reception on the one hand and prevention against illegality on the other.
question no 44 by mr ignasi guardans cambó (h-0523/04) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: terrorismthe council framework decision of 13 june 2002 on the fight against terrorism invited member states to legislate in certain areas related to the fight against terrorism in order to establish common definitions in the light of the threats that exist. under article 11 of that framework decision, the commission and the council were to examine by the end of 2003 the specific measures taken by the member states to combat terrorism. these texts were finally submitted by the commission on 8 june 2004 (com (2004) 0409/final) and by the council on 12 october 2004 (11687/2/04/rev.2). both reports state very clearly and factually that the member states have failed to act and to implement the objectives set out in the council framework decision. the commission has no binding instruments to require member states to implement the framework decisions. however, in order to ensure the credibility of europe in the fight against terrorism, how does the commission intend to promote and achieve a genuine european counter-terrorism policy and thus ensure that member states fulfil their commitments in terms of legislative action?
vice-chairman of the commission . the commission will begin to explain to the informal council of ministers of the interior and justice at the end of this month the action plan for implementing the hague strategy. the action plan will be presented in may this year and i hope that it will be approved by the european council in june. the action plan against terrorism will contain concrete measures and indications, precise deadlines for the member states and binding obligations for a common policy of strengthening cooperation, exchanges of information and protection of victims of terrorist attacks. these are the measures which the commission intends to put before this parliament in advance, which we shall do at the beginning of february, so that before we formulate our proposal we shall be hearing parliament's views on the specific proposals.

commission. mr president, the commission has taken careful note of this discussion on the important issue of debt relief. a number of important and useful suggestions and comments were made today. i should like to respond as follows. first, it should urgently be emphasised that poverty is not just a question of debt relief. the real issue is appropriate levels of development financing. second, it is important to distinguish between different countries, in particular between the least developed countries and other developing countries. third, the per capita figures on debt relief were not presented to you with the aim of cutting back on aid, but rather the opposite: to use this criteria in order to alleviate the debt burden for those countries that really need it most. fourth, the un and the commission will coordinate their efforts with other international organisations on the hipc and other initiatives. fifth, a new world bank-imf sustainability framework recognises the inadequacy of existing debt relief efforts. the new framework will: first, set indicative debt burden thresholds that are country-specific; second, take account of external shocks; third, ensure greater transparency and dialogue in assessing that sustainability. that is what the new sustainability framework is all about. lastly, relief for iraq should not be at the expense of the poorest countries, and a debt moratorium for countries hit by the tsunami would be appropriate. the commission will closely follow the issue of the external debt of developing countries, in particular the least-developed ones. there also remains much to do as regards considering debt relief for the countries of southeast asia hit by the earthquake and tsunami. the commission will maintain a continuous dialogue with the european parliament in all the above fields of action. we all agree that for some developing countries external indebtedness is a major obstacle to growth and development. debt relief can indeed be a useful tool in that quest, but by no means can it offer a full response. aid, socio-economic policies, trade policies, etc. that ensure the sustainability of these countries in the long run are crucial. that is what they would want and what they deserve.

commission. mr president, on 9 june 2004 the previous commission took the decision to terminate the contracts of 43 language teachers. this decision has been perceived by certain parties as 'untransparent' and 'unjustified'. in this respect the questions put by the chairman of the committee on employment and social affairs reflect the concerns expressed by the teachers themselves. before i reply in detail to the questions put by the honourable member, i would like to make four introductory points. first, the decision was taken in order to conform to the principle of sound financial management. since 1997, commission language courses have been delivered either by internal teachers with direct contracts with the commission or by language schools selected via an open tender procedure. each formula accounts for approximately 50% of the courses. quality-wise, surveys have shown there to be no difference between the courses given by internal trainers and those given by language schools. on the other hand, there is a significant difference in budgetary terms: one hour's training delivered by an internal trainer costs four times as much as an hour delivered by a language school. on a yearly basis, taking 2003 as the reference year, the costs are approximately eur 3.5 million as opposed to eur 900 000. second, the language teachers have been granted generous compensation. the commission offered compensation payments that went well beyond the minimum legal requirement. minimum compensation would have been three months' salary per five years of service. that would have resulted in compensation equivalent to between 12 and 19 months' salary. the commission opted, however, to calculate the compensation on the basis of the maximum amount ever granted by belgian courts. this resulted in compensation of between 14 and 24 months' salary. this means gross amounts of between approximately eur 19 000 and eur 152 000. furthermore, the commission opted to pay this compensation without requiring the teachers to serve out their period of notice. third, the decision to terminate the contracts in question is not a unilateral initiative by the commission, but rather the outcome of moves initiated by the budgetary authority in the mid-1990s. in order to understand the decision of 9 june 2004 one must go back to the origins of this matter. the whole process started in the early 1990s, when parliament externalised its language training in luxembourg. at this time, the language courses at the commission and the council were delivered by internal trainers who were granted private law contracts, without any call for tender or selection procedure. in the mid 1990s, the committee on budgets criticised both the commission and the council for the costs associated with this practice. after lengthy discussions, the trialogue – the chairman of the committee on budgets, the secretary-general of the council and the commissioner in charge of personnel – concluded that gradual full externalisation was desirable. as a first step the parties agreed to launch a call for tenders for the supply of language courses, and also, by way of derogation from this principle, to allow existing internal teachers to continue their activities within their existing contract framework. fourth, the trialogue agreement did not constitute a commitment on teachers benefiting from lifelong employment. in detail, the trialogue agreed to allow the language teachers to continue working under contracts of indefinite duration without having to participate in the call for tender. this point was made explicit to the unions at the time, as the minutes of meetings show. at the same time, the possibility of terminating a contract of indefinite duration is governed by belgian law and cannot be waived. any agreement between parties not to apply the law is null and void. after that basic introduction, i will now turn to the specific questions asked. the first is: did the commission inform and consult the council and parliament before unilaterally breaching the trialogue agreement? there are three elements that need to be considered here. firstly, the commission did not breach the trialogue agreement because this agreement did not constitute a commitment on teachers benefiting from lifelong employment. secondly, the commission accepts that it could have informed the trialogue co-signatories – the committee on budgets and the council – of its intention to proceed with the second phase of externalisation. nevertheless, the commission considers that its decision was broadly in line with the stated orientations of the trialogue and the budgetary authority. the second question is: when did the commission inform the teachers' representatives, the union representatives and the local personnel committee? the commission informed the teachers' representatives, together with the teachers concerned, at the general assembly held on 18 june 2004, before the decision was notified. under the social dialogue agreement, staff representatives and the local personnel committee represent persons employed under the staff regulations. since language teachers do not fall into this category, no staff representatives were involved in the case in point. the third question is: what kind of information was communicated to the teachers' representatives? the commission informed the teachers and their representatives of the decision taken on 9 june 2004, giving the reasons for this and explaining the practical consequences and arrangements, which included the commission's plans for compensation payments. the fourth question is: does the commission consider that its handling of this matter stands as a good example of best practice in terms of prior consultation and the provision of information in good time? looked at from a legal point of view, then i would reply in the affirmative: the commission complied in full with all the relevant obligations, even if, as already stated, the commission could have informed the co-signatories of the trialogue agreement before adopting the decision. the fifth question is: does the commission feel it has fully faced up to its social responsibility to the teachers concerned? the commission has not only fulfilled all its legal obligations but has also interpreted its obligations in the most favourable way for the persons concerned. the sixth and last question is: can the commission comment on and provide copies of any opinions given by the commission's legal service on the dismissal of the teachers requested by dg admin? the opinions given by the commission's legal service are governed by the rules applicable to relations between lawyers and their clients. therefore, the commission will not release the opinions or comments of its legal service. in conclusion, the commission's position can be summarised as follows. firstly, as regards the substance of the matter, the commission considers that the decision to terminate the contracts concerned was sound. it was no longer tenable to continue a dual system where half of the courses were provided by internal teachers at a cost approximately four times greater than the courses provided by language schools, with no difference in quality. secondly, the commission implemented this decision in full compliance with its legal obligations. thirdly, the commission accepts that it could have informed the co-signatories of the trialogue agreement before adopting the decision. however, the commission considers that its decision was broadly in line with the orientations of the trialogue and the budgetary authority. finally, the commission has no intention of reducing the number of courses. it reaffirms its commitment to multilingualism and to continuing to provide its staff with opportunities for a high standard of language learning without compromising on quality. obtaining better value for money without any loss of quality is obviously a means of attaining this goal.

the next item is the report by mrs sophia in 't veld on aid to compensate for public services.
i am speaking on behalf of the group of the european people's party. the commission has already made a number of proposals. first of all, i would like to thank the rapporteur for her excellent work. it has dealt with a very difficult subject with great expertise and enthusiasm and has produced a very transparent report. we liberals and democrats take it for granted that the public sector must ensure the provision of certain services. but taxpayers' money must be used very carefully and only where it brings real added value to the consumer. clear regulation is therefore necessary. in principle, we welcome the commission's attempt to set up a framework which gives transparency, objectivity and traceability to the use of funds. we want a solution which ensures that competition is effective and that the regulation of public services is not abused to distort competition. the completion of the internal market must not be hampered by the unrestrained distribution of aid, and even more so by the principle of the pot. on the contrary, we want to advocate a solution which will make it possible to achieve the following objectives: the definition of social security should be made in the member states; even if it's not the same, it has to be comparable. we do not see any breach of the principle of subsidiarity. state aid must be targeted and focused where it helps to secure the future. their use in the future should be more restrictive than it is now. the scheme must not impede the further completion of the internal market. we condemn attempts, such as that of the federal minister for economic affairs in germany, to prevent the possible opening up of areas of public service provision by derogating from the services directive. finally, i would appeal to the commission to facilitate the application of the rules by further clarification. the commission should develop benchmarks and best practice examples as reference points. the best practice approach can provide input to other member states on the basis of successful examples.
the commission has already done so. one of the main problems in the application of european state aid law to the provision of services of general interest is legal certainty, or legal uncertainty. it is not always clear to decision-makers in local administrations, cities, municipalities and counties whether compensation for the special costs associated with these services is covered by the aid rules. so, do these benefits have to be notified to the commission or approved by it? failure to do so, even though it would have been necessary, has serious legal consequences. however, if, in the face of doubt, such a notification procedure is carried out, even though it would have been unnecessary, valuable time is lost during the procedure. this legal uncertainty should now be addressed. i welcome and support this. the basis is the judgment of the european court of justice in the altmark trans case, as mentioned above. on this basis, the commission's proposal for an exemption decision is in line with our request in the resolution on the green paper on services of general interest of 14 january 2004. this proposal is an expression of support for a control policy focused on the cases which are essential for the functioning of competition in the internal market. compensation payments which have only a negligible effect on the internal market are exempted from aid control procedures. this is a crucial gain in legal certainty for the local actors. compensation for services of general economic interest which have only a minor impact on the internal market is very often provided in a very limited, local environment. they are therefore a typical application case for the exemption decision in question. provided that the other criteria, such as a clear description of the tasks and compliance with the principle of transparency, are respected, they must also benefit from the increased legal certainty sought. the rapporteur has produced an excellent report. it has had it streamlined by vote in the committee on economic and monetary affairs. i hope that we in the house will understand this as well.
member of the commission. mr president, i wish to apologise to mrs in 't veld for failing to mention at the outset that i was impressed by her report. i know it was a difficult job, but the result has responsibilities of national, regional or local authorities to define, organise, finance and monitor public services. i very much agree with the idea that we should occasionally review what we are doing. when we consider the altmark court case, it is not that difficult to make a clear decision on three of the four criteria. therefore, i do not agree with the member who said that it is difficult the commission's vice-president mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to be able to present to you today the proposal for a directive on river information services. this directive, which was also requested by parliament in its resolution on the white paper on european transport policy, aims to harmonize information services on community waterways. the commission has long recognised that inland waterway transport has great potential as a substitute for congestion problems in other transport sectors. in other words, water transport is often cheaper, more reliable and more environmentally friendly than other modes of transport. river information services offer an extraordinary opportunity for inland navigation. they are based on modern information and communication technologies and allow better planning and management of traffic and transport. they include services such as information on waterways, navigability conditions, traffic situation, capacity in ports and terminals. they also include disaster mitigation services. by making it possible to plan journeys more precisely, to adapt more easily to traffic conditions and to navigability conditions, river information services lead to a reduction in fuel consumption and thus have an impact on the reduction of emissions. in addition, river information services offer the possibility of controlling the transport of dangerous goods and thus responding adequately in the event of accidents and possible ecological damage. the deployment of information services will contribute to the modernisation of the river network; it will increase safety, reliability and efficiency. the directive has a twofold objective. on the one hand, it wants to give the administrations that provide the services, the users who use them and the industry that produces hardware and software the security necessary to invest in this area. the directive also aims to make applications interoperable and compatible at national and european level, with the obvious possibility of ensuring continuity with services of other modes of transport. the directive does not oblige the private user to use river information services, but we are confident that the strengths of these services will lead users to exploit them and that industry will understand the commercial opportunity presented by river information services technology. she'll offer it at a reasonable and affordable price. this is all the more important as the companies in the inland waterway transport sector are small and medium-sized enterprises. the commission will be following this development closely. the council reached a general approach. i am glad that the rapporteur and the committee on transport and tourism responsible for this matter have sought agreement at first reading. it is a constructive approach between the two institutions which should enable us to adopt the directive quickly and start the implementation of river information services. i would like to thank mrs sommer and the committee on transport and tourism very warmly for supporting this approach. three points are worth highlighting: the interoperability of services, the implementation deadlines and the matching table. parliament has done well in emphasizing what is at the very heart of the directive: the interoperability of services and the compatibility of ministerial meeting in the hague on 29 and 30 november 2004, which confirmed the centrality of the barcelona process, reinforced by the european neighbourhood policy for the mediterranean. it is a process in which the european union and the mediterranean partners jointly participate in the achievement of political, economic and social reform objectives involving the societies concerned. these same objectives are also reflected in the european union's strategic partnership with the mediterranean region and the middle east. more than ever, the euro-mediterranean partnership constitutes an essential and privileged regional framework for dialogue and cooperation between the two shores of the mediterranean. the hague meeting was the second ministerial meeting after naples and before the mediterranean partners, the ministerial meeting in the hague confirmed progress in cooperation on the fight against terrorism, regional security and non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, network of foreign policy institutes, are making a substantial contribution to bringing the euro-mediterranean partners closer together. these efforts shall also aim at the implementation of political reforms and cooperation on human rights and democratisation, and shall be supported by civil society through commitments made either in the framework of association agreements or, where appropriate, in the framework of the european neighbourhood policy. in this regard, the action plans concluded with a number of partners give a central role to human rights, democratisation, good governance and strengthening the rule of law. similarly, the establishment of the anna lindh euro-mediterranean foundation for intercultural dialogue is a decisive step in the implementation of the social, cultural question no 9 by mr jonas sjöstedt (h-0017/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: storage of traffic data a framework decision on the retention of traffic data is currently being worked on at eu level. this question has been raised before, and each time the so-called article 29 group (eu data protection leaders tasked with ensuring that data protection rules are applied to personal data) has responded with very critical statements. the draft proposal proposes to introduce a common eu regime allowing data from publicly available communication networks to be retained for 12 to 36 months for the purposes of 'prevention, investigation, detection and prosecution of criminal offences, including terrorism'. the proposal goes far beyond telephone services and includes extensive traffic data, i.e. information on who visits which websites and who has sent an e-mail to whom. moreover, it is not only a matter of retention for law enforcement purposes but also a preventive measure, which means that all citizens are considered as potential suspects. the article 29 group has, of course, strongly criticised this proposal. in its opinion, the group considers that this draft law not only violates the provision that traffic data may be used only for the purpose for which it has been stored, but also violates article 8 of the convention on human rights, which states that 'everyone has the right to respect for his private and family life, his home and his correspondence'. does the council intend to take appropriate action on the basis of the criticism of the article 29 group?

capacities, which involves infrastructure, smes, regions and research potential. here, we would like to address the question of new member states, but not in a way that would undermine the excellence of the programme. researchers in those countries should be supported so that they develop and become more visible. we should establish actions which allow us to access the structural and cohesion funds. the worst thing for the new member states and their researchers would be to create conditions under which they would not be able to compete. it is best for them to develop rapidly so that they are competitive from the very beginning. they are doing that already. i am very much aware that conditions in some countries mean that they cannot compete. we have to help them, but the question is how we do this. our programme seeks to achieve excellence and competitiveness in the eu, which is crucial. we have structural and cohesion funds for solidarity. if we are using these funds for road, the average life of ships destined for export to the countries affected by the tsunami will be between 5 and 20 years. so, it's not about the very old boats. as regards the question of the experts, i would like to say that they have already been and will be sent on the spot. in addition, it is at our request that the fao should carry out an assessment of needs and this will be on the agenda of the ministerial meeting on 12 march, where mr borg will represent the commission. we are all in favour of good cooperation with the fao; the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. in principle, liberalization is good. but with gas, it will be almost ineffective. why would you do that? for two main reasons: first, let's look at the producer level. we have only russia, norway and algeria. this oligopoly determines what happens in the gas market in europe, and this market power allows, for example, that the price of gas in europe is 90% tied to oil. there's no economic reason for that. this is pure market power or, to put it bluntly, it is pure rip-off. there is no sign of competition among the producers. what is the point of downstream regulation if upstream there is only an oligopoly of the big three? it's like the weekly market. if there are more strawberries, the price will drop! for example, the russians would have to bring more gas to the world market and compete with the norwegians to bring down prices. they won't do it willingly. we need a council and a commission! the second obstacle is the large national and international distributors. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not undermined by the current crisis. who, for example, supplies gas to a medium-sized utility in germany? russia would laugh if a german utility wanted to buy directly from gasporm and have a direct pipeline. in this context, it is worrying that the largest electricity suppliers in europe are now also the largest gas suppliers. if we want competition and liberalisation, then the industry must not be vertical and have everything in one hand, from extraction to the last distributor. we must effectively prevent the big four in germany, for example, from setting up a wider vertical and buying up all the smaller and medium-sized distributors. the same is true in italy with enel and eni, and in france with gdf and edf. in an industry determined by grid lines, there must be distributors independent of the big producers. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. if we do not address these challenges, then our efforts today, however good, will be largely ineffective.

member of the commission. the enlarged eu depends on imported energy for 50% of its needs and is increasingly dependent on external energy sources. by 2030, this dependency could grow to almost 70%, with 90% of oil and 80% of gas consumed coming from outside the eu. imports of gas from russia currently make up 26% of total gas consumption in the eu and the relevant figure for oil is 25%. in this respect it is important to know that russia has always been a completely reliable energy supplier to the eu. the eu-russia energy dialogue has established a good relationship in the energy field, and the commission believes that russia will be the most important and reliable energy supplier to the eu for the foreseeable future. notwithstanding this, however, the community needs to ensure diversity of supply and make maximum use of its own indigenous energy resources. such a policy makes sense in terms of security of supply, sustainable development and the pursuit of our lisbon objectives. for these reasons the new commission will be pursuing the following energy priorities: first, energy efficiency. a simple comparison of the way in which the different eu member states have addressed energy efficiency will show the possibilities for energy savings, which will contribute significantly to meeting the eu’s kyoto targets. it will also enhance our competitiveness. this spring i will present a green paper on energy efficiency, outlining the concrete measures to be taken at community, national, regional and local level that will lead to those savings. second, supporting renewables: towards the end of this year the commission will publish a communication on renewables, in particular assessing the efficiency and effectiveness of existing support mechanisms in the member states. i will closely monitor the situation so that there is a clear move towards achieving by 2010 the target of 12% of the union’s overall energy consumption coming from renewable sources. third, supporting clean coal: approximately one-third of eu electricity is produced from coal. if we wish to retain this, a major effort needs to be made to increase the efficiency of coal generation and to succeed in developing co2 capture and storage. europe should take a leading role in research in this area, and the commission will be examining the possibility of a joint european project. finally, i should like to mention establishing and improving energy dialogues with a wide range of energy producers, consumers and transit countries. enhanced dialogue between the eu and opec was recently agreed upon at the regular ministerial-level meeting. a dialogue with the caspian countries will be pursued and the existing annual high-level meeting with norway will be continued. in addition to this, and to ensure that these policies fully meet this challenge, it is clear that a wide public debate should take place on increasing eu external energy dependency. for this reason the commission intends to adopt by the end of this year a new green paper on security of the eu energy supply, with the aim of promoting a large public debate. the input of the european parliament during the preparation and follow-up of this green paper will be vital.

president of the council. mr president, five years after its adoption, the european council will be called upon to discuss the relaunch of the lisbon strategy again, at the time of the mid-term review of the strategy. as the commission has proposed, we must give this strategy a new start by focusing our action on achieving stronger and more sustainable growth and creating more and better jobs. the european council will thus be able to confirm the relevance of the strategy by clarifying its challenges and its purpose. the objective of growth and jobs must be pursued through synergies to be developed between the three dimensions of the strategy: the economic, the social and the environmental. in this context, the european council will also set priorities for union action in the social field. the review of the social agenda should complement and support the mid-term review of the lisbon strategy, in particular as regards the promotion of the social dimension of economic growth. on the environment, the european council should underline the contribution of environmental policy to growth and employment and confirm the need to integrate environmental considerations into the lisbon process. the european council will also be discussing the commission's communication on the sustainable development strategy, but i will come back to it later, because it is a separate item on the council's agenda. the european council will also consider how to improve the governance of the strategy, at both union and member state level. the issue of governance is really at the heart of the mid-term review. it will be decisive for the success of the strategy. for the presidency, this complex issue can be reduced to a few essential points. firstly, the adoption of a set of integrated guidelines, which will allow the synchronisation and rationalisation of the various processes that currently exist. the multiplicity of processes and reports contributes significantly to the lack of legibility of the strategy in public opinion and to its effective implementation. in the light of the guidelines given by the european council, the commission should now present proposals for guidelines comprising the broad economic policy guidelines and the employment guidelines, integrating them into a single and coherent text. these integrated guidelines would then be endorsed by the european council and, where the treaty so requires, formally adopted by the council. it goes without saying that parliament's views will be taken fully into account in this process. secondly, the introduction of national action programmes over three years. the aim is to give each member state greater latitude in choosing the priorities and means of action for implementing the strategy, within the framework defined by the integrated guidelines i have just mentioned. on the basis of these integrated guidelines, it is proposed that member states draw up national action programmes after as wide a consultation as possible between all the actors concerned. in order to facilitate consultation and coordination and the implementation of what has been decided, each member state could appoint a person responsible for the implementation of the lisbon strategy. thirdly, a follow-up procedure based on regular evaluation of implementation at intermediate meetings. the idea is that each autumn from 2006 onwards, member states will present a single report on the implementation of their national action programme. on this basis, the commission will present an evaluation report each year in january, possibly accompanied by some proposals for adjustment, without this however being able to lead to a total revision of the integrated guidelines, which will be valid for three years. the european council will then decide on these adjustments. the various council configurations concerned are continuing their work on all these issues relating to the revision of the lisbon strategy and the general affairs council will return to them just before the european council on 16 march. these are the major projects which are currently being discussed and prepared for the european council on 22 march.
president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, a month ago at the conference of presidents i presented our ideas for a partnership for sustainable growth and employment, thus giving a new impetus to the lisbon strategy. our objective for this partnership is simple: we must modernise and revitalise our economy, our social model and improve our quality of life through truly ambitious reforms. we must recognise that appropriate environmental policies can produce results with a double benefit in terms of jobs and ensuring sustainable growth, and in a context of economic stability we must improve the capacity of our companies, from the largest to the smallest and medium-sized, to create new and better jobs. we also need to boost productivity through more investment in knowledge, innovation and people. today is the first opportunity for one of the partners with whom we want to work - one of the most important partners, the european parliament - to state its views and set its priorities. i, like other members of the commission, welcome this debate. we want to thank the political investment that has been made in bringing forward a comprehensive motion for a resolution that reflects a wide range of views within this house. we share many of your priorities, we are sensitive to your concerns. later today we will debate the forthcoming european council. that summit will be the start, and not the end, of the journey as far as the renewed lisbon strategy is concerned. i fully support the remarks made by the distinguished representative of the luxembourg presidency. we will only succeed if everyone feels that they have a stake in europe's success. that success depends on presenting a vision that mobilises popular support, gives a real sense of ownership and, above all, leads to real action at national, regional and local level. however, to mobilise support it must be clear why these reforms matter and that they are part of our wider vision. they are about people and the issues that matter most to them: the chance to work, a decent start for their children, security in retirement or ill-health, and quality public services. they are about a better quality of life and a better standard of living in every part of an enlarged union, from our city centres to the heart of our rural and coastal communities. they are about binding the union together through 21st-century infrastructure and regional investment. they are about making the most of european excellence in our business community addressing, in particular, the concerns of small and medium-sized enterprises and in all areas of creativity, but also in science and technology and in our unique model for society. they are also about achieving all this in a way that guarantees future generations the same or better possibilities than we ourselves enjoy. this goal of sustainable development underpins the lisbon strategy as it does the action of the union in every area. these are broad economic, social and environmental objectives. they were at the heart of the lisbon strategy when it was launched and remain at its heart today. i can promise you that this commission will fight to ensure that they do so tomorrow, not least as we discuss the future financial perspectives over the coming months. then and there we will test the real commitment to cohesion and solidarity of those who are today at least in their political discourse on the frontline of defence of the european social model. nevertheless, we need to face facts. the first five years of the lisbon strategy have not delivered the desired results. there has been insufficient delivery, little ownership at national level and even less among society at large. in key areas, from productivity to research and education spending, early school-leavers or poverty, we have barely made an impression on closing the gaps that existed five years ago. we can add to this the challenge of intense global competition and an aging population. these are no longer challenges for the future, but the day-to-day reality for our businesses and workers. this is why lisbon needs a new start, with fresh ambition. this is why we propose a new focus on growth and jobs in order to meet those challenges. a dynamic and innovative europe offers us the best chance to do this. vice-president verheugen will set out in more detail how this new focus translates into concrete action and results. this does not mean downgrading action in other areas. our new social agenda, our review of sustainable development and our action on climate change show the commission's commitment to moving ahead across a wide range of areas. let me turn to two specific concerns that your resolution addresses. the first is the balance within the lisbon strategy. i know a variety of concerns have been raised about the new focus on actions to promote growth and jobs. this is not at all in contradiction with our social and environmental policy. growth is a necessary precondition for an effective and more ambitious programme in terms of solidarity, just as fighting unemployment is the best protection against exclusion and poverty. without growth, without a dynamic economy, there will be no sustainable development; we will not foster convergence between regions and our social and environmental goals will slip out of reach. however, i fully accept that lasting growth relies, in turn, on parallel progress on cohesion, our social agenda and addressing unsustainable and damaging environmental trends. with regard to the services directive, we need an open and thriving internal market for services in the union, as well as high-quality, accessible public services. they are key factors for a successful society. yet we have identified a number of areas where changes will be required for the broad consensus that we would like to see emerge. we have said that we are ready to work pragmatically with you, the parliament, and with the presidency, in preparation for your first reading. in particular we need to ensure a framework that removes the risk of social dumping, has a broad coverage but does not necessarily cover healthcare or services of general interest and addresses genuine concerns about the operation of the country of origin principle. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to conclude with a few words on the governance of the lisbon strategy. i do not think it is necessary for us to completely rewrite the lisbon strategy in the coming weeks. that being so, a number of innovations have been suggested by the commission, as well as - it must be remembered - by the parliament. we have proposed the creation of a european institute of technology; greater priority to be given to improving regulation, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises; a greater propensity to re-examine existing proposals; the use of state aid and tax rules in a way that encourages entrepreneurship, innovation and research; the refocusing of labour market reforms on measures to help women, young people and older workers to find and keep a job; the european union is also committed to the development of the european union's youth policy and the conclusion of a european youth pact. in reality, i think it can be said that people have a fairly clear idea of what ought to be done. the political challenge this time is to find out how we can help them to really do it at community level. it is a question of appropriation. it is above all because the member states - and society in general - have not really done their job that the structural reforms of the last five years have produced disappointing results. in reply, we have made the following proposals - which you seem to approve, if i may say so - of your draft resolution. first, the formulation of integrated guidelines at the level of the european union, including the current economic policy guidelines and the employment guidelines, in order to give the member states a clearer idea of what they are committed to doing. for the first time, micro-economic reforms will be dealt with in detail. it will therefore be an integrated vision, encompassing macroeconomic policies, microeconomic reforms and employment policy. thus, lisbon will not only play a decorative role, but will really be at the heart of our economic policy. secondly, the development of national lisbon programmes adapted to national situations. the initiative is of course for the member states, but we have already prepared a european union programme on the lisbon strategy which presents the community-level initiatives and therefore specifies what must be done at community and national level. thirdly, a simplification of information obligations, both at community and national level, so that member states spend more time on implementing reforms and less time writing reports on them which most people are not familiar with. the reports should therefore be given less importance than the integration of a vision on the reforms in progress. our ambition is to develop active support for these reforms and to integrate them into the heart of national political debates. the spring european council will not be the end of the road, but will give political impetus to the new approach. but to be perfectly coherent, the political guidelines defined in march will have to guide the financial decisions to be taken in june. the union must not be content with being ambitious. if it wants to succeed, it must also mobilise the means to match its ambitions. in this respect, a voluntary agreement on the financial perspectives, giving its rightful place to cohesion, would be a decisive element for strengthening and developing our social model in the coming years. at the same time, the european council will also open the way to national and regional debates on the action programmes which the member states are invited to present this autumn. i personally attend a lot of these debates. the lisbon strategy must be inspired by the partnerships and dialogues that cohesion policy has put in place in recent years between the different national, local and social actors. without this, it will not be possible to mobilise the partners concerned by its implementation. let me say to you, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, that following my talks with the economic and social committee and the committee of the regions, i find the very good reception given by these institutions in general to our review of the lisbon strategy very encouraging. i am particularly pleased to see the joint declaration which has been presented in recent days by the two major trade union and employers' organizations at european level. it is therefore possible to reach a balanced consensus for ambitious reforms. it goes without saying that in this partnership, the members of the european parliament play a major role if we really want to put these reforms into effect. that is why i ask you to make your contribution each year to the work of the european council in spring by setting, in accordance with the treaty, the guidelines which guide the process and, of course, to take the lead in political discussions by mobilising support at national, regional and local levels. that is our concept of partnership which the commission wishes to establish with you. we believe that on this basis, with this commitment, it will be possible to do much more for our europe. to put it mildly - has been languishing for some time. we need a clear political direction. it must be clear that better regulation is something that has a direct and immediate impact on the productivity and quality of the european economy. this is again something we can only do together. parliament must play a major role in this, as must the council, the member states and the commission. it is not just about future legislation and how we ensure that it improves competitiveness; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. secondly, there is a huge, almost untapped potential for economic power in europe, which is before our eyes and which is also talked about a lot, but little is done. i am referring to the 25 million small and mediumsized enterprises in europe, which provide two thirds of our total workforce. we should not be content to say to these 25 million people: you are the backbone of the european economy, and then do nothing. we need a policy that exploits the enormous potential for innovation, investment and creativity that exists in this area and translates it into jobs. i shall be proposing to you very soon a comprehensive modernisation and upgrading - i emphasise the word upgrading - of european policy for small and mediumsized enterprises. the third is industrial policy. the word itself is already causing anxiety in some member states. we need a modern definition of industrial policy for the 21st century. this can no longer be the policy of the past, where protective fences were erected around certain industries. again, the only thing that can be done is to maintain and increase competitiveness. but it is necessary to realize that we need a strong industrial base in europe on a lasting basis. this will require looking at european industry sector by sector and talking to all those involved - businesses, trade unions, parliaments and governments - about what framework is best for each sector to exploit its growth potential. the last point i would like to make is the issue of innovation. the commission will also be making new and far-reaching proposals in this area. innovation is the link in the chain between research, development and production where europe is not strong enough. we need to improve our ability to translate research into innovation, and we need to do that everywhere. here, the americans and others are much better. this commission is firmly convinced that europe is strong enough to face the challenges of global competition. we have at least one european company or european country that is world-leading in almost every sector of the economy. in other words, we can. we can learn from each other. we can support each other in realising the potential that exists in our societies. but we will also have to give the european institutions the capacity to implement such a policy. i cannot therefore conclude without pointing out that growth and employment policy, as an effective instrument for achieving our long-term political objectives, must be reflected in a set of figures, in the next financial perspective. i think there is only one thing to be said here: it would be a serious blow to the success of our growth and employment policy if the uncertainty about the next financial perspective were to continue for a long time. i urge the member states to be aware that large projects also need their preparation time. we're running out of time. it is also a question of credibility to the citizens of europe that we are prepared to demonstrate that our words will indeed be followed by action. and actions i can't change cost money. without a budget that is efficient and without a clear financial perspective, it will be difficult, if not impossible, to achieve our objectives. mr president, mr president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i would also like to thank my colleagues, especially mr lehne and mr goebbels. it was a very constructive cooperation, for which i thank you very much. five years after the start of the lisbon strategy, we are at a crossroads. i would like to take this opportunity to make a fundamental point about the situation in europe. as in the 1930s, europe is suffering from the ulcer of structural mass unemployment. in my home country of germany, unemployment is higher than at any time in the history of the federal republic. in north rhine-westphalia alone - my home and that of commissioner verheugen - it has now exceeded the one million mark. at the same time, we are witnessing a growing debt in many member states and the exodus of science and research, while the intellectual, moral and political consequences of mass unemployment are spreading. declining voter turnout, dissatisfaction with politics in general, rising racism, anti-semitism, right-wing and left-wing extremism -- these are consequences of mass unemployment that we have to face. after five years of wanting everything and achieving nothing, europe must make a choice. we have the courage and the strength to finally take up the fight against mass unemployment. do we have the courage and the strength to achieve the reversal to more employment and growth? do we have the courage and the strength to focus not only on those who still have work but also to finally take into account those who want to work but cannot? my answer is clear: we must summon the courage and the strength, and it is equally clear that this requires our concerted efforts and an unconditional focus on greater competitiveness. let us finally see it for what it is: a prerequisite for more growth and employment. and growth and employment are the prerequisites for achieving the ambitious social and environmental objectives which we all support, as expressed in the resolution. the completion of the internal market as a development engine will play a key role in this. we must all no longer ignore the fact that the european single market has created more than two million jobs since 1993. in this context, can we afford to continue to have the european market for services on paper? the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the removal of barriers to crossborder services holds enormous growth potential. if we want to put europe on a growth path and combat mass unemployment, we must start here. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the first thing to be said is that the unholy alliance which met this week across the rhine in westphalia is now the first thing to be said. mr chirac and mr schröder are waging a campaign of fear, full of half-truths and untruths. it is therefore particularly good - and i want to make this very clear - that the commission has finally started to fight this polemic. i want to congratulate charlie mccreevy on his passionate speech yesterday. let us have the courage to fight against mass unemployment. i think that we should not have this debate in strasbourg, but in brussels. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr lehne, because you have specifically mentioned it, it is not that we in the green group have taken it easy in debating this text. you will remember that in our lisbon coordination structure we have introduced many amendments into the discussion process. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would remind you that when we started discussing this text in the steering committee, we agreed that there was no point in agreeing again on a general level, but that the lisbon process must also be concretized in this parliament. we shall continue to do so as the green group. we believe, for example, that it is absolutely necessary to reach an agreement on the freedom to provide services in the european union. my impression - mr president, mr president of the commission, mr president of the council, ladies and gentlemen! the difference between the majority of this house and my group in the mid-term evaluation of the lisbon strategy and the conclusions that follow from it is that they want to continue on the path of supply-oriented economic policy with increased competition, but we say that this is the wrong way! we are in agreement in this house on the objectives of the lisbon strategy, but we are completely different on the ways in which we can achieve them. the creation of jobs is the main objective and i can only achieve this if the demand for products increases and the economy is forced to make expansionary investments to meet the increased demand. the data should also be a reason for the most neoliberal economic thinking to accept that tax cuts do not create any new jobs when there is no demand, but on the contrary, they are either destroyed by rationalization or the increased yield is not reinvested or is fed into the state budget through taxes. the lisbon strategy must not mean competition for the highest incomes, but competition for highly qualified jobs, excellent education and training, quality of products, high environmental standards and high consumer protection. this also means that lower income groups, whose saving rates are not rising, despite what is often claimed, either need to get higher wages or have their taxes reduced - all the more so because there is more than enough policy space available, as productivity has developed much faster than wage growth in recent years. this is also reflected in the positive balance of trade of the majority of the member states of the european union. despite high social transfer performance, global marketable products were offered. low-wage jobs, part-time jobs do not help to eliminate the scourge of unemployment. if we want to become the world's strongest economic region by 2010, we must give priority to the social and ecological european union. this is the best economic support we can give.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. the enlargement of the european union is objectively ushering in a new era of entrepreneurship. that's how people in other parts of the world see us. the european union is a great example of the european union's ability to act in a new era, to be and remain internationally competitive, while maintaining and developing high social standards. are we able to make economic, technological leaps into the new age and at the same time produce the new generation of products with the highest and highest environmental standards? mr president, commissioner verheugen and the president of the commission have given us very bold prospects. commissioner verheugen spoke of values, values in business management, values in social standards, values of social participation in business and in social life, and described these as a vehicle to drive this process of modernisation. i emphasize this, but i think it does not reflect the reality of many people's lives. they have fears of insecurity, they have fears that these goals will not be achieved in their daily lives. if we are to build this bridge, then our instruments must be reformed and then this bridge must also be built, for example in the general outlines of economic policy. i do not want to read any more of the old ideologies, but more of the social reality of people. we must reform our own instruments to achieve what we are working together to achieve here.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. one of the most successful commission presidents was jacques delors, who had a vision of creating and completing the internal market. the vision for this commission could be the lisbon strategy. however, jacques delors had to deal with heads of government such as kohl and mitterrand, who also had a vision and a goal in europe. the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the european union is able to play its full part in the development of the union. that is one of the fundamental problems you have, mr president of the commission: to overcome this and to make lisbon a reality, so that in the end it is not said: i had a dream, but nothing productive came of it for us. this is the decisive point. the commission can do a lot to help. i see commissioner mccreevy here, who in his field can make a very important contribution to this. i hope that you will be able to prevail against the member states where it makes sense to move europe forward. it is necessary to point out to the member states what they have to do. this is about transparency and comparability. we are currently seeing that the stability and growth pact does not apply the law in force, so i doubt that progress reports are sufficient. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. in future, we must ensure that the economic, ecological and social objectives of the lisbon strategy are not in conflict with each other, but rather that they are all subordinated to the objective of the lisbon strategy. this makes it all the more important to focus on improving legislation in national implementation. there are member states - i come from one of them myself - which manage to tighten up the rules again and again. the most important thing will be to give the people of europe the confidence that the lisbon strategy can become a reality. our main problem is that some parts of europe no longer believe that we can stand up to the americans. if you can do that, we have achieved a great deal in europe. parliament is with you!

mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. as a german, you are in a particularly difficult position here when it comes to talking about the forthcoming council and the stability and growth pact, because you know how hard the germans have had to part with the d-mark! the only way to convey the idea of separating from the deutsche mark to the german public in germany was to give them a clear assurance that there was a stability and growth pact, which would build on the tradition of the deutsche mark and maintain the stability of a currency in the long term. it is therefore particularly difficult, of course, when it is precisely the large countries such as germany and france that do not respect this stability pact, which they have won from the small countries, including those in southern europe, when they violate its rules and even change it - if they themselves have problems. i can therefore only encourage the luxembourg presidency of the council to stick to its position at this summit, and all the other members of the european council to do the same. we could consider changing this pact. we have also heard important arguments here as to why it can be applied differently at certain stages. the worst thing is to change the pact at the very moment when you have broken the rules yourself and got away with it. the 16 points proposed by jean-claude juncker are therefore the right way to reform the pact. the commission must remain strong, it must remain in the game. it cannot be left to the member states to decide when and where the special arrangements for the stability pact are to be applied. that is our position on this question. the commission must be strengthened, some amendments can be discussed and this should be borne in mind by the european council when it decides on 22 and 23 march. the council has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is important that we now stand on the side of the democrats and human rights there too. i would therefore like this council to take a clear vote on terrorist activities, on hezbollah and everything related to it, unlike what we have heard from the council in this parliament so far.
