question no 1 by mr bernd posselt (h-0107/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: kosovohow does the presidency of the council assess the state of preparations for the clarification of the status of kosovo and what steps are to be expected under the luxembourg presidency?
president of the council. madam president, the council agrees with the honourable member that developments in kosovo, under the auspices of un security council resolution 1244, will be particularly important in 2005. the luxembourg presidency will fully support the efforts of the united nations and the action of the special representative of the un secretary-general, mr jensen petersen, to stabilise kosovo. the council was able to discuss the situation in that country in the presence of mr jensen petersen at its meeting on 21 february. mid-2005 will provide a first opportunity to make a comprehensive assessment of progress towards effective compliance with un standards. the positive outcome of this assessment will determine progress towards a process to determine the future status of kosovo, in accordance with security council resolution 1244. the european union has been closely involved in this process, in strict compliance with the role of the united nations in determining the future status of kosovo. the thessaloniki summit clearly stated that the western balkans, including kosovo, regardless of its future status, are destined to join the european union. this means that the union will have an important role to play in the review of kosovo's status, to ensure that it is fully compatible with the european integration process. the council stressed in its conclusions of 21 february that kosovo should not return to the situation before 1999. its future could only be conceived in the form of a multiethnic and democratic kosovo, which ensures effective protection of minorities, preserves the cultural and religious heritage of all communities and respects the right of return of refugees and displaced persons, thus contributing to the stability of the region and thus adhering to the values and principles of the european union. the council invited the secretary-general/high representative and the commission, in close cooperation with the presidency, to examine with the united nations and other relevant actors what the future contribution of the european union to the efforts of the international community in kosovo to implement resolution 1244 could be and how it could contribute to the overall assessment of the implementation of the standards and its contribution to the subsequent stages of the process and then to report to the council.
the council has already taken a decision on this. the un resolution 1244 does not say a word about the future status of kosovo. the resolution is already five years old. the european union is not prepared to accept the new position of the united states, which has been in the forefront of the negotiations on the status of the union. in kosovo, unemployment is at 70%, and investment will only be made if the future is at least clear in the long term. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
president of the council. firstly, on the protection of minorities, i believe that this is part of - i have made it clear - the european union's approach to a political solution in kosovo. there will be no political solution for kosovo without the protection of minorities, without the right of all refugees to return to their homes. i see. as regards the question of sovereignty, i believe that it is precisely at this level that a political solution must be found without anticipating the question of sovereignty. we are aware that the question is extremely complex and difficult; it must be the subject of negotiations which will have to be opened in due course. so i cannot give you a clear answer, but what guides us today is resolution 1544.

question no 8 by mr van hecke (h-0131/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: human rights violations in uganda efforts to resolve the 18-year conflict in uganda have failed and violence has flared up again. the conflict has led to immense human suffering, massive displacement of populations, the collapse of social and economic structures and serious human rights violations. the lord's resistance army rebels continue to use extreme violence against the civilian population in northern uganda, abducting children to use as soldiers or sex slaves. what action has the council taken or will it take in the light of the european parliament's resolutions on human rights violations in uganda to ensure the safety of the ugandan people, especially children, and to put an end to the atrocities?
president of the council. the council remains deeply concerned by the conflict in northern uganda. it repeatedly condemned the serious violations of human rights and the atrocities committed against the civilian population, in particular by the lord's resistance army. the conflict in northern uganda is one of the main points of the political dialogue between the european union and the ugandan government. in this context, the representatives of the member states and the commission have regularly raised their concerns about the continuing violations of human rights in the north of the country. they stressed the need to put an end to the suffering of the civilian population through a peaceful and negotiated solution to the conflict. representatives of the european union and other international partners reiterated this position to the ugandan government. the union as such has also declared its willingness to support the peace process and to contribute to the economic reconstruction of the north of the country. a significant part of the union's humanitarian assistance to uganda is intended to support the most vulnerable population groups in that part of the country. despite the resumption of fighting following the recent expiry of the ceasefire declared by the government, the council hopes that the talks with the resistance army will be able to continue. it is also prepared to consider how it can increase pressure on both sides in order to achieve a lasting settlement of the conflict in uganda.
president of the council. indeed, perhaps the wording which puts the government and this so-called resistance army on the same level is not quite appropriate. however, i believe that the only way to achieve a settlement of this conflict is to push the ugandan government and the ugandan army into a phase of dialogue. i believe that without dialogue, there is no peaceful settlement possible. as far as responsibilities are concerned, i believe that we really need to examine the extent to which these responsibilities can be fixed, determined, and we must not exclude any option, including the option of the international criminal court.

vice-president of thecommission. mr president, the commission shares the overall concern that member states are aiming to address with the envisaged framework decision on data retention, which is to guarantee the capability of law enforcement authorities to access certain data related to electronic communication to underpin their efforts to fight crime, including terrorism and organised crime. from a legal point of view, the initiative of france, ireland, sweden and the united kingdom on data retention currently under discussion was tabled under title 6 of the treaty on european union. however, the commission is of the opinion that the provisions of the draft instrument that deal with the harmonisation of obligations on electronic communication providers to retain data related to the provision of electronic communication services fall under the european community treaty, notably in view of the existing provisions of community law on the subject. as a consequence, the commission will present an alternative proposal on data retention based on article 95 of the european community treaty by early spring 2005. personally, i hope that the four member states in question will withdraw their proposal. the commission is fully aware of the possible cost implications of data retention obligations on the providers of electronic communication services. an impact assessment will be carried out to determine to what extent the creation of obligations to retain data will have economic implications. regarding a third pillar general data protection instrument, the commission intends to issue the first comprehensive proposal in the second half of 2005; in october or november. to that end, the commission has started consultations with experts representing the relevant ministries and data protection control authorities of the member states and the schengen states. as regards the transfer of passenger data to the united states joint review, a number of questions concerning the transfer of passenger data – the pnr issue – are related to the implementation of undertakings by the us customs and border protection agency. those undertakings provide for a joint review on their implementation to be conducted by the us authorities and the commission, the latter assisted by representatives of european law enforcement authorities and data protection supervisors. this joint review will take place in the first half of this year, i.e. during the first year of operation of the agreement and associated undertakings, which entered into force on 28 may 2004. the review aims to provide a clear picture of the way the undertakings function. it is my intention to inform this parliament of the outcome of this joint review and any important developments in this file. as i have already mentioned, national data protection authorities will be part of the commission-led team conducting the joint review. this should allow the article 29 working party to participate to assess fully the implementation of the undertaking. i am pleased to tell you that, in spite of differences of opinion on the us pnr package, there is excellent cooperation on the implementation of this package between the article 29 working party and the commission. as regards passenger information, as an example of that excellent cooperation between the article 29 working party and the commission, the working party has issued a passenger information notice, which airlines and travel agents use in order to inform airline passengers of the fact that personal data are transferred to the us customs and border protection agency for the purpose of preventing and combating terrorism and other serious crimes. as regards data transfers to third countries, according to information we received from the united states, no passenger data have been transferred so far to third countries. no doubt this issue will be looked into during the joint review exercise that will take place very soon. as regards ‘secure flight’ and capps ii, you will be aware that the us transportation security administration has dropped its controversial computer-assisted passenger pre-screening system – also known as capps ii – in favour of a new programme called ‘secure flight’. that programme will use passenger data for pre-screening passengers on us domestic flights against a terrorist watch list, with the aim of helping to identify potential terrorists. unlike capps ii, ‘secure flight’, for the time being, is limited to us domestic flights, which make it much less problematic than capps ii from a new data protection point of view. ‘secure flight’ is only in its testing phase. that is why, for the moment, no negotiations are planned. this is an issue to be watched very carefully. as regards the eu’s global plan for pnr policy, the commission issued a communication in december 2003 on the eu’s global approach on passenger data, advocating a comprehensive and balanced approach. the commission indicated in the communication that it will pursue its task with other third countries requesting passengers’ data. the commission has entered into talks with canada and australia. concerning canada, we will soon seek parliament’s opinion on a draft commission document and an accompanying international agreement. talks with australia are also well advanced. in both cases the article 29 working party has issued a positive opinion. as you can see, the commission’s strategy as outlined in the communication of december 2003 is being put into practice. finally, as regards the international civil aviation organization, that organisation established the passenger name record access study group in june 2004, following an initiative by several states within that organisation. they called for the development of a harmonised set of principles under the auspices of the icao. guidelines are currently being prepared. the european commission and several eu member states are participating actively in the work of the study group. i will keep you well informed about further developments in that programme.
the socialist group will be voting in favour of the report. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. i am grateful to you for having already announced an initiative by the commission. i am concerned about some other questions on the subject of data retention in telecommunications networks, which i hope will be answered in your proposal. the first is cost. for smaller telecommunications companies in particular, long-term storage represents a major financial burden. the proposal from the council and the four countries does not contain any compensation scheme. who's gonna pay for this? what is the total benefit in relation to the cost? the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the data are not stored for a long period of time. data protection experts, and even law enforcement agencies such as the federal criminal police office in germany, cast doubt on the necessity of the measure proposed in the council decision. the bundestag has even expressed its opposition to the minimum retention period for traffic data and calls on the federal government not to support the proposal. how can we achieve greater security if there are loopholes for terrorists and organised crime which the proposal does not even address? what about internet cafes, flatlines, public phone booths, calling from overseas phone providers? who's going to be able to track and store all this? data protection is another very, very important issue, the sharing of data with third parties. one thing is clear: we need more effective security. no one is against the fight against international terrorism or organised crime. but we don't need any more superfluous surveillance. i hope you will answer all these questions as well. one thing is also clear, and we stand by it: control is good, trust in control is better. but the proposal of these four countries will not achieve that in this form.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank all the members who have spoken. the first is that the commission intends to reconcile two great european values, namely the right of citizens to security and the right of citizens to the protection of their freedoms and fundamental rights. i do not think that these two fundamental rights are in conflict. we in the mentioned an initiative on data protection under the third pillar. the commission will of course rely on article 8 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. there are principles which i can briefly put to the house: the principle that the data processed must be used transparently and only for specific purposes, the principle that the consent of the data subject is required, the principle that the legal basis must be established in advance by law, and that it cannot be uncertain, and finally the principle that control by an independent authority is required. these are guidelines which will lead the commission to present a proposal under the third pillar, indicating a new generation of guarantees, before the end of this year. more guarantees are needed, taking account of the times and the evolution of technology. as regards the initiative of the four member states on the first pillar, i have stated our intention to make an alternative proposal, as i am convinced that the legal basis on which these states have proceeded is not correct. i have therefore also added that i will try to persuade them to withdraw their proposal. as regards the question of system.

member of the commission. mr president, i should like to begin by thanking mr daul, mr fruteau and the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development for all the work they have done. the drafting of the resolution and the hearing on 30 november last year make valuable contributions to our thorough preparations for this important reform of the common organisation of the markets in sugar. allow me to make a few introductory remarks before responding to your questions. the need for reform of the sugar sector is inevitable. based on the consultations i have had with stakeholders in recent months, it is my clear impression that this view is widely shared. the question is ‘how far’ and ‘how fast’ we should move. i sincerely believe that we need an ambitious reform. i should now like to make a few comments on the major issues you raised in your resolution. with regard to price and quota cuts, i am convinced that there is a future for sugar production within the european union, but that it must be based on competitiveness. we therefore need to accept that sugar production should be concentrated in the areas where it has a sustainable long-term perspective. the price cuts proposed in the communication will keep us well below current world market prices. i am therefore convinced that the proposed 33% price cut and the 2.8 million quota cut are a necessary minimum to achieve an effective reform, balance the market and respect our international obligations. the less thorough we are now, the more likely it is that we will have to reform again in the near future, with ensuing uncertainty for the sector. it is clear that the reform will force farmers and producers to take important, and sometimes difficult, decisions about their future in the sector. we have to offer them a clear outlook. i therefore consider predictability to be a key issue. i have taken good note that this is a concern shared by parliament. i therefore do not intend to include the idea of a mid-term review in two or three years in the legislative proposal. instead, a long-term perspective will be offered. farmers will receive compensation equal to 60% percent of the reduction in the institutional price, through the single farm payment scheme. this will offset the loss in revenue. past experience shows that income loss at farm level does not equal the price cut. that is especially true for sugar, where the farmers will no longer carry the cost of the production levy. in any case, the reform needs to be budget-neutral, which limits the degree of compensation. if we go beyond 60% then other sectors will have to pay, through a reduction in their direct payment. with regard to the quota transfer between member states, the communication introduces this as one of the key elements in driving the necessary restructuring within the sugar industry. quota transfers could facilitate production moving to regions where the production conditions are best, and at the same time provide regions that are not competitive with an opportunity to give up their quota and invest the proceeds in alternative economically viable activities. your concerns about the quota transfer have not gone unnoticed. if our objectives can be achieved through alternative instruments then that deserves thorough consideration. i have been particularly interested in the ideas put forward in the resolution on making the transfer subject to some degree of control by member states and farmers, and on the setting-up of a special fund. i am currently exploring those ideas. the creation of a specific fund forms a particularly important element of my reflections. let me be very clear on the ‘everything but arms’ – eba – initiative, which is one of the cornerstones of our trade relations with the least-developed countries, the ldcs. it was the result of an unprecedented unilateral concession made by the european union, and a logical step given our commitment to the development of these countries. it would be a wrong signal to roll back our privileges to the ldcs, particularly in a year where we are trying to convince the rest of the developed world to follow our example and increase market access to developing countries. i am therefore against a renegotiation of the eba initiative. furthermore, a system with regulated imports at remunerative prices would lead to a price reduction which is too small and thus inefficient. we should not give incentives for unsustainable investments within the eu or in third world countries. we recognise that the sugar reform will imply certain adjustments of the sugar sector in the acp countries concerned, but we have also clearly indicated that we are prepared to accompany this process. on the basis of an action plan the commission presented on 24 january, a dialogue with the acp countries is currently taking place. it is the commission’s intention to submit the final action plan on accompanying measures in the form of a communication to the european parliament and the council in mid-2005. the last point i want to address is the wto. the final ruling of the wto appellate body is fixed for 28 april 2005. our reform proposal will take due account of its outcome, and with that we will have brought the common market organisation for sugar into line with our existing wto obligations. let me conclude with the timetable. for internal and external reasons i consider it absolutely necessary to reach an agreement on the sugar reform by november at the latest. in fact, the current sugar regime expires on 1 july 2006. the sector has to know sufficiently in advance what the new sugar regime looks like in order to make their decisions for the common marketing year 2006-2007. furthermore, we have a clear interest to indicate to our wto ministerial partners, before the conference in december this year, what the basic elements of our sugar reform are. otherwise we run the risk of the sugar issue spoiling the hong kong meeting in the same way that cotton did the cancún meeting. the uk presidency has scheduled discussions in the council in order to reach final political agreement in the november council. to meet this timeframe i will present the legislative proposal to the european parliament and the council by the summer. i know that i can count on your cooperation to make this timetable possible.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. as the shadow rapporteur for the epp-ed group, i would like to thank in particular the rapporteur, mr jean-claude fruteau, and the chairman of the committee on agriculture, mr joseph daul, for their excellent cooperation on the motion for a resolution on the reform of the common organization of the market in sugar. i would also like to thank all the other members who have worked constructively on this resolution. when i travel in my constituency in bavaria, the sugar beet growers ask me why the market organization for sugar, which has been proven to work for decades, should be changed so fundamentally. the disappointment of the farmers and workers concerned with the proposals of the european commission of 14 july 2004 is very great. i then explain to them that a reform of the market organization is necessary so that sugar beet can continue to be grown in europe. we want to see sugar beet growing in the european union, sugar cane growing in the peripheral regions and sugar production in the sugar factories. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the sugar industry is not left behind. the commission's proposals go too far. in many regions of europe, sustainable sugar beet cultivation and, in the peripheral regions, sugar cane production would disappear altogether. the reform would benefit a few large producers, such as brazil, which, unlike the eu, consistently produces with very low environmental and social standards. our environmental organizations would cry out if in europe, as in brazil, whole rivers were pumped dry for irrigation agriculture, if hundreds of thousands of hectares of land were burned and the animals living on these areas had no chance of escaping the fire. such a sugar production cannot be the benchmark for european sugar production. the argument that the european consumers would benefit from a reduction in sugar prices is not one i can understand. for although grain costs less than a third of what it did 40 years ago, the price of bread has increased many times over the same period. the council of agriculture ministers of the european union, at its meeting on 18 november 1997, defined the multifunctional tasks of european agriculture as follows: 'the council believes that european agriculture must be a multifunctional, sustainable and competitive economic sector, spread over the whole of europe. it must be able to maintain the landscape, preserve natural spaces, make a significant contribution to the vitality of the countryside and meet consumer concerns and requirements in terms of food quality and safety, the environment and animal welfare.' if we want such a multifunctional agriculture in europe, we must also give it the appropriate protection. we therefore call for the production of imported sugar to be subject to the same social and environmental standards as the production of sugar in the eu. the commission is urged to comply with the acp states' requests and to consider how the eu can continue to control sugar supply in terms of quantity through a similar scheme under the 'everything but arms' initiative. in the commission's legislative proposal we also not ecologically oriented. i do not want a world market in which people and whole regions are exploited! i would like to ask you to give the motion for a resolution a large majority so that the the commission is therefore proposing to extend the period of validity of the directive to the period of 1 january 1999. the commission has already done so. you said that reform was needed. i agree with you. the sugar market regulation has been perverted by the sugar industry itself. it was aimed at consumption plus the privileged access of acp sugar. then there was a development where c sugar was also dumped on the world market and the quantity of sugar coming from the acp countries was re-exported, which also cost the budget another 1.5 billion euros. but you say you want to bring back the 1.8 million tonnes. we have to reduce them by 4 to 5 million tonnes if we include the c sugar. that's the way the world works. so you have to go back in quantity, not in price. we can accept a reduction in price, but if you propose that 33% should be reduced and the least developed countries should not be given a quota - extensively addressed. we have also brought to the attention of the chinese authorities the situation of tibetan individuals, together with individuals from all over china, who have been sentenced for existing respective positions. we hope that those developments will encourage the start of a meaningful and direct dialogue between beijing and the dalai lama, which will lead to the recognition of genuine autonomy for the tibetan region. we firmly believe that only such direct dialogue can be conducive to a lasting solution of the tibetan issue. in our view, the opening of a direct dialogue should not be subject to any precondition. on the other hand, the respective parties should refrain from taking any steps that would compromise the establishment of a climate of confidence, which appears indispensable if a solution is to be reached. in all circumstances, we would condemn violence from any quarter as a solution to the problem of tibet. the commission would certainly be prepared conditions which allow the tibetans to fully exercise their basic political, religious and cultural rights and allow the cultural identity of tibet to be preserved.

president of the council. mr president, i do not share the presentation that some of you have tried to make by giving parliament the fine role of defender of freedom and the ministers in the council of ministers for justice and home affairs the role of champions of security. i can tell you that in all the decisions we take, we try to maintain the balance between the three components of the area of freedom, security and justice. we have said many times that we want these three aspects to be developed in parallel. it is something that we care about and i therefore challenge the claim that parliament should hold us back in our ambition to create more security because it would be at the expense of freedom. that is simply not true, and i will give you several examples of that. the day a murderer or a rapist can be prosecuted because we find in dna databases of genetic fingerprints the evidence to convict them in a court of law, the citizens will find it a good thing, and so will you. today, this person can travel to another member state of the european union and, since there is no interconnection of dna databases, he remains unpunished. and that is when parliament asks the council why we have done nothing in this area. the same applies to the interconnection of criminal records. when a person who has committed sexual offences against children moves to another member state and the member state is not informed of the person's history, it is right to ask why we did not do anything. we are currently looking at how we can better interconnect the data we have in the different criminal records. after 11 september 2001, we were also rightly asked why we had not moved forward on the european arrest warrant, although this text had been on the council's table for some time. we have done so since then, but in the absence of dramatic events we are somewhat forgetting, and i think you are too, that in order to be active in the field of crime and terrorism prevention we must take a number of measures, while obviously maintaining the balance between freedom, security and justice. it is a concern we share, so let us forget the fallacious notion that there are defenders of freedom in this parliament and those in the council who want to reduce our fundamental freedoms. secondly, it concerns the retention of data. what i have just said about principles also applies to data retention. i am, however, extremely surprised, if not shocked, by some of the statements made here, in which data retention and torture chambers are equated. has the european parliament forgotten that three years ago, i believe, we adopted a directive on data processing, which allows member states, in the framework of their national legislation, to retain telecommunications data for certain specific purposes and for limited periods of time? this directive was adopted by codecision. so today, what we're doing is not storing the wiretaps, the content of the phone conversations. we are simply trying to fight crime better by putting in a text, which we are discussing and which will perhaps be amended, that what we can do at national level we can, in some cases, also do at european level. i ask that we think 'more european' when it comes to fighting crime. of course, there will need to be clear conditions and objectives regarding which data are retained, for how long and how to access them. it is nothing more and nothing less than what we are already doing in many of our member states. many drug cases, many terrorism cases in our member states have been solved by the retention of data. so let us be realistic about the possibilities that this opens up. of course, if the legal basis - and we will look at it - is such that we are partly in the first pillar, the council has no problem in discussing it with parliament and i shall be happy to come back to the committee on civil liberties and to discuss it in detail. i believe and remain convinced that it is a judicial area; i am not in favour of the idea of a european court of justice, but i am in favour of the idea of a european court of justice, and i am in favour of the idea of a european court of initiatives. we have defined a road map, a set of actions and principles that we will tackle; we're already dealing with some of them. i have mentioned earlier the issue of child protection, and this the fundamental principle that racism must not have entered europe. the commissioner's group has dealt with this and will continue to do so. much has been said about the protection of personal data, but nobody is going to - and the commission is obviously not thinking about that - to create a big european ear that listens to everything, that records everything. we are thinking of a balanced initiative, which first of all takes account of the specific needs of investigating certain serious transnational crimes, terrorism for all, but also human trafficking, paedophilia, and makes itself available to specifically designated authorities for an appropriate period, so nothing to do with an eternal database which none of us considers compatible with the european charter of fundamental rights. the commission will present its proposal, but we have doubts about the legal basis which the council has put forward. i have said it many times and i will say it again, within a few weeks our proposal will be ready for the council to consider. we shall take account of parliament's assessments on this subject, just as we have taken account of the assessments - we must never forget this - of those personal data protection authorities, who, meeting in a body of undoubtedly technical and technical level, have often given critical opinions on the commission's proposals. we certainly take these opinions into account and will take them into account, but once, for example, that opinion on that proposal is positive, we have a strong argument in favour, in the sense that the proposal respects the fundamental right to data protection. finally, a word on asylum and european asylum policy. here again, our approach must be, and will continue to be, balanced: minimum procedural rights are essential, they are a first step. we have the ambition to arrive tomorrow, and i hope soon, at a european system for recognising or withdrawing refugee status without any differential treatment, a high quality standard, not a common rule to the bottom, as some have said. we do not think that european policy can again be unbalanced in the sense of looking only at the opposition and not at the reception and integration, but both aspects are preserved, there is no adequate policy of prevention, of opposition, if we are not ready to integrate those who come legally to europe. we are certainly not going to help people who want to work honestly unless we show that we are clear, firm and strict with those who are trading in human beings. these two aspects are linked and will be the guiding principle of european policy as far as the commission is concerned.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, first of all i would like to welcome parliament’s support for this important proposal. our proposal has two main elements. the first aims to set common minimal standards as regards certain procedural rights applying to criminal proceedings throughout the european union. the intention is to promote compliance as a consistent standard, rather than to duplicate the echr. the areas where common minimal standards are proposed at this first stage are: firstly, access to legal advice both before and during trial; secondly, access to interpretation and translation free of charge; thirdly, ensuring that appropriate attention is given to persons who are not capable of understanding or following the proceedings; and fifthly, the right for foreign suspects to communicate with consular authorities, and a letter of rights notifying the suspected person of their rights in writing. a decision was taken to draw up proposals relating to these five rights initially, because they are of particular importance in the context of mutual recognition. it is not the intention to suggest that these five rights are more important than others, simply that they are of more immediate relevance to mutual recognition. in seeking to enhance fair trial rights generally, this framework decision will have the effect of ensuring a reasonable level of protection to foreign suspects and defendants. finally, mutual recognition can only operate effectively in a spirit of confidence. this proposal for a framework decision will strengthen the mutual trust that member states have in each other’s criminal justice systems. it is important not only to have trust in the integrity of one’s partner’s rules, but also to trust that these rules are correctly applied. that is why a monitoring mechanism is proposed.

member of the commission. let me answer the question concerning the application of early retirement. i think it's absolutely clear that with demographic aging, which will mean the loss of millions of available jobs, it's very necessary that we expand the supply of labor to increase the employment of the entire population. it is also clear, and this is the experience of all employment policies, how serious the situation is. the training for the profession takes approximately 22 years. a person is out of work for about 5 years during his active life and is retired for about 20 to 22 years. so in the human lifetime, we're 50 years out of work. this is a situation which is not sustainable in the long term and is also why, for the overall stability of our social systems, we need to expand the supply and make it easier for people who are already older to stay in the labour market. another question that was asked was why social policy is not somehow clearly incorporated and described in this question no 43 by mr bushill-matthews (h-0175/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: de-election of expatriate citizens and referendum on the constitutional treatyis the commission aware that many british citizens who are retired in other eu member states will not be able to vote in the national referendums on the proposed european constitution? if they left the united kingdom more than 15 years ago, they no longer have the right to vote there under the current national legislation, but they do not automatically have the right to vote in their new country of residence. it is up to the individual member states to grant such a right, but should there not be some coordination between member states so that these people can also have a say? it is certainly completely wrong to deny european citizens the right to vote on such an important issue. does the commission know how many eu citizens are affected and what measures does it propose that the member states should take to tackle this problem together?
member of the commission. it is true that a citizen of the union who has exercised their fundamental right to free movement could be affected, as they might have no right to participate in referenda either in their member state of residence or in their home member state. however, we should not interpret current community law so that it leads to the conclusion that this issue could be an obstacle to free movement, or might dissuade citizens of the union from exercising their right to it. community law on free movement would be violated as a result.
question no 44 by mr liam aylward (h-0204/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: bioethanol from sugar beetin view of the continuing rise in oil prices and in particular the current reform of the sugar sector, does the commission not consider that it is time to seriously consider, with the participation of governments, all relevant commission directorates, experts in the field, industry and trade, the possibility of developing an industry for the production of bioethanol from sugar beet in the eu?
member of the commission. the july communication on sugar reform recognises the importance of various industries, and particularly the bioethanol industry as sugar users. it therefore proposes the production of sugar beyond the quota at a price closer to that on the world market, for the processing of specific products like bioethanol. as you know sugar beet for the production of biofuel can already be cultivated outside the quota limits. the forthcoming legislative proposal will have to ensure that sufficient sugar is available at competitive prices for these industries, including for its increasing use in biofuel. under the biofuels directive, member states are required to promote and to set targets for the use of biofuels. bioethanol from sugar and grain is a good way to meet this objective. the commission is taking steps to ensure that all member states fulfil their obligations under the directive. the commission will review the implementation of the directive in 2006 and will, if necessary, propose measures to reinforce it. the commission is aware that some firms in the bioethanol industry have expressed reluctance to invest in processing facilities in the eu because they are concerned about the possibility of tariff reductions, leading to large-scale imports from low-cost sugar cane ethanol producers outside the eu. the commission believes that a ‘win-win’ solution should be found that leads to a rapid increase in eu bioethanol production and consumption, combined in a proportionate manner with increased imports. the fuel quality directive places a limit on the ethanol content of petrol. the commission is reviewing certain aspects of the directive and will take into account the need to encourage the use of alternative fuels, including biofuels, as well as the need to introduce modifications for other parameters in the fuel specifications. the commission continues to support targeted research action aimed at developing cost-competitive alternative fuel technology, including ethanol production from sweet sorghum, cereals, agricultural residues and other ligno-cellulosic feedstock. the commission currently contributes to the creation of a european biofuels industry by supporting and facilitating initiatives to create a biofuel technology platform. stakeholders on this platform will include, amongst others, the agricultural and forestry sectors, bioethanol producers and the sugar industry.
member of the commission. i can be quite clear: there will be economic analyses to find the most efficient source for biofuels, taking into account the fact that the commission is really aware of the importance of this. various options for out-of-quota sugar are already being analysed. however, this question will only be answered when the commission tables the legislative proposal for reform of the common organisation of the market in sugar. the reform proposal will have to take into account the outcome of the wto sugar panel, which is expected to be known in late april. the commission cannot, therefore, table the legislative proposal before june or july 2005. the commission will set up a biomass action plan for the second half of 2005. this plan will contain a table and make it quite clear how to achieve the eu targets for renewable energies. that is my answer to the last question.
question no 45 by mr staes (h-0164/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: competition rules and state aid in the nuclear power sectoron 22 september 2004, the commission announced that it would approve the uk government's assistance of eur 6 billion in the restructuring of the energy company british energy. on 1 december 2004 it also announced that it would carry out an investigation to determine whether the establishment of the nuclear decommissioning authority was not contrary to the treaty. the nda is to be given responsibility for the sellafield mox plant and the magnox nuclear power plants and to relieve bnfl of its obligation under the polluter pays principle, which can be considered as the granting of state aid. can the commission state what the amount in the second case might be and whether it shares the view that state aid should actually be internalised in the cost price of nuclear energy and not be borne by the taxpayer?
member of the commission. i can assure you that the commission intends to apply the ‘polluter pays’ principle to the nuclear sector as well. both the commission’s final decision on the restructuring of british energy and its decision to open proceedings on the nuclear decommissioning authority make it clear that under the polluter pays principle, operators of nuclear stations bear the primary responsibility for the payment of the management of their waste and other nuclear liabilities, including planned decommissioning. however, one has to keep in mind that, as with all principles of community law, the polluter pays principle must be reconciled with other community principles and objectives, which may, in certain circumstances, conflict with it. in the british energy case, for instance, the polluter pays principle had to be reconciled with the need to preserve nuclear safety, which is also, as you know, a major community objective enshrined in the euratom treaty. in such cases the commission seeks to strike the best possible balance between diverging principles for the benefit of the community.
question no 46 by mrs batzeli (h-0218/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: mergers in the audiovisual sector in addition to the basic provisions of the treaty on the regulation of concentrations between undertakings, the relevant regulation (ec) no 139/2004 oj l 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1 applies, which states that the control of concentrations between undertakings is in principle the exclusive competence of the commission and that member states may not adopt national competition law (the exclusive competence principle) except in specific cases where the commission considers that national intervention is necessary. how does the commission intend to respond to the activities of corporate groups and large media groups and to the dominant position of the mass media in order to promote pluralism and objective reporting?
member of the commission. according to the merger regulation, the commission cannot take pluralism of the media into account as a legal criterion when it decides whether a merger with a community dimension is compatible with the common market. in carrying out its assessment, it is entitled to take account only of competition-related or economic criteria when determining whether the transaction in question significantly impedes competition in the common market. however, notwithstanding the commission’s sole jurisdiction to examine mergers with a community dimension, article 21(4) of the regulation provides that member states may take appropriate measures to protect legitimate interests other than those taken into consideration by the regulation, provided that they are compatible with the general principles and other provisions of community law. the legitimate interests specifically recognised by the merger regulation include media plurality. ‘the member state’s right to plead the plurality of the media recognises the legitimate concern to maintain diversified sources of information for the sake of plurality of opinion and multiplicity of use’. this would appear to include the objective information referred to in the question by the honourable member. it is clear from the foregoing that the member states should as a matter of priority take appropriate measures under their national law to safeguard the plurality of the media if that legitimate interest were to be threatened by a merger with a community dimension. lastly, the commission points out that in practice the aim of the merger regulation, namely to preserve and develop competitive market structures, can go hand in hand, at least to some extent, with safeguarding media plurality. when the commission considers whether a merger with a community dimension hampers competition on a media market, it necessarily examines the degree of concentration and hence indirectly the degree of pluralism on that market.
question no 47 by gay mitchell (h-0245/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: state aid the irish government has recently abandoned its attempt to obtain approval for state aid of eur 170 million for a new microchip manufacturing plant in ireland. the commission considers that the project is not sufficiently linked to innovation or job creation to justify the aid. it is argued that the commission's interpretation of the state aid guidelines is very narrow and that this decision frustrates all attempts by member states to be competitive in a global market of high-technology industries. what is the commission's response to this allegation?
member of the commission. the commission doubted the compatibility of the investment project with the ec state aid control rules for two main reasons. firstly, there was a real risk of distortion of the conditions of competition since intel has very significant market power in microchip production, and the aid would allow the company to reinforce its dominance. secondly, on the basis of the information submitted, the investment project appeared to be for the large-scale manufacturing of microchips. there was no indication that research and development activity would be transferred to europe, nor of the creation of new jobs at the leixlip site. as you know, leixlip is located in a prosperous region that may not be eligible for regional aid after 2006. any regional investment aid therefore needs to refer to a project scheduled to start before the end of 2006, which was not the case with modules ii and iii of the investment project. for these reasons the commission envisaged to launch an in-depth inquiry according to state aid rules, in order to analyse the balance of the positive and negative aspects of the aid. however, the irish authorities decided to withdraw the notification before any commission decision was taken.
member of the commission. i understand your reason for asking this question. it is worthwhile in itself and therefore i am quite happy that the matter has been raised, because it gives me an opportunity to explain. we should not underestimate the importance of the facilities in leixlip for the local economy. this is aid for a mobile manufacturing project, which will maintain a large number of jobs in the region for seven years, but will not create any new employment. to be quite frank, ireland is an example that proves how important the european union and our policy to stimulate the economy is. however, in this case no new jobs would be created. there is no indication that the project would lead to a transfer of any significant part of the company’s research and development base to europe from the us, for example, or would develop other synergies or spillover effects, which would in turn contribute to innovation in europe, going beyond the specific manufacturing operations concerned. this is a pure manufacturing project for the large-scale production of microchips that will help intel to maintain its position as a leader in the relevant market. it was exactly the combination of those points and arguments that led us to think what we were thinking until the irish government withdrew the notification.
member of the commission. we are talking about different types of aid which are not comparable. i do not see the logic in saying that if we could not move an activity to another part of the european union then aid should be allowed. we have to be consistent in accordance with our rules. only with a consistent policy on state aid, whereby people can expect reliability and can be assured that there are no differing measures, can we face not only you as a member of parliament, but also the outside world and the people involved in the case.

member of the commission. the commission does not plan to propose amendments to the nitrates directive, as it is convinced that its full implementation is crucial to reduce the impact of nutrients from agricultural sources on european waters. we are fully committed to ensuring that the nitrates directive will be correctly implemented in the member states with a set of actions including, as i mentioned before, legal pressure through infringement procedures for member states that do not implement the different steps of the directive. significant steps have been taken by the commission to support a better knowledge of the pressures on the environmental status of european waters through regular monitoring; reporting exercises; exchange of technical information and best practices with regard to agriculture and their impact on nutrient losses; and tools for measuring, modelling and forecasting their impact on water quality. a relevant contribution to the implementation of the nitrates directive has also been made by including this directive in the codes of practice underpinning rural development since 2000 and, from 2005 onwards, under cross-compliance with direct payments to producers according to the new agricultural policy.

president of the council. mr president, mr president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, on 12 january in this house i presented to you the programme of the luxembourg presidency for the next six months. today, as is the custom, i shall briefly present the results of the recent european council. briefly because, in view of the overwhelming presence of members of parliament, the debate may not be sustained. so i will not feed it, except to tell you that we agreed on the reform of the stability and growth pact after bitter debates, after exchanges between men and men, even if women's voices were heard in this heated debate. the result we have achieved is a balanced result, since it attaches the full importance it deserves to stability and does everything in its power not to hinder, by applying the rules of stability, the growth opportunities that exist and that must exist in europe. to do this, we have not touched on the fundamental principles of the pact, but we have broadened its scope, since the stability and growth pact will now apply to all stages of the economic cycle, and in a differentiated way. this reform, which we have achieved, is the result of excellent cooperation - i should like to emphasize this here - between the commission and the council, more specifically between the presidency of the commission and the presidency of the council, between the commissioner for monetary affairs and the president of the council of finance ministers. it was a real pleasure for me to work hand in hand with the commission. everything has been said about the reform of the pact and much of what has been said is a lie. those who say that after the reform of the pact all deficits will be allowed, those who claim that the message is now being sent that europe can move towards the unproductive lands of massive debt are gravely mistaken. neither the basic rules of the treaty nor those of the pact have been changed. the 3% and 60% criteria remain the cornerstone of a system which will continue to be based on clear rules and clear legal rules. i would like to repeat here that as soon as we see that the 3% value is exceeded, the commission will draw up a report and the member state concerned will be placed under close surveillance. i am saying here that, as has always been the case, exceeding the reference value, i.e. 3%, does not automatically lead to the initiation of infringement proceedings. some people say that this is an innovation, but they are not familiar with the maastricht treaty, which has provided for this rule since 1992. the commission's powers have not been reduced, but they have been strengthened by the reform of the pact. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the second item on the agenda of the brussels european council was the interim review of the lisbon strategy. you will recall that in our debate on 12 january there was great concern that the council was upsetting the fundamental balance of the lisbon strategy. after the commission presented its communication on the lisbon strategy on 2 february and after the commission communication on the social agenda, the commission and the council - again acting together - managed to maintain the basic balance of the lisbon strategy. of course, we have refocused the lisbon strategy on growth and competitiveness, but we have not abandoned its social and environmental dimensions. as i have said for several months, i have to say that europeans still do not understand the importance of the lisbon strategy, because we are talking about competitiveness, productivity and growth, and these are concepts and expressions that do not speak to the hearts of europeans. in fact, what europeans want is work, to be able to set up a business, to find the necessary financing, to have open markets, efficient communication and transport systems at their disposal. they would like to be able to better balance work and family life, to be able to keep up with new technologies and the internet world. they want to be able to have a good education for their children; they want to have at their disposal services of general interest and efficient public services; they want to have decent pensions; they want to be able to grow in a healthy environment. the lisbon strategy is all about this and to give credence to the idea that governments and the commission will henceforth have to be more proactive and more consistent in the way they implement the decisions under the lisbon strategy, we have grouped the steps to be taken around three axes concentrated on ten areas and illustrated in one hundred individual measures. the lisbon strategy has many actors: the commission, the european parliament, the european parliament, the council, the commission, the european parliament, the council, the commission, the european parliament, the council, the european parliament, the commission, the council, the european parliament, the european parliament, the council, the commission, the european parliament, the council, the commission, the european parliament, the council, the commission. there are national parliaments. there are national governments. there are local and regional authorities. all these authorities and bodies must be able to take better ownership of the lisbon strategy. i say this especially for national governments, who, because they are accountable to their national parliaments and to european public opinion, on the three main subjects which, as you know, were discussed at the spring european council. first, the stability and growth pact. as we all know, consensus on the pact broke down in november 2003. a new consensus on a proper fiscal framework has now been reached. the commission made a very important contribution to this end. the commission launched discussions in its 2004 public finance report and in september 2004 the commission adopted a communication on strengthening and clarifying the stability and growth pact. since then, the commission has actively contributed to the debate on the reform of the pact and supported the presidency in its efforts to find a consensus, while preserving the essence of our budgetary framework. the european council's agreement was a very positive outcome, restoring credibility to the pact and preserving the commission's prerogatives. under this agreement the treaty principles are maintained. the budget deficit of member states cannot exceed 3% of gdp and government debt is still limited to 60%. to avoid excessive deficits any overstepping of these limits can only be temporary and only in exceptional circumstances. a new feature is that member states are being asked to exercise more discipline. they must step up their efforts to reduce deficits in growth periods, while a degree of flexibility has been introduced for periods of economic difficulty. the commission intends to present its proposals for amending the relevant regulations before the end of this month so that reform can be completed by june. it is in everyone's interest that we make rapid progress on finalising the reform of the pact in order to offer greater transparency and predictability regarding public finances and budgetary developments. this is an ambitious timetable but one that can undoubtedly be achieved with the cooperation of all the players involved: the member states, the european parliament, and the european central bank. i am sure that i can count on your cooperation in attaining these objectives. the commission will do what is necessary to ensure the success of this joint project and is ready to work closely with you to do this, as requested in the joint motion for a resolution. in order to be effective, the pact must count on the broadest political support, which is why wide support within parliament is of the utmost importance. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thanks to the very active role of the presidency, the recent european council has given the necessary political impetus to the lisbon ambition. we have objectives, including sustainable development. the commission is extremely pleased with this result because its proposals were the basis of the work and conclusions of the european council. president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the council is continuously and strongly concerned about relations between the western balkans and the european union, which remains strongly committed to the stabilization and association of this neighbouring region. under the european security strategy, this region is a high priority for the european union, which is documented, among other things, by the european union's police and military presence in the western balkans, in addition to the civilian aspects. the future of this region lies in the european union. the thessaloniki summit of 21 june 2003 clearly underlined the european vocation of the western balkans. while the eu's commitment to the western balkans is unequivocal, it is up to the countries of the region to make good use of it. the countries concerned must demonstrate, through policies and concrete actions, their willingness and capacity to become, in due course, candidates for membership of the european union with a view to joining it one day. the union will continue to actively support them in their efforts to bring about political and institutional reforms. this will undoubtedly require perseverance and a strong commitment on both sides, as the challenges to be met remain considerable. but they can be reversed and controlled, because it is in the interest of the peoples of the western balkans, who have definitely gone through dark times, to reverse them. it is also in the interest of the european union to promote this path to europe, because our primary objective must be peace and stability on the european continent. the stabilisation and association process remains the overall framework for the european path of the western balkan countries towards future membership. the process aims to help countries in the region to establish peace, democracy, stability, prosperity and respect for minority rights in a sustainable way. these are the very objectives of the european project which, after the most terrible of wars, reconciled the enemy nations and enabled them to build a common future. it is important to note that this same ideal, this same vision, also enriched the experience of the last enlargement. this morning we have just taken a very important decision, your parliament has just taken a very important decision in this respect, in this case with regard to bulgaria and romania. each year, the council shall examine both the progress made by the countries of the stabilisation and association process and the outstanding problems, on the basis of the commission's annual reports. this review is an important exercise which reminds us that the western balkans are making progress towards the european union. as agreed at the thessaloniki summit, the union concluded european partnerships with the countries of the region for the first time in 2004. they were presented by the commission together with the reports on partnerships and the stabilisation and association process. these partnerships, which are modelled on the accession partnerships of the candidate countries, serve as individualised roadmaps, adapted to the specific situations of each country. they indicate the precise actions to be taken as a matter of priority. the commission and the council shall monitor the progress of the implementation of these partnerships. the union's approach to the balkans is therefore already highly individualised and based on the principle of own merits. all the participants at the thessaloniki summit accepted that the speed with which the countries of the region progress towards future membership will depend on the pace at which they implement the necessary reforms and comply with the existing copenhagen criteria and the stabilisation and association process. the top performers can move up the ladder faster. only two countries currently have a stabilisation and association agreement with the european union, namely croatia and fyrom. croatia is now the first country in the region to become a candidate country. the process is therefore global, but it follows a merit-based approach. the prospect of accession, which is the only guarantee that the development of these countries is for all, is, however, applied according to the own merits approach. the last review of the stabilisation and association process by the council in may 2004 welcomed the progress made in the region. it noted a lasting stabilisation of the security situation. but despite the successes of recent years, the possibility of slippage, of violence, of questioning the fundamental values on which the european construction is based cannot, unfortunately, be ruled out forever. this is why we must remain particularly vigilant and alert to possible developments. peace and stability are not final achievements in this region. the legacies of a dark past, where destructive nationalism has wreaked havoc, have not been totally erased. the year 2005 will be a year of significant opportunities for the region. the council will therefore closely monitor the continued implementation of the ohrid framework agreement in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, which has applied for membership of the european union. the political developments in albania, particularly in the run-up to the parliamentary elections due to take place this summer, deserve our full attention. as regards serbia and montenegro and bosnia and herzegovina, the council should, inter alia, express its opinion during this six-month period on the advisability of negotiating a stabilisation and association agreement. negotiations for such an agreement are continuing with albania. and the council will have to consider the application for accession of fyrom later this year, on the basis of the commission's opinion. for kosovo, mid-2005 will provide a first opportunity to assess progress in effective compliance with un standards. the positive outcome of this assessment will determine progress towards a process to determine, in dialogue and cooperation with all relevant parties, the future status of kosovo. finally, as regards croatia, the intergovernmental conference for accession negotiations will be convened by mutual agreement as soon as the council - and i hope it will be soon - has established that croatia is cooperating fully with the hague tribunal. this full cooperation with the court is a key requirement for all the western balkan components. real progress has been made in recent times, but it still needs to be made. the european union's initiatives to promote regional integration in the western balkans, particularly in the areas of infrastructure, education, the return of refugees, the fight against crime and cultural exchanges, are essential. regional cooperation promoting the economic integration of the region is an important instrument for promoting reconciliation, promoting reforms and, above all, improving the economic and social situation in the region. endemic unemployment, which is at record levels and largely due to insufficient private investment, is characteristic of parts of the western balkans and is a major factor in social as well as political instability. the council therefore attaches particular importance to the promotion of regional cooperation, which is a key element of the stabilisation and association partnership. in its assessment of this process in may 2004, the council welcomed the significant improvements in regional cooperation, particularly in the areas of infrastructure, trade and energy. assistance projects in the areas mentioned in the question are being implemented by the commission under the cards programme and, in particular for croatia, through the pre-accession instruments which are of particular importance in this respect. the objective of the cards regulation is, among other things, to implement reconstruction projects, to provide assistance for the return of refugees and for the stabilisation of the region, but also to encourage regional cooperation. discussions are currently under way in the council on the new financial instrument for preaccession assistance proposed by the commission. from 2007, it should be the framework for eu assistance to candidate and potential candidate countries, categories in which the western balkans are included.

talking about tonight. ten million vehicles are scrapped in europe every year. the fact that cars are no longer piled up and spoiling the landscape as in the past has something to do with the high recyclability and recyclability of an automobile. the aim of the vehicle type-approval directive is to lay down provisions to ensure that cars and light commercial vehicles are designed to meet the minimum reusability, recyclability and recoverability ratios set out in the altauto directive. the altauto directive sets binding targets for manufacturers. from 2006 onwards, at least 85% by mass and from 2015 onwards at least 95% by mass of a car must be recoverable and reusable or recyclable. in particular, the 95% target from 2015 is a very ambitious target, because it would mean that the car of the future would produce almost no waste. the achievement of this objective will depend not only on the use of certain materials by manufacturers, but also on the further development of recycling technology and the definition of recyclability. the recyclability of cars and the prevention of waste are important environmental policy objectives in europe. but cars still account for a staggering 1% of the total amount of waste in the eu. the prevention of waste from cars is particularly well regulated in the eu, alongside packaging, electronic scrap and batteries. now, to the main points. the types must be given priority to ensure that all new types that will be introduced in the eu in the future meet the binding objectives of the altauto directive. the commission's proposal of 36 months should therefore apply to new types. the existing models will then be tested successively. we have agreed in parliament and with the council on 54 months. this corresponds to the arithmetic mean between the commission's original proposal and my original proposal of 72 months, which corresponds to the life cycle of an average car. the definition of the representative vehicle is another point. called on the commission to inform parliament regularly, and in particular the committee on culture and education, of the negotiations taking place in unesco. the commission responded to the invitation positively. following the provisional unesco timetable for the negotiations on the future convention, the intergovernmental negotiations were launched in september 2004, and the negotiations on substance started in december 2004, with the first meeting of the drafting group. a few weeks after the end of the drafting group meeting, the commission accepted parliament's invitation to take part in a mini-hearing on the unesco negotiations. this meeting was held on 25 january 2005 with members of the culture committee, with mr schmitt in the chair. it gave rise to a substantial discussion with the commission and the luxembourg presidency on the current negotiation process. the commission remains available to take part in similar meetings in the future. the culture committee has already envisaged one such meeting for later this month. negotiations are well under way in unesco. from an eu point of view, the last negotiating session, in february, took place in a good collaborative spirit, on the basis of a code of conduct adopted by coreper on 27 january 2005. the unity of the eu's representation has been strictly respected throughout the session on the basis of common positions established through numerous community coordination meetings. with a single voice, the european union has become a reference for the debate and a major partner in the negotiation. however, the commission’s observer status in unesco entails numerous restrictions that limit its ability to negotiate. the european union has thus introduced a request for full participant status for the european community in this negotiation, and this will be discussed at unesco in april. although the february session has not been able to produce a new consolidated draft convention, the overall results of this negotiating session on substance are positive in relation to european union expectations and positions. the general trend resulting from the plenary debates is in line with the european union's common positions, including the articulation with other instruments. the april session of the unesco executive board will have to confirm the convening of a new intergovernmental negotiating session, provisionally scheduled for 25 may to 4 june 2005. it will also discuss the request made by the european community for a reinforced status in the current negotiations. the main next steps in the provisional timetable for the negotiations in unesco are as follows. the spring executive board will be held on 18-28 april 2005. notably, this session will discuss the request from the european community for a reinforced status in unesco for the purpose of the current negotiations on the future convention. the next session of intergovernmental negotiations is scheduled for 25 may to 4 june 2005, while the autumn executive board is to be held on 13-29 september 2005. finally, the general conference is to take place on 3-21 october 2005 when, on the basis of the provisional timetable, the convention on cultural diversity should be adopted. on behalf of commissioner figeľ i wish to thank parliament, and in particular the culture committee, for its early and active involvement in the unesco negotiations, and for its general support for the commission in this process.
