member of the commission. madam president, first of all i would like to thank the european parliament, and in particular the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection and the rapporteur, mrs klaß, for their contribution to this report at first reading. groundwater is an important natural resource, used mainly for drinking water as well as for industry and agriculture. it also has high environmental value as it interacts with surface waters and water bodies, and is therefore an important part of the water cycle that needs to be protected. prevention of groundwater pollution has been the subject of community legislation since 1980, most recently the water framework directive adopted in 2000. however, some gaps remain. there are no clear criteria for the definition of environmental quality objectives for groundwater, and in particular good chemical status. in addition, specific measures are needed to prevent and control pollution of groundwater. this was recognised when the water framework directive was adopted, article 17 of which calls on the commission to submit proposals to address the needs in question. in this context and after extensive consultation with the parties concerned, the commission has put forward the proposal under discussion today, which contains the following main elements: - a compliance regime for the assessment of good groundwater chemical status for a limited number of pollutants where community standards already apply; - the criteria for assessing the chemical status of groundwater on the basis of environmental quality standards to be established by the member states at the appropriate national, regional or local level, taking into account the specific characteristics of the natural groundwater conditions, the pressures detected and the pollution-related chemicals; - the criteria for determining the degradation of groundwater quality and for reversing pollution trends; measures to prevent or reduce the direct and in particular indirect discharge of dangerous substances into groundwater. the proposal contains clear specifications which will ensure that the environmental objectives of the water framework directive are met in respect of groundwater. the proposal also strikes a satisfactory balance between issues which need to be addressed at community level and those which are better left to the member states.
the rapporteur. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. water is life, and groundwater is our largest reservoir of fresh water and therefore of drinking water, as 60% of drinking water in the european union is treated from groundwater. groundwater is not only an important resource for our drinking water, but it is also essential for agriculture, industry and our ecosystem. in all our efforts to keep our water, and in particular our groundwater, clean and to restore it when it is already polluted, we must - also at european level - strike a sensible balance between the demands of water management, the concerns of agriculture, ecosystems and the resources available for water treatment and restoration in the member states. since it is very difficult, very time-consuming and, in particular, very costly to clean up polluted groundwater, the precautionary approach and the protection of the groundwater ecosystem are of particular importance. groundwater bodies, like rivers - at least on the european continent - do not stop at borders. the protection of groundwater is therefore a european task, since the different requirements in the member states inevitably lead to distortions of competition for industry and agriculture. i'm glad we're not starting from scratch. the european commission's proposal is a subsidiary directive of the water framework directive, which has been in force since 2000 and should be implemented in all member states by the end of december 2003. the first task of the water framework directive is to have all member states take stock of all water by 22 march 2005. if all the member states have done so in time - mr dimas can perhaps tell us about that - then every member state should be informed about the state of its waters and groundwater by now at the latest. the water framework directive sets objectives and measures for all community waters, including groundwater, both in terms of quality and quantity. the subsidiary directive now seeks to settle two outstanding points. first, the criteria for classifying groundwater as 'good' or 'bad' and second, the time from which action must be taken when deterioration is documented. in addition, the absence of regulations on indirect releases of pollutants from point and diffuse sources must also be covered. we must put all the relevant directives in context: the water framework directive, the priority substances directive, the nitrates directive and the plant protection products directive. the costs of the effort, implementation and monitoring must be sustainable without jeopardising the achievement of the goal of good chemical status of groundwater in all 25 eu member states. but this objective would be jeopardized if we groundwater directive. this amendment must not be accepted! the hard-won compromise of the water framework directive must not be changed by a subsidiary groundwater directive! we have two other member of the commission. mr president, first of all i would like to thank and congratulate the rapporteur, mr maaten, for his work on this difficult dossier. as regards the european commission's report on the 2004 bathing season, i should like to inform you that it will be published by the end of the month, and not only in greek but also in other languages. the commission's original proposal was to modernise the existing directive, which dates back to 1976. it proposed tougher standards for water quality, updating bathing water management schemes, streamlining monitoring requirements and improving public information. the commission accepted at first reading, in whole or in part, 22 of the 37 amendments adopted by parliament (commission position on parliament's amendments: see annex). the text of the proposal has been improved, but its basic structure and in particular the water quality standards have remained in line with the commission's original proposal. the council held discussions during the greek, italian and irish presidencies. it was quickly found that a significant majority of member states considered the commission's proposals for quality standards to be too ambitious and too costly. the council also made clear its desire to distinguish between quality standards for coastal waters and those for inland waters. other changes resulting from the council's discussion concerned the timing of the new standards and an alternative approach to dealing with short-term pollution and emergencies. the commission considers that many of the changes made to the common position improve on the commission's original proposal. however, on the question of the sufficiently high water quality standards and the establishment of a classification category, the commission would prefer to maintain its original proposal. however, after long and arduous negotiations in the council, it was found that the commission proposal would never gather the necessary support. the commission has therefore decided to support the common position which, while far from ideal, is nevertheless a significant improvement on the arrangements currently in place under the current directive. the modernisation of existing legislation, which is nearly 30 years old, is urgent. when adopting the common position, the commission made a statement to the minutes underlining its intention to fund an epidemiological research programme to examine in more detail the possible effects on bathing and in particular the health effects associated with freshwater bathing. the results of this programme are expected to be ready in 2008 and may allow the resolution of some issues on which the positions of the council and parliament are currently different. i would ask parliament to seek, with the assistance of the commission, to find a common position with the council on this matter as soon as possible. we urgently need a new directive with targeted management practices, more rational monitoring regimes and more effective communication with the public.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the bathing water directive of 1976 was the first to establish uniform minimum standards for bathing water in the european community. whereas the 1976 directive on the assessment of water quality still provides for 19 physical, chemical and microbiological parameters, the present council common position has reduced the test criteria to only two microbiological pathogens, supplemented by visual checks and measurements of the ph value in fresh water. in general, the commission's proposal for a new bathing water directive is part of the european union's overall water policy. it is based on the latest scientific findings, in particular on studies by the who. whereas in 1976 levels considered "sufficient" for an assessment level were still associated with a health risk for 7-9% of bathers, the who now requires levels allowing a maximum risk of 5% of disease cases among bathers. the council has introduced a new level of 'sufficient' in its common position, but it does not provide for any improvement on the 1976 standard. opinions are divided. commissioner, you said it yourself: the main argument is that the cost would be too high. however, many of the alleged additional costs are already incurred by meeting the standards of the water framework directive, the nitrate directive and the municipal waste water directive. the low additional costs actually incurred in meeting the higher quality standards are now being offset by reducing the social costs, simply because fewer people are ultimately sick. i personally support the introduction of the higher quality standards proposed by the who and the commission with immediate effect. you can't put off health care. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the quality standards are met. this should enable those countries which feel that they are particularly hard hit by the new quality standards to prepare themselves for the stricter standards for a longer period and to eliminate any problems. i would ask the house to support this compromise amendment.
the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal. the commission has already made a number of proposals. i would like to thank the rapporteur, particularly for his question as to whether we need such a directive at european level. 'if it is not necessary to make a law, then it is necessary not to make a law', montesquieu said several centuries ago. the bathing water directive is, in my view, a good example of a directive which europe can certainly do without. the constant quest for european harmonisation has resulted in over-regulation, which has led to the european union becoming increasingly distant from its citizens. conversely, more and more citizens are turning their backs on a european union that stands out above all because it is overlaid with a wealth of bureaucratic regulations. to put it more specifically in this case: any region with bathing or recreational waters has an existential interest in ensuring the quality of the waters in the event of penalties for absent visitors and tourists. the creation of a legal framework in this area should remain a matter for the member states. i do not see any relevance to the internal market. and i do not need to explain how bad the practical implementation of many environmental regulations in the eu is, given the abundance of infringement procedures. if europe wants to become more transparent for its citizens, we must also focus on what is necessary and feasible in the european context in the field of environmental and health protection. this means that if we have doubts about whether a task should be regulated at european level or not, we should leave the responsibility to the member states. i think that the bathing water directive is not one of the requirements of european integration.

the next item is the report (a6-0105/2005) by mr alejandro cercas, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending directive 2003/88/ec on certain aspects of the organisation of working time (com (2004) 0607 - c6-0122/2004 - 2004/0209 (cod)).
i have to say, madam president, i would like to remind my colleagues once again that we must really take responsibility for social europe, especially since many believe that this will be a utopia after the accession of the ten new member states. minimum standards are essential for a social europe. we therefore reject the commission's amendments to the working time directive, because they remove the minimum standards and leave the directive to its own devices. this includes the invention of dividing the standby duty into active and inactive working time and not recognizing parts of it as working time. we're gonna keep the on-call hours to be working hours. the protection of workers and public safety must continue to take precedence over economic considerations. health care services of 30 hours or more pose a risk to patients. i see no room for compromise here! this position is also clearly supported by the ecj judgment. i thank the rapporteur for including this crucial phrase in the report. however, we do not bear his compromises that come after. we want to improve this because we think it is necessary that the standby time remains working time.
i have to say, madam president, the revised lisbon strategy is aimed at growth and jobs. we need more flexibility and competitiveness agreed! but that is precisely what is contained in the cercas report on the working time directive, on which mr silva peneda, the epp member, and many of us have worked on compromises. we do not want a rigid corset for the whole of the eu, but a reasonable framework for action, which leaves room for national regulations, such as extending the reference period from four months to one year, provided that the social partners agree. the possibility of extending the 48-hour week is also in their hands and in the collective agreements. this is the practical application of the principle of subsidiarity and flexibility. the court of justice's ruling defining the standby period as working time must remain the basis. i think that the commission's proposal to divide paid active and unpaid inactive working time is far from realistic. commissioner spidla, i worked a night shift at the largest accident clinic in hesse. what paramedics, nurses and ambulance drivers did there was highly active emergency response. the short breaks between missions were not enough to regenerate. employees are not only entitled to job security and job satisfaction in hospitals. the directive does not apply to fire services, including those at airports, and to emergency and security services in environmentally sensitive companies. i've spoken to all of them. i know the financial problems of hospitals. but they must also - as in other areas - find intelligent ways to save costs, better coordinate the work of their skilled staff and make better use of technical facilities. let's not forget that there are other costs that come with having a staff that is so overworked on a daily basis that they are at risk of permanent health damage, not to mention possible misdiagnosis or inadequate treatment by overtired staff. putting patients at such risk is unacceptable!
i have to say, madam president, i'm focusing on the standby. many colleagues are asking why there seems to be a particular problem in my country, because, as in the case of germany after the ecj judgments, the hospital authorities are taking a strong stance against the proposed amendment to the social affairs committee. therefore, it is clear that: germany has also been implementing ecj legislation since 2004. since then, the entire period of on-call duty has been regarded as working time under the german labour code, just as the report by mr cercas demands. secondly, it is also possible in practice without any major problems. this is evidenced by a study cited by the german federal minister of health. the necessary introduction of innovative working time models and the partial re-employment of doctors have been supported financially in my country since 2003. of course, problems can still arise. but that is precisely why our committee wants the opening clause, which allows for different arrangements for the calculation of periods of inactivity to be made by collective agreement and, if necessary, by law. the problem is not the european working time directive but the inability of the german hospital system to reform. for example, in germany, a region which is much smaller than sweden, has much more hospital beds and hospitals. and the emergency room is about patient safety. prolonged wakefulness for more than 24 hours has the same negative effects as a blood alcohol level of 1 per mille. but doctors often work 30 hours a day, and that needs to change.
we as members of the european parliament have a responsibility to ensure that the people of europe have a good chance of a future. and that includes protecting their workers' rights, their rights in the workplace. there must be rules for that, yes, but what are they? how many? how detailed? the central task, i think, is - and i have heard this repeatedly over the last year - that we first of all make sure that they keep their jobs or have jobs at all. and then i see a directive on working time being put forward, which is being made worse by the relevant committees of parliament, and made worse by the criteria of the lisbon strategy. that means we're going to make more regulations! we will not have less regulation, we will not have more flexibility, but the opposite will be the case. i'm gonna try to tie this to a few questions. firstly, why do we have to dictate in europe what the emergency services look like? does this have to be the same in every hospital, in every city, in every country in europe? why would you do that? the truth is that the situation in a trauma hospital, where you have to go out more often at night, is different from that in an orthopedic clinic, where at night everything sleeps! it is not appropriate to put all this on the back burner. it's wrong! secondly, why can the extension of working time be regulated only by collective agreement? why can't an individual worker make an agreement for himself? who gives us the right to forbid workers from making their own agreements on their place of work and working hours? i know young doctors who would like to work a little longer in the future and earn a few more marks because they are rebuilding their lives, because they have just built a house. and we want to ban that in the future? what right do you have? and why do we now want to impose strict working hours on family members? why do we not want to allow the proven flexibility of family farms to be maintained in the future? different work situations require different solutions! if we do not do this, we will not be doing justice to the people and we will be doing europe a disservice!

president of afghanistan. mr president, honourable members of the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen, i am delighted and honoured to address this distinguished gathering, particularly as this is my first visit to the european parliament. it gives me great confidence for the future of afghanistan and our region to see the countries of europe come together here in a spirit of unity and cooperation. it was not long ago that the iron curtain divided europe into west and east. yet, today, that curtain has been removed to reveal a mosaic, where each piece retains a distinct identity, but together form a greater entity. two days ago, europe celebrated the 60th anniversary of the victory in europe day, the anniversary of europe’s new beginning. while in the past, european conflicts had global implications, today european cooperation is improving lives and is a source of admiration across the world. as you rebuilt after the second world war, you had security guarantees, the marshall plan, and an international long-term commitment. we, the people of afghanistan, are also grateful for the international security and economic support we have received over the last three years. the european union, in particular, has been one of the largest supporters of afghanistan. we are grateful for your generous contributions, the commitment of troops from your nations, and the technical assistance you have provided and continue to provide. most importantly, you show us what our region’s future could be: a future of peace, a future of unity, and a future of cooperation. afghanistan was one of the least-developed countries, even before its invasion by the former soviet union. ten years of fighting the soviet invasion, followed by more than a decade of foreign interference and factional conflict, further impoverished our country. our infrastructure was almost totally destroyed, our communities devastated and our state institutions crippled. the long and dark years of suffering, however, did not dampen our aspirations to build a stable, democratic and prosperous afghanistan. given that opportunity in 2001, the people of afghanistan enthusiastically began the process of rebuilding our country. today, we have an enlightened and progressive constitution which safeguards human rights, guaranteeing the equality of men and women, provides for a free-market economy and creates a framework for responsible government. the first presidential election in our history was held last october in which more than eight million people participated. the success of the election graphically illustrated the defeat of terrorism in afghanistan. (applause)in particular, the massive participation by the women of afghanistan, 42% of the national turnout, demonstrated emphatically that a new era of social and political rights for women had arrived. (applause)here, i would like to narrate a story to you that i witnessed about two and a half months ago. two and a half months ago, i was having lunch with a group of tribal elders from a very conservative part of afghanistan, and i noticed that with these tribal elders and clergy there were women. i felt as if the women were from the urban parts of the country, and i greeted the tribal chiefs by name. i knew many of them by name, and i said: ‘mr so-and-so welcome and how are you?’. when i had finished greeting the men, i said to the ladies: ‘welcome and good to see you’. suddenly one of the ladies got up and said: ‘mr president, you greeted the men by name. you did not greet us by name’. i was shocked. i said: ‘well, madam, i am sorry i did not know your name’. she said: ‘you know, you are elected because of our vote. next time i see you, you had better know my name or you will not be elected!’. (laughter and applause) that is the change in afghanistan for which we are very happy. the presence of the international security assistance force, led by europe from the beginning, has provided us with a secure environment to exercise our political rights. with help from europe and others in the international community, we have trained a new police force of some 50 000, along with a special force to conduct counter-narcotics operations. the new afghan national army, currently 20 000 strong, is increasingly taking responsibility for supporting security across the country. we are accelerating the disarmament process, disarming both regular armed forces and illegal armed groups. more than 50 000 former combatants have been disarmed, and over 95% of the heavy weaponry has been cantoned. extensive reforms are also under way in other sectors, including the judiciary and the civil service – the administration. our judicial system is gradually recovering in effectiveness and credibility from the damages of war. institutions of government and civil society are gaining increasingly in strength, giving the citizens more confidence, more services and more rights to enjoy. the afghan independent human rights commission continues the important work of promoting human rights throughout the country. thanks to the open political atmosphere in afghanistan, the free press has enjoyed great development and success, as demonstrated by the publication of more than 300 independent papers, more than 30 independent radio stations and four independent television channels in less than two years. we realised that political and security developments can be sustained only with corresponding improvements in the economic area. over the last three years, we have introduced a new currency, stabilised inflation and enacted numerous legal and administrative reforms to simplify our customs and investment processes. as a result, hundreds of millions of dollars in international investment have flowed into afghanistan. certain industries, such as the hospitality sector, banks and mobile communications, have particularly benefited. wages have increased, as has trade and commerce with countries of the region, notably pakistan, iran, tajikistan, china and beyond. i should like to give an example here of the changes that have occurred. three years ago, afghanistan’s trade with pakistan was less than usd 50 million. last year, this trade – in less than three years – surpassed usd 1 billion. today, trade between pakistan and afghanistan amounts to usd 1 billion. the same applies to china and other countries around us. much has been done so far, but daunting challenges remain ahead of us. afghanistan’s social development indicators are still dismal: we have one of the highest infant mortality rates and one of the lowest life expectancy rates in the world; and we have unacceptable levels of illiteracy, particularly among women. sadly, these social indicators place our country close to the bottom of the human development index: in fact, fifth from the bottom. terrorism has been defeated as a force, but its residues disturb our peace and tranquillity. while critical steps to establish an effective government have been taken, the ability of the new institutions to provide security and help lift the population out of extreme poverty is far from adequate. poppy cultivation and the drug economy are still afflicting our communities and remain obstacles to afghanistan’s stability. i wish to depart from my prepared speech to explain to you what is happening in afghanistan with regard to the drug economy – the cultivation of poppies. thirty years ago, when the former soviet union invaded afghanistan, afghanistan was a somewhat well-to-do agrarian society. in the years of conflict, drought and difficulties for the afghan people, afghan men and women – families, fathers, mothers, daughters – had no hope for the future. a father, a mother did not know whether their son or daughter would be alive or dead the next day; whether they would have food to eat or be hungry. in that situation, people destroyed vineyards and replaced them with poppies; people destroyed pomegranate orchards and replaced them with poppies; people destroyed apricot orchards and replaced them with poppies, because poppies were easy to grow – there was not much need for irrigation – and easy to sell. therefore, because of a lack of confidence in the future and a lack of means, society became involved in that easy crop. last year, we began action against poppy cultivation, and the people responded because they have more hope for the future: they have more confidence in their country and in themselves. we hope that there will be a considerable reduction in poppy cultivation this year in afghanistan, a great part of it voluntarily. my hope, and that of the afghan people, is that the international community will continue to assist us in decreasing poppy cultivation in afghanistan and to replace it with legitimate forms of agriculture. in other words, to replace it with alternative forms of livelihood, so that our people can return to growing vines, pomegranates, apricots and the other agricultural products which afghanistan is very good at cultivating. (applause) afghanistan produces the best pomegranates, the best foods; it can compete in international markets. please continue to help us bring a legitimate economy to the afghan people again. nobody wants to have a bad name in the world, and afghanistan is no exception. afghanistan wants to live an honourable life, a life where it can return to generating its own legitimate income. i am grateful for what you have done for us so far, but please continue to help us. parliamentary elections in september will mark the culmination of the bonn process in afghanistan. the afghan constitution decrees that at least 27% of members of the afghan parliament should be women. (applause) yet, while we will have met all the benchmarks set out in the bonn agreement by the end of september, we will only be at the beginning of a long road towards achieving the vision set out for afghanistan in that document. the end of the bonn process, therefore, must not be the end of your commitment to and support for afghanistan, but the beginning of a long-term and more comprehensive partnership. the end of the bonn process will not mean the success of afghanistan or the total success of afghanistan. the end of the bonn process, the coming of the parliament, will lay the foundations for the success of afghanistan but not constitute success itself. success itself will take many more years to come, and for that your help is needed. from europe, we need support and the assurance that afghanistan will continue to receive assistance in a sustainable manner. in particular, as you deliberate here about the european union’s future international commitments, i hope you will see the need for multi-year pledges of aid to afghanistan to support our efforts at rebuilding our country. we also need the united nations, the united states, japan and others who have assisted us so far to reaffirm their commitment to partnership with afghanistan: a partnership that is essential if afghanistan is to achieve lasting stability, democratisation and development. allow me to take this opportunity to thank you once again, on behalf of the afghan people, for the generous support that the european union, as one of the largest donors to afghanistan, has provided over the last three years. the people of afghanistan are especially grateful to your sons and daughters in uniform who are serving courageously in our country. to those who have given their lives to provide us with security, we offer once again our gratitude, our prayers and our pledge that we will never forget. today in afghanistan, in a country which, not long ago, was totally isolated from the world, something unprecedented is taking place. in a true spirit of cooperation, people from all corners of the world, people from different faiths, cultures and backgrounds, are together helping to secure the lives of the afghan people and rebuild our country. it is clear that without this cooperation afghans would never have accomplished what we have accomplished over the past three years. afghanistan is as much in need of your help today as europe was 60 years ago. then, a long-term commitment from your friends around the world gave you the support you needed to rebuild your countries, your lives. today, we are asking for that same opportunity. thank you for what you have done so far for us. we are very grateful. climate regime that is not only a decisive step in winning our battle against climate change, but also allows us to do so in a way that strengthens our competitiveness in clean technologies. such a regime will get us much further – also in climate terms – than trade sanctions. with regard to the developing countries, i agree about the importance of assisting developing countries to adapt to the president of the council. mr president, on the question of small arms and light weapons (salw), we all know that the world is faced with many regional conflicts in which these weapons, sometimes even used by children, create extremely dangerous and destructive situations. the european union therefore supports the secretary-general's call for the development of long-term strategies to end the scourge of the illicit proliferation of small arms. one such strategy is the united nations programme of action to prevent, combat and eliminate the illicit trade in small arms in all its aspects. it was adopted on 20 july 2001 and the european union is actively working to implement its recommendations at national, regional and global levels. the consequences of the illicit manufacture, transfer and trafficking of small arms and light weapons, as well as their excessive accumulation and uncontrolled spread, are at the heart of four of the five major challenges identified in the security strategy adopted by the european council in 2003. small arms and light weapons contribute to the escalation of terrorism and organised crime and are a major factor in the outbreak and spread of conflict and the collapse of state structures. as the european strategy points out, conflicts in which these weapons were by far the main instrument have since 1990 claimed the lives of nearly four million people and forced more than 18 million others to flee their homes or their countries. the increasing access of non-state actors to these arms stocks has changed the nature and duration of conflicts. in the face of this situation, which may jeopardise our own security, the european union must react in close cooperation with its international partners. we are therefore actively preparing for the second biennial meeting of states to implement the un programme of action on salw, to be held in new york in mid-july. in the context of preparing for this important event, the presidency has drawn up a list of topics which should be dealt with as a matter of priority in the relevant international fora. the list, which is in the process of being approved, includes, inter alia, illicit salw brokering, transfer control, end-use verification, security-development link, military and security force arms management, the establishment of a mechanism to implement the un action plan, civilian possession of small arms, transfer to non-state actors and technical assistance for submission and reporting. the european union stresses in particular the importance of establishing a group of governmental experts in the immediate wake of the review conference of the action programme to be held in 2006 in order to consider further measures to strengthen international cooperation aimed at preventing, combating and eliminating the illicit trafficking in small arms and light weapons. another key element of our priorities is the negotiation of an international instrument for the identification and tracing of these weapons. the european union gives its full support to the open-ended working party responsible for negotiating this instrument. in the two sessions held so far by this group of diplomats and experts, the european union and the other parties have set out and confirmed their priorities on the various aspects, including the nature of the instrument, its scope and definitions, the marking and tracing of small arms and ammunition, and registration and international cooperation. the european union notes the progress made in these negotiations, but regrets that the participating states remain divided on the two major issues of the nature of the instrument and the inclusion of munitions. the european union is working to secure the adoption of a legally binding instrument to supplement the united nations protocol against the illicit manufacture and trafficking of firearms. it also insists that the instrument should include appropriate provisions on ammunition. indeed, only a steady supply of ammunition allows illicit small arms and light weapons to continue to wreak havoc. but if we can stop the smuggling of munitions, we can silence these weapons. if the group reaches a positive result at its final session in june 2005, the union will make every effort to ensure the swift entry into force of this instrument. as you know, honourable members, the european union is also very active in this area, both internally and in its bilateral assistance to third countries. within the union itself, in 1998, the council adopted the code of conduct on conventional arms exports. it allows for improved exchange of information between member states and enhanced mutual understanding of their export control policies, including provisions on the requirement of an end-user certificate or appropriate documents or a form of official authorisation issued by the country of final destination, which must be subject to close scrutiny. as you know, the code of conduct is currently under review; it will cover virtually all activities related to, or having a direct or indirect connection with, arms transfers. as regards assistance to third countries, following a number of specific joint actions, the european union adopted a joint action in 2002 and launched specific actions on the basis of this action on arms collection and destruction projects in africa, asia, latin america and the balkans. the council is prepared to report regularly to your parliament on these weapons and to work closely with it.
member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european commission naturally welcomes the constant efforts of the united nations and other actors to combat the serious effects of the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons. we welcome the renewed attention to this issue and look forward to participating in the biennial meeting of the states in new york city in july 2005. we are very grateful to the european parliament for taking the initiative to draw attention to this upcoming event. the commission will study very carefully the proposals which are formulated in the parliamentary resolutions. we recognise that the accumulation and spread of these weapons exacerbate conflicts, fuel terrorism, hamper post-conflict reconstruction efforts and reduce prospects for sustainable development. it is therefore essential to use multinational partnerships combining prevention and response measures to address these issues and it is also essential to use the instruments of the united nations to this end. the effectiveness of the fight against the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons depends on communication and cooperation between states. the commission, which favours a multilateral approach, has involved several of these services in various projects in this field. it is important to stress that to remedy this problem, action must be taken in several directions, ranging from development aid proper to security sector reform and the effective destruction of armaments. some of these areas fall within the community's competence, others unfortunately do not. in its programme for the prevention of violent conflict, the european union recognises that by working to eliminate the destabilising and conflict-inducing source of small arms, it would make a major contribution to preventing further violence. the european union is striving to achieve this through international cooperation, financial and technical assistance programmes and effective arms control. the commission is financing a number of actions under the european development fund to help demobilize and reintegrate former combatants into society and to collect and destroy these weapons. in many cases, these actions are implemented through specific demobilisation, disarmament and reintegration programmes. in other cases, however, the reintegration of former combatants has been integrated into larger post-conflict development/rehabilitation programmes. these programmes aim to improve overall economic and social structures in conflict-affected areas, contributing to the reintegration of former combatants and their families into civilian life. a number of issues related to the transfrontier transfer of these weapons are also currently being considered for next year's conference. the commission is also considering the possibility of a new agreement on the trade in arms. the commission will actively participate in the council's debate on these issues. it is premature to go into these points in detail now, as some of them will require a thorough study involving several commissioners. the european union has also repeatedly called for legally binding instruments on arms brokering, marking and tracing of small arms and light weapons at the united nations conference and the monitoring meeting on the illicit trade in small arms in 2001 and 2003.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the number of 4 million victims just mentioned by the president-in-office of the council shows how important this issue is. we've all made a decision to prevent small arms from falling into the wrong hands. we in europe, in the european union, have the monopoly of violence of the state, and that is a great achievement. we have different conditions here than in the united states, where this is not the case in the same way. this means that the use of small arms is reserved for soldiers and police officers and that there are special regulations for hunters and for sport shooters. it is of the utmost importance that every single weapon in our european union is actually registered, that we know where it comes from. the problem arises when these weapons also reach countries outside the european community. that is why it is so important that the code on arms exports, as it is now, be further tightened and that we ensure that at least the supply of arms to areas of tension - where this incredible number of victims actually arises - is prevented as far as possible. this includes the development of a system for tracing these weapons, the registration of each sale or acquisition of these weapons, i.e. in an international register, and the possibility of tracing a particular weapon back to its origin, to the manufacturer, and the identification of those responsible for the sale and transfer of these weapons. the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the projects initiated by the united nations are actually carried forward and finally brought to fruition.

other objectives as well. that's not right. if we start to be specific about this and say, for example, that only certain authorities are allowed to access the confidential data of individuals and not other authorities, we start to make firm points. i'll just give you an example. the ministers of the interior have asked me to develop greater powers of access for the investigating authorities to existing databases. my answer is that the right of access can be extended if we simultaneously increase the protection of that data with a third pillar proposal, which i assure you will be tabled by the end of this year. i think the answer is "we must be clear". there are narrowly defined goals, as the legal scholars say, so if access to data is allowed for one goal, it cannot be allowed for another goal. this is the starting point on which i started working. the last theme: victims of crime: we will also be putting forward proposals to help financially, not directly individual victims, but for example organisations and institutions that are concerned with the care and psychological care of those who escape violence, trafficking in human beings, who escape traffickers. there are many forms of assistance, including concrete assistance, to individual persons who have been victims of crime. we cannot have individual funding relationships but we can develop them through specific institutions and organisations; we will be concerned with alleviating the consequences for those who have suffered the tragedy of crime.

question no 29 by eoin ryan (h-0350/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: imports of textiles since the expiry of the international textile quota system on 1 january 2005, and due to lower labour and production costs, exports of certain chinese garments to europe have increased by more than 500%. does the commission accept that excessive imports of textiles from china are causing market distortions and that thousands of jobs in the textile industry could be at risk if china does not limit its imports? will the commission now invoke wto rules and introduce an annual limit on chinese imports of 7.5% until 2008?
member of the commission. the european union is abiding by the rules of the wto, which set out quite clearly what should be done at this particular stage. that is why commissioner mandelson awaited factual information regarding exports from china into the european union for the first three months of this year. the commission has now initiated further action. as a result of this particular action, a number of categories are now being investigated. however, as my colleague mr mandelson has pointed out, under the agreement in the wto, member states throughout the union have had ten years to prepare for this. therefore, it should not have come as a great surprise – or any surprise at all – that the chinese exporters would avail of the opportunity. furthermore, irrespective of what action might result as a consequence of the investigation now taking place, it can only last until 31 december 2008 in any event. i am not anticipating what decision might be reached as a result of these investigations; however, whatever happens, this can only last until the end of 2008. furthermore, the honourable member raised the question of customs cooperation. the fact-gathering that the commission’s services have done gives details from all the member states as to what the volume of imports from china has been in the first few months of this year. there has been good customs cooperation between the authorities in the relevant member states and the commission in order to provide that particular precise information on the real data regarding imports.
question no 30 by mr evans (h-0285/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: protection of air passengers in the event of insolvency many air passengers who book separately a flight and a hotel on the internet instead of a package holiday do not have adequate protection against being stranded in another country or losing their money in the event of the airline's insolvency. the european commission stated on 29 march 2005 that it was looking into the problem and would consider the need for new legislation. could the commission say when the study will be completed and when proposals will be made to protect the millions of eu citizens who book their travels online?
member of the commission. the honourable member is right in highlighting this particular lacuna in the existing legislation. as he will know, the package travel directive covers travel as part of the total package. however, as he has pointed out, in the specific instance where a consumer has purchased his or her flight separately from the package, it is not covered. that means that the difficulties mentioned can arise. that is why the commission carried out a study in this particular area. the first part of the consultancy is being done by commissioner barrot, and will cover the general review of regulations in this regard. the second part will deal with the possibility of bankruptcies and what should be done when they occur. i should also point out that dg sanco is carrying out an ongoing review of the package travel directive, which will also deal with this issue. since 2000 there have been 40 such bankruptcies, but the method of dealing with them varies between member states. some member states take it upon themselves to look after their stranded nationals. others have agreements with each other. therefore, it is necessary that we review this in its entirety. hopefully, we will have the consultancy study by this summer. commissioner barrot will then propose some amendments, if he thinks necessary, on the basis of the study.
member of the commission. i should like to point out that, whether or not one has insurance, it does not necessarily mean the standard passenger involved would be flown back. he or she might have the insurance to get compensation later, but it would be no use to him or her when the actual event occurs. the study being done will look at all aspects and i am sure we will put forward proposals to address some of these problems. as you know, one of the great successes of opening up markets in europe in recent years has been the airline industry. people can fly around europe now for very little, compared to a short number of years ago, and that has been good for consumers in general. of that there is no doubt. all these matters will be looked at in the consultancy study.
question no 31 by mr giorgos dimitrakopoulos (h-0288/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: relevance threshold lawwhy did the european commission not examine, in accordance with articles 1 to 5 of the european constitution, the possibility of discussing the points of disagreement in the relevance threshold law at expert level with a three-person panel appointed by the greek government, following the model of the well-known european arbitration procedure, before sending its reasoned opinion or reply to the greek government's letter of 6 april 2005?
member of the commission. it has been pointed out to the greek authorities that the commission believes that this law infringes both the eu directives and the treaty itself. we have pointed out to the greek authorities that neither the article in the constitution nor the law are compatible with either the eu directive or with the treaty provisions. we also pointed out that the same applied to the previous law, which was not implemented or executed. we sent a letter of formal notice to the greek authorities on 23 march, they replied on the same date. from that, we saw the case they had put forward. then, on 28 april, we sent our reasoned opinion. that is the situation. of course, we need to have dialogue with the greek authorities, but they know our position on this matter.

vice-president of the commission. not only that, but by putting it in the constitution, these rules and fundamental rights will be legally enforceable to european citizens. that is another argument that has to be put to our citizens. we try to do it in different ways. the best way is often to show the text as it is so that people can read for themselves what are actually set out as fundamental rights for european citizens and explain what that means. we can also do that through information on the web-page or other information materials that we have. there is a constant dialogue with citizens in trying to explain and discuss it with them. you did that successfully in spain. we are grateful to spain for that. you set an example. in many member states they actually advertise the full text of the constitution, including the fundamental rights.
question no 33 by mr bernd posselt (h-0281/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: commission communication there is growing criticism of the commission's communication activities. what steps does it plan to take to improve relations with the media and to bring publicity about the eu closer to the citizen?
vice-president of the commission. the barroso commission has proposed a partnership for a renewed european order to tackle the complex challenges ahead, where vision, leadership and delivery are the key elements for building renewed trust and confidence. the only way to develop this partnership is by bringing in the european citizens and taking their interests into account. the first responsibility of the present commission is, therefore, to connect with citizens. let me add immediately that this is not just the commission’s responsibility. in fact, it is very much the responsibility of all players: parliament, the council and the member state governments. the commission will, therefore, put forward a white paper on communication, which will address the role of all involved and which will give the other institutions the possibility to define and organise their input. the commission for its part will pursue a new approach on communication, which will focus on the need to interest europeans in eu politics. this demand-driven communication approach has to involve a better understanding of target audiences and those who act as multipliers, a better use of modern and effective communication tools and techniques, and a more professional attitude to all our communication work. what the commission will have to do first is to improve its listening process. the commission needs to make better use of its polling and intelligence services – if i may call them that – in its consultation procedures and to use its communication tools according to the needs and interests of its audiences. in order to reach people, the communication of political priorities will be adapted to demographic and national specificities, instead of taking the classical one-size-fits-all approach. our representation offices in the member states will have a central role to play here. the commission will explain its policies and their impact on eu citizens’ daily lives and communicate the tangible benefits of europe rather than overload people with technical information. last, but not least, the commission will encourage and support efforts to establish and improve a dialogue with europeans. the commission will, therefore, need to professionalise its communication activities. that involves improving research, planning, coordination and evaluation of communication activities and making better use of the excellent communication tools the commission has at its disposal and the representations in the 25 member states. communication will be integrated into the commission’s working culture and into policy formulation from the very beginning, and this needs to be maintained throughout the whole political process. since communication is an across-the-board challenge, all actors – from the european institutions and member states to civil society and the media – have a role to play. interinstitutional cooperation is a key element. the commission has kept parliament regularly informed on the development of the communication strategy, which was also discussed at the last meeting of the interinstitutional group on information and in the committee on culture and education during the discussion on the herrero-tejedor report. the commission will invite the european parliament and the council to comment on its white paper. the commission will also continue to improve relations with the media, in particular regional and local media in the member states, as a key element for ensuring that information reaches the citizens.

guarantee payments, liability payments and even a continuing training obligation may be required if necessary. the debate on the future of the community is a debate on the future of europe. the council was divided between the first and second readings and showed a certain hesitancy. i would like to emphasize that it is not luxembourg, but the council as a whole. it is not true that a three-month course at a technical college is sufficient for a heating engineer to be able to work afterwards. however, despite all the controversy in certain newspapers and especially from certain trade associations: the result is a success! it is feasible, it is important for the opportunities in the single market and for the citizens. we should now do everything we can to seize these opportunities and enable citizens to experience europe as we have always imagined it.
the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. i would like to begin by emphasizing the clear desire of all the parties to reach a good agreement on this difficult matter. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr zappalà, and my colleagues from the various groups, mrs weiler, mr wuermeling and my own colleague, mr manders. the cooperation was really very constructive. this is also true of the commission and the council in the final phase. i think there are three main points which we are now able to achieve with the directive. firstly, we are moving further towards the completion of the internal market. secondly, we are doing something for consumer protection. thirdly, we are actively contributing to the reduction of bureaucracy. the first point is the completion of the internal market. the vocational qualifications directive is an essential step towards overcoming the de facto limits of free movement and freedom to provide services in our common internal market. it is therefore of crucial importance for improving the mobility of union citizens. the directive is also to be seen in the context of the freedom to provide services. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's citizens are able to travel freely, without complaints or discrimination, to the countries of the union, either to settle there or to offer their services temporarily. at the same time, everything that is subject to the specific provisions of this directive is excluded from the scope of the much-discussed services directive. i hope that our agreement here will help to make the debate on this important project more concrete. second point: consumer protection: while the services directive will regulate the conditions under which a service provider may operate, the aim here is to ensure the necessary level of professional qualifications. this is already an important objective in terms of protecting the european consumer, namely to guarantee that service providers always act only in accordance with their respective recognised qualifications. we have succeeded in introducing a safeguard against the stealthy use of qualifications by excluding qualification shopping. this is also an important aspect of consumer protection. i would like to say again in this context that i am very pleased that the trade unions have been able to be involved in the comitology procedure. your knowledge will be very valuable. it is important, however, that most craft professions should be included in annex ii in order to ensure that their specific qualifications are properly recognised. third point: reduction of bureaucracy: in recent years, the existing rules on professional recognition have become a patchwork of parallel rules and variations which have proved to be complicated, confusing and difficult for the citizen to handle. the regulatory objective of this directive, which aims to bring together the different legislative acts, is a necessary paradigm shift from the unmanageable multiplicity of regulatory approaches to a general approach which finally subjects different professions to a single legal regime linked to certain levels of qualification and thus will also contribute to deregulation. the adoption of this draft directive tomorrow is therefore a decisive step towards the completion of the european internal market, which my group will support. i think that we should not have this debate in strasbourg, but in brussels.
the commission is therefore proposing to extend the period of validity of the directive to the period of 1 january 1999. the commission has already made a number of proposals. i am glad that the commissioner has taken this opportunity to say that the commission is very much aware of the problems which the european parliament is facing in the field of the internal market. the new directive replaces a bundle of 15 old directives and thus provides for greater transparency and legal certainty. this directive will make it easier for eu citizens to take up their work opportunities in other european countries, which is becoming increasingly important in the light of the difficult labour market situation in many member states. unjustified restrictions on mobility due to bureaucratic over-regulation in member states are being reduced, but there is still no need to fear a race to the bottom in qualifications. if you are settling permanently, you may need to pass an aptitude test or undergo further training. the notification is made in the host country and not in the country of origin as originally planned. the right of inspection is also retained by the country of destination under the directive. for some particularly sensitive fields, such as doctors, pharmacists, midwives and architects, minimum standards are set at european level and the level of qualification is also guaranteed by five levels of professional qualification according to the length and level of training. in addition, there is a duty to inform the customer or consumer of one's qualifications. we believe that this directive has struck a good balance between freedom of movement and quality protection. i hope that this balance will not be jeopardised by the proposed services directive.

the next item is the statements by the council and the commission on the world bank.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. the biggest problem in the world bank's policy is structural adjustment policy. decades of structural adjustment programmes by the world bank have often produced grotesque results, such as the privatisation of services. take the water supply as an example. water supply is being privatized, infrastructure is being built, but the price of water is rising so much that the poorest of the poor can no longer afford it. or take trade policy. the forced liberalization and market opening as conditions for lending weakens the bargaining power of developing countries in the wto's world trade rounds. all this is contrary to the objectives of european development policy, which, for example, places water at the centre of the fight against poverty or, as we say, of strengthening the negotiating capacity of developing countries in world trade negotiations. so this is the central lever that the world bank needs to change its policy. the reform which is now beginning will not change anything in principle. the so-called selective lending policy which is now to be re-introduced is basically a bankruptcy declaration for over 30 years of world bank policy. in short, this new policy means: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. those who have not properly followed this policy should receive even less money. this division into good performers and bad performers is highly problematic. i believe it is the task of the commission and the council to ensure and to insist that this classification is at least based on clear, transparent and comprehensible criteria, and also to insist that the world bank must fundamentally change its strategy for combating poverty in the context of the un reform, in the context of the millennium development goals.
president of the council. mr president, i should first like to thank the honourable members for this extremely interesting debate and for the very useful messages they have sent to the leadership of the council and also of the commission. i'll pick out two or three questions. i shall begin with the weight of the union in financial institutions, and particularly in the world bank. let me speak for a moment on behalf of the presidency and not as a representative of the council. it is true that if we were shareholders in a private company, we would be mismanaging our share of the capital in that company. but as you know, it's a little bit more complicated and we're not in that configuration. we are in another configuration, political in nature. nevertheless, i must say that the message that the european union must coordinate its positions better within these organisations, and in particular within the world bank, is absolutely necessary because, as many of you have said, we are far below our real weight, our financial weight, but also our political weight. i would like to point out that there may be an article in the treaty which should be read twice and perhaps used as a follow-up to the debate we had this morning. i am referring to article 99 of the treaty, which is also included in the draft constitution and which provides that the member states may, on the basis of a proposal, coordinate their positions more closely within the financial institutions and international financial conferences. i therefore believe that the question of the union's representation in international forums -
