the next item is the statement by the council and the commission on the situation in kyrgyzstan and central asia.
president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am particularly pleased to have the opportunity to speak on behalf of the council on these important subjects concerning this vital region of central asia. this region is important for the european union from many points of view: geopolitical, geostrategic and economic. despite a number of recent improvements, the situation in kyrgyzstan remains critical. the new political dynamic is structured along lines of personal and regional allegiances and political parties play a purely nominal role. the presidential election is scheduled for july 10 and a runoff could take place on july 24. the risks of security issues and the uncertain economic situation could complicate the presidential campaign. the electoral campaign for the presidential elections is increasingly turning into a competition between the two main candidates on the country's political scene, namely mr. koulov and mr. akayev. the stability of the country thus depends to a large extent on a possible rapprochement between these two political leaders. a compromise between them could include a commitment to respect the election result, which should be normal in a democracy, provided the losing candidate can hold the post of prime minister. however, informal contacts between the two sides have not yet produced tangible results. in this regard, the main message of the international community, including the osce and the european union, during this presidential campaign should emphasise the importance of holding free and fair elections. however, holding democratic elections will not automatically guarantee a fully successful democratization process. several political issues will remain on the agenda, including constitutional reform, early parliamentary elections, media independence and the development of political life based on organically developed political parties. the question of constitutional reform has already been raised in the electoral debate. the parliament has set up a constitutional council, which should establish the principles of constitutional reform to be implemented after the election results. however, different political actors have quite opposite views on the matter. the economic situation is not improving significantly and public order remains precarious. the seizure of land around bishkek poses acute risks of disorder. ethnic issues are at the heart of political discussion. in general, the situation of ethnic minorities remains a cause for concern. all major international actors, including russia, are in favour of maintaining stability and internal security in kyrgyzstan. the new leadership of the country successfully maintained good relations with all its neighbouring countries, especially with kazakhstan and uzbekistan. the osce's work for kyrgyzstan will soon be finalised and the kyrgyz government is expected to approve it in the coming days. the european commission recently announced its intention to allocate eur 25 million to kyrgyzstan for 2005. as you know, the general situation in central asia remains a matter of concern. several factors create an atmosphere of uncertainty around the countries of this region. first, the most important threats to regional stability in central asia lie in the lack of economic reforms, the persistence of authoritarian regimes and the widespread presence of corruption, organised crime and drug trafficking. we discussed yesterday the question of drugs in afghanistan. these countries are on the drug trail. the political rights of the people are deteriorating in most of these countries. regional cooperation has not reached a sufficient threshold due to lack of confidence and political will among the regional state actors. the impoverishment and lack of growth in the central asian countries have exacerbated socioeconomic tensions. the geopolitical proximity of afghanistan and certain internal factors have allowed islamic extremism to spread and, as i have just pointed out, facilitated drug trafficking. potential conflicts within and between the states of the region can be fuelled by the intermingling of ethnic minorities within the territory of these countries. there are many specific questions to be raised in relation to the situation in some countries in the region. i'll run through them in a second. the parliamentary elections in kazakhstan in september 2004 did not meet the normally accepted international standards. the opposition, despite growing support in the population, only won one seat. the current president is inclined to call for presidential elections before the end of his presidential term in january 2006. the government's grip on the legislative process, the opposition, the media, civil society and financial systems is a cause for concern. the human rights situation is deteriorating. in uzbekistan, the legal opposition was not allowed to participate in the parliamentary elections on 26 december 2004. the country's reform programme has not advanced and poverty has spread further. there is a real risk in this country that islamic fundamentalism is increasingly gaining ground among the population. in turkmenistan, the lack of freedom of expression and democratic debate, the inability to maintain an effective opposition to the government and the absence of any programme of structural reforms are major concerns. finally, in tajikistan, the situation of the country is characterized by two main problems: endemic quarrels between provinces and a prolonged economic crisis. despite the problems and difficulties of the region i have just described, the european union considers relations with the region to be of paramount importance and the european union is ready to support the transition of these countries to efficient market economies but also to functioning democracies. the european commission's deputy director-general for external relations recently visited four central asian republics. on 12 may, the eu-turkmenistan joint committee will be held in ashgabat. an ad hoc meeting will be held on the sidelines of the joint committee with the aim of advancing the dialogue on the human rights issue. a european union troika will meet representatives of the five countries of the region at the end of june in tashkent. the cooperation committee with kyrgyzstan will be held in brussels in june and the cooperation councils with kazakhstan and kyrgyzstan in july.
member of the commission. mr president, it is an honour for me to be here in this plenary session to discuss with you the situation in a region of great strategic importance: central asia and, in particular, the situation in the kyrgyz republic. following the overthrow of president akayev, following the mass protests on 24 march, which were triggered by the violation of international and osce criteria in the parliamentary elections in february and march, both the eu high representative for the common foreign and security policy, mr solana, and the commissioner for foreign affairs, mrs ferrero-waldner, who apologises for not being able to be present at this debate, have encouraged the kyrgyz republic to seek a path towards national reconciliation based on building dialogue and consensus to deepen the process of political reform. the kyrgyz republic has a unique opportunity to establish a genuine multiparty democracy in central asia and to eliminate the corruption that has contributed so much to the recent political crisis. this opportunity is in the hands of the political leaders of that country, who must demonstrate their strong commitment to real progress in the field of political reform. the best way to achieve this is to implement measures to ensure the establishment of a multiparty democracy, respect for human rights and the rule of law, in line with the international commitments undertaken by kyrgyzstan. i would like to stress that political liberalization and the preparation and holding of free, fair and transparent elections must be applied to the next presidential elections, which according to our information will be held on 10 july. the elections will be closely monitored by the union and the international community as a whole. the democratic credentials of the kyrgyz republic will improve if the interim government implements the recommendations contained in the final mission report of the osce office for human rights and democratic institutions, published in march this year. under the osce umbrella, the union is preparing, through its rapid reaction mechanism, a package of electoral assistance measures and electoral legislative reforms. the union encourages kyrgyzstan to create an environment in which the media and journalists in that country can fully exercise their rights and freedoms, in line with international commitments. i understand that the osce is in a position to provide the authorities with advice on this matter. it is important to fight corruption more effectively in all central asian countries, as it has been identified as one of the main causes of the events in kyrgyzstan. i now want to talk about cooperation between the union and all the countries of central asia. at the end of last year, the union launched an initiative to improve political dialogue with the region. to this end, the eu troika of regional directors met with their central asian counterparts in bishkek last december. this political dialogue between the european union and central asia can certainly help to change the future of relations between the two regions, provided it is developed in a constructive way. the commission welcomes the interest shown by the five central asian countries in this process. the success of the dialogue depends on the degree of involvement of both parties. in this sense, the union will always be in favour of economic liberalisation and, of course, political democratisation in central asia. the dialogue process could focus on common concerns to both regions: the fight against terrorism, drug and human trafficking, money laundering, illegal immigration, energy, transport and increased economic cooperation. political dialogue between the union and central asia would facilitate regional integration in the area and provide political guidance to cooperation between the two areas. the union is considering the next steps to be taken. the meeting between the union troika and the foreign ministers of central asia in tashkent at the end of june will be a good opportunity to continue discussions on the dialogue process. the union encourages the five central asian countries to persevere in the process of political liberalization. the only way for a country to prosper for the benefit of its citizens, to enjoy stability and security, to make a significant contribution to regional integration, is to ensure that economic development goes hand in hand with political liberalisation, the rule of law and the development of an active civil society, one of the essential components of which is freedom of the press. i am convinced that this is the best way to strengthen the ties between central asia and the union. the commission hopes for improved cooperation between the union and the caspian sea countries, as agreed at the ministerial conference on energy and transport held in baku last november. from a political point of view, energy has become a security issue. it is in the interest of both regions to cooperate in order to achieve a more efficient and deeper integration of our energy systems and markets. the intensification of cooperation between the union and central asia depends on both political and economic aspects and, in this context, the union remains ready to help this important region.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals. this region is often overlooked because it was once hidden in the darkness of the soviet union and had no independent development. today it is a region of great strategic importance - a strategic importance that has to do with the issues of gas, oil, energy supply and similar things, with the growing interest of china in this region, the emerging islamic fundamentalism and also with the fact that some of these countries are going on routes that have to do with drug trafficking. we must see that the increasingly poor development of democracy, the rule of law and human rights makes it increasingly difficult to cooperate with this region, to fulfil existing partnership and cooperation agreements or to conclude or ratify new ones, and that such regimes - as the experience of the elections in kyrgyzstan and previously in ukraine has shown - are becoming less a threat to stability and more a threat to instability. the more instability there is in such a critical geographical situation, the more our interests are affected. i would therefore like to invite us to think about this issue much more in terms of a common strategic concept than in terms of progress on individual points, and to attach importance to genuine support for the democratic process in these countries. i believe that we should try to reach an agreement in the common interest with the united states, which does not regard this country merely as a short-term base camp for afghanistan, and with russia, whose understanding of these developments is often shaped by old ideas. the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force. this is where a new emphasis should be placed.
the commission is therefore proposing to extend the period of validity of the directive to the period of 1 january 1999. the commission has already made a number of proposals. i have only a minute, so i want to focus on one aspect and emphasize what i said before: i am particularly concerned that we recognise the importance of the osce in central asia, particularly when it comes to conflict prevention, but also when it comes to crisis management, when it comes to the enforcement of the rule of law, when it comes to helping to enforce human rights and democratic standards. but also think about supporting civil society or working for minorities. we should expressly welcome the activities of the osce in this region, particularly also on the issue of election observation and preparation for the next elections in kyrgyzstan in june 2005, so that they can be held in accordance with international and european standards. in this context, the question of training the police plays a very central role, particularly in kyrgyzstan. in conclusion, i ask the council and the commission to cooperate closely with the osce. in this respect, we should draw on the experience of mr alojz peterle, the osce representative for the region.

acting president of the council mr president, mr president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, sixty years have passed since the end of the second world war. this commemoration of 8 may 1945, the date of the capitulation of the third reich, is a burning obligation and i would like to congratulate the european parliament for not failing to commemorate 8 may 1945 today. the obligation to remember is a burning obligation. it is especially ardent, i think, for those born after the second world war, the men and women of my generation. and when we remember 8 may 1945, the surrender of german democracy in 1933 and the terrible period between those two dates, we young people, at least in relation to the generation concerned, must do so with great restraint. those of us who were born after the second world war, in 1954, 1955 and later, must remember with a certain reserve because we were not the first to witness the tragedy that befell the european continent. we have not seen, as those before us have seen, the concentration camps and prisons where men were killed, tortured and humiliated to the point of utter degradation. we did not see the battlefields as they did, because we did not have to cross them, death in the soul, not to mention physical death very often. we could not and should not have seen, as they could and should have seen, the long processions of prisoners from all nations passing through europe, in effect constituting a single continental funeral procession. we who were born after the second world war were not faced with dramatic choices, either individually or collectively. we didn't have to say no, we didn't have to say yes, we could live in the post-war sun, all the dramatic choices were spared us. remembering may 8, 1945 is an act that feeds the collective memory. this is very important at a time when direct memories, where the lived experience of war or the immediate post-war - the direct lived with the package of personal experiences and noble feelings - are being transformed into history, with all that history in relation to memories involves distance and so-called objective reading grids. today, the firsthand witnesses of this terrible era in continental history are disappearing. it is moving to see the russian veterans in their trucks on red square, moving to see this long procession of those who fought for them and for us and who, even today, can no longer walk, while we all know where they are going. the obligation to remember is a burning obligation. to remember, for the men and women of my generation, also means that we must remember with restraint but also with a lot of gratitude. first of all, we should be grateful to the generation of our fathers and grandfathers who, after returning from the battlefields, from the concentration camps, from prison, had so many reasons to give up, to do nothing, to mourn their fate. but they rebuilt europe and they made europe the most beautiful continent there is. let us be grateful for the extraordinary achievement of a generation of people who had to fight and who wanted to make peace! (applause) i would like to thank when we remember, when we feel this burning obligation to remember, we must also speak the truth. may 8, 1945, was a day of liberation for europe. may 8, 1945 was also a day of defeat. but it is the defeat of fascism, the defeat of national socialism, the defeat of the capitulation of the democrats to the terror of the war that has been going on since 1933. but it is also war for germany and above all a day of liberation! (beifall) i would like the elected representatives of the german people in this house to say: never were the germans such good neighbours as they are today! (beifall) to tell the truth on 8 may, 9 may and 10 may is also to show gratitude to those who have joined forces and energies with the european forces and energies to free the european continent. i would like to say, not with a delay of 60 years but with a distance, how grateful we europeans must be to those young american and canadian soldiers who, from across the ocean, came to europe to liberate europe, unaware even of the existence of a number of countries whose liberation they helped to bring about. we should never forget that. (applause) my remarks are directed to the soldiers of the red army. what a waste! how many interrupted biographies among the russians who gave twenty-seven million lives for the freedom of europe! it is not necessary to be a fanatic, although i am, with a great love for the russian heart and for the eternal russia, to recognize that russia has earned europe. (applause) i would like to thank i would like to pay particular tribute to a european people who said no when others were tempted too often to say yes. i would like to pay tribute here today to the british people who said no and without whose contribution nothing would have been possible. (applause) i would like to thank but the freedom that was restored in early may 1945 was not the same everywhere. we in our western part of europe, comfortably established in our old democracies, could, after the second world war, live in freedom, in a newfound freedom for which we knew the price. but those who lived in central europe and those who lived in the east did not have the freedom that we have had for fifty years. (applause) they were subject to the law of another. the baltic states, whose arrival in europe i would like to welcome and to whom i would like to say how proud we are to have them with us, have been forcibly incorporated into a whole that was not theirs. they were not subject to the pax libertatis, but to the pax sovietika, which was not theirs. these peoples, these nations, who have gone from misery to misery, have suffered more than all the other europeans. (applause) the other countries of central and eastern europe have not experienced this extraordinary volume of self-determination that we have been able to experience in our region of europe. they weren't free. they were to operate under the system of principle that was imposed upon them. i say this with great sadness in my heart, all the evil that is being said today about enlargement. but now, when the second world war has finally ended, i say: long live enlargement! (applause) this post-war europe, which, without the war, could never have become the europe it is today; this europe, born of the ashes of war, would never have come into being if it had not been for the so-called founding fathers of europe - the schumans, the bechs, the adenauers, the gasperians and others - who, for the first time in the history of the continent, made of that post-war phrase 'never again war', a hope, a prayer and a programme. today we must remember with emotion and gratitude those who had the courage to say yes after saying no. they could not have done so if they had not been moved by the noble and deep feelings of their people. nothing great is done against the will of the people. the reason why europe was able to do what we did after the second world war is that the people of europe never again wanted to experience what the european continent had experienced as a tragedy, twice, in the 20th century. there are the founding fathers of europe who are known; there are the people who walked in the shadows and shared these noble sentiments, and then there are the philosophers, the thinkers, the politicians who, too often, are not remembered: leon blum, who dreamed of europe in a french prison; the great spinelli imprisoned on an italian island by the italian fascists; others who have no name but to whom we owe much. i would like to pay tribute to those who, forgotten or anonymous, made possible what was achieved after the second world war. (applause) i would like to thank there was the free part of europe and the part of europe which was paralysed by that fatal historical decree, the yalta decree, which wanted europe to be divided forever into two parts, parts which very often looked at each other as dogs of the mud and between which we were too often unable to build bridges. the cold war - that is how the other tragic period of european history was affectionately called - paralysed europe's best energies; it has not allowed europe's best talents to express all that they would have been able to do if they had been allowed to. i was born in december 1954, but i prefer to say i was born in 1955. i grew up first of all in respect for the performance of my father's generation, if i may venture this digression, which suffered a doubly terrible fate, because luxembourgers born between 1920 and 1927 were forcibly conscripted into the wehrmacht and wore a uniform that was not theirs, a uniform that served ambitions that were not theirs. terrible fate to have to wear the uniform of one who is your enemy. the same applies to the alsatians and lorrainians to whom i pay tribute. i grew up in the atmosphere of the cold war, where the world, it seemed, was easier to understand. there were those who were with us and those who were against us. we didn't know why we loved those who were with us, but we knew we had to hate the others. we knew the threat was on the other side and those on the other side thought the threat was on our side. what a waste of opportunity! what a waste of time in europe, with all this stupid post-war analysis. let us rejoice today that we no longer have to resort to the relentless logic of the cold war and that we can make peace between the two parts of europe. (applause) i would like to thank i often think - perhaps because i am not - of the wise men of europe, churchill for example. the great churchill, in 1947, when the first congress of the european movement met in the hague and when the idea of creating the council of europe was born in the face of the soviet union's refusal to allow the other countries of central and eastern europe to participate both in the marshall plan and in the construction of the council of europe, declared with this prophetic gift of his: 'we are starting today in the west what we will one day finish in the east.' ladies and gentlemen, let us be proud of what we have achieved. (applause) i would like to thank i am reminded of the words of victor hugo who, in 1949, wrote: "a day will come in europe when the only battlefield will be the opening of markets to ideas; "will come to europe the day bullets and bombs are replaced by votes". we should be proud of what we have achieved today. let us be proud to say so in the european parliament, the elected representative of the peoples of europe, whose members are the heirs of those who said no when they had to say no, the heirs of those who said yes when the only option left was yes. let us be grateful to those who said no when it was time to say no and let us be proud of all those who today say yes to the great europe, to the europe which has seen its history and its geography reconciled. let us be proud of those who do not want europe to become a free trade area and let us be proud of those who, like us, like millions of others, think that europe is a complicated continent that deserves better than a free trade area. let us be proud of the europe that those who came before us built and let us behave as worthy heirs. president of the commission. mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, dear friends, it is a great honour for me to represent the commission at this ceremony in the parliament which represents the europeans. we are looking at the past and the future at the same time today. we are here to remember, to acknowledge and also to build. but first, let's look at the past. the greatest conflict on a global scale has been a source of conflicting feelings for all who survived it. a source of relief for many, a source of exhaustion, no doubt, often a source of fear about the future, the fear that the post-war was not better and might even be worse than what had been before. that's why we remember. we remember the scale of the destruction that struck europe in particular. hardly any country has escaped unscathed. what some have called the "european civil war" has witnessed the inhumanity that man can prove to man. we in europe, who are often rightly proud of the great achievements of our civilization, our culture and the great works of the european spirit, must humbly consider that 20th century europe also experienced some of the greatest horrors that mankind has ever committed. however, we should also remember the great stories of triumph over adversity, the personal journeys which so many europeans made to find a better life, some crossing mountains and seas to reach their goal of a happy, peaceful existence. some found it simply by returning home. we remember those who did not have that chance, those for whom the light of freedom went out almost as soon as they saw it; those for whom one nightmare was replaced by another. let us recognize that something remarkable came out of the ruins of europe in 1945. let me give you a quote from one of the visionaries of that time, speaking in zurich in 1946. he said: "i am now going to say something that will astonish you. the first step in the recreation of the european family must be a partnership between france and germany. in this way only can france recover the moral and cultural leadership of europe. there can be no revival of europe without [...] a spiritually great germany. churchill was right. it's easy to forget now the courage it took to say those words at that time. what he said was astonishing. even more astonishing were the deeds that turned those words into reality. we should remember the extraordinary determination shown by robert schuman, jean monnet, konrad adenauer, alcide de gasperi and others and what they achieved, reconstructing rather than retreating into retribution. we should also remember and recognise the vision of transatlantic leaders who helped shoulder the burden of reconstruction rather than turn their backs on it. before we get too carried away, let's pause, because what the founding fathers started was remarkable but incomplete. as the commission said in its declaration of 9 may: for millions, true freedom was only to come with the fall of the berlin wall, not the end of the second world war. after 1945 they lost their liberties and opportunities almost as soon as they had regained them. in some cases they lost political control of their countries; in others, they lost their independence. for many people in europe the end of the war meant peace and freedom; but for some it meant only peace, not yet freedom. we should not forget what europe was. sixty years ago here on this continent we experienced the holocaust. about 30 years ago several countries in southern europe, including my own, were still living under dictatorships. until about 15 years ago half of europe did not enjoy freedom and democracy. that is why i have difficulty in understanding how we can fail to be optimistic about the future of europe when we see where europe is now compared to where it was only a few years ago. (applause) however, that, fortunately, was not the end of the story. what european leaders of the 1940s and 1950s built was a light and a magnet: a light through dark years for those who had no prospect of the peace, prosperity and stability that other europeans enjoyed, and an extraordinary, powerful force of attraction for those peoples and countries that were breaking free and saw the european community - as it was called then - as the catalyst for the transformation of their countries. for my generation, europe was always synonymous with democracy. as an 18-year-old, i, with others, was determined to set my own country free from a deadening, authoritarian, backward regime. that is why i and many people of my generation especially admire the extraordinary efforts of the peoples of the czech republic, estonia, hungary, latvia, lithuania, poland, slovakia, slovenia and romania and bulgaria to fight for democracy, and how they relate the very idea of europe to that of democracy. it should be, and is, with enormous pride that the european union and its institutions embrace those new members and peoples, as well as those of malta and cyprus. so this transformation is worthy of recognition and commemoration. because it appears at times to be almost forgotten. today it is too easy to take for granted the firm foundations of the new europe in which we live, a europe of freedom and shared values. that is why it must be said: the european union cannot be a victim of its own success. the integration of such a variety of members united by a common project is a truly extraordinary achievement. it is an extraordinary challenge, one which concerns us all. i am convinced that the implementation of this formidable project, which will soon involve 27 countries and 500 million people, will continue in spite of the turbulence which will inevitably arise from time to time. however, this implementation is sometimes so peacefully done that we run the risk of forgetting the foregoing. the accounts of the murderous conflicts ravaging europe seem now to be confined to the history books. they were still making the news ten years ago, when there were massacres in some balkan countries. on our continent, one can say: never again! it is easy to say this, but the history of europe has shown that we must work for peace and not have it for the sake of it. this is probably not a very good prospect, because today in europe there are problems and fears. in berlin, in the grand building which once housed what the gdr called its parliament, is inscribed the word zweifel, which means 'doubt'. there are doubts and fears, especially among young people. their fears are serious: the fear of finding or not finding a job, the fear of a more competitive world sometimes perceived as a challenge. it is more a question of the fear of finding or not finding an employment, not the fear of finding or not finding one's own country. it is now necessary to find an effective way of addressing the real or perceived difficulties connected with the integration of markets. there is no question of armed conflict between competitors who become adversaries or enemies. the european union is not a party to the treaty of rome, but it is a party to the treaty of rome. we must have the same imagination and courage. let us remember that the ambitious partnership we have concluded in europe has been the source of the peaceful revolutions which have brought freedom and democracy to millions of europeans! the example of europe - the europe of the six, the ten, the twelve, the fifteen and now the twenty-five - has been the real driving force behind democratization in southern europe, latin america and, subsequently, central and eastern europe. we must remember that freedom is the driving force behind growth, employment and investment, and that it offers a greater number of europeans the chance of a better life. the vitality of democracy and the modernity of our societies are evidence of our capacity to reinvent our continent. from its internal market to its external borders, from the promotion of internal cohesion to the defence of sustainable development and the environment, from the dimension of solidarity to that of justice in the four corners of the globe - because we do not want a europe that is self-sufficient - the european union is still building europe. it does so by taking concrete steps to improve the daily lives of its citizens. the ratification of the constitution will consolidate these achievements and lay the foundations for even more important progress in the future. today, therefore, let us remember this terrible war and its aftermath. in our work for the future, let us be inspired by the visionary ambition and determination of the leaders and citizens who have gone before us, from reconciliation to cooperation and from cooperation to the union! (applause from the centre)
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. 1945 sixty years ago europe is a field of ruins. a barbaric war has claimed over 55 million lives. millions and millions of people are uprooted, millions are displaced or displaced, fathers without sons, women without husbands, children without fathers. my father was a private soldier and went missing in late march 1945. we learned much later that he had fallen; i never saw him. in 1945, many of europe's cities were devastated. europe's economy is in ruins. the name 'europe' is a source of fear and terror throughout the world. there can be no doubt about the responsibility for the outbreak of the second world war: the national socialist regime of injustice in germany increased its racial madness and power claim to an inferno of aggression against all other peoples of europe. the holocaust of the jews of europe became his worst crime. national socialist totalitarianism led all of europe to ruin. in the end, the german people themselves became one of his victims. but few were victorious in 1945. there were lucky and unlucky survivors, some in western europe, others in central and eastern europe. in the west, with the help of the united states, a new life was born, one of freedom, respect for human dignity, democracy and a market economy based on the rule of law. winston churchill - as has been pointed out - drew up the vision of a united states of europe, and i would add that without britain europe would never be complete. after 1945, europe was rebuilt from its western atlantic edge. exhausted but happy to be free to start over, the peoples of western europe rallied. it is always robert schuman's merit to have helped the germans to make this new beginning. without france's greatness, europe would have remained an empty idea. in the midst of the new beginning of a european union with a common constitution, i would add that europe will need france's constructive cooperation more than ever in the future. (applause from the centre) the peoples of central, eastern and south-eastern europe were also filled with hope for a new beginning in 1945. as people of the same cultural area that we all share in europe, they hoped for a new chance at life in freedom and peace. they learned the hard way that peace without freedom was only half the freedom from the yoke of totalitarian injustice. the soviet takeover shattered their hopes. in 1945 the national socialist totalitarianism was defeated. but stalinist totalitarianism has divided europe and has overwhelmed the peoples of central, eastern and south-eastern europe with its unjust regimes. but there was hope among the unfortunate survivors of the second world war: the hope of a common europe, spiritually, morally and politically renewed, with prospects of prosperity for all its citizens. this hope they finally realized in a peaceful revolution and solidarność is the expression for this. but it took decades for the wall to be broken. (applause from the centre) if we are to hold this debate together today - and i have been a member of this parliament since it was first directly elected in 1979 - with dignity and the necessary seriousness, it is a happy hour for me that europe is united today and that we have among us equal colleagues from eight central european nations. (applause from the centre) in 1989 the double burden of totalitarianism in europe ended. 1989 taught us the power of europe's values for all of us and how much we always depend on the example of the brave to uphold our freedom. after 1989, europe could once again breathe with both lungs, as the unforgettable and great pope john paul ii said. (applause from the centre) the peoples of western europe have made a valuable, indispensable and lasting contribution to this process. the construction of the european union with common values, with human dignity at its core, and the transnational integration into a legally binding community of freedom were the logical response to the chance of the end of the war. the european union is a project of peace and freedom. the common path of a united europe is the opportunity and the task of all europeans. now let us build together a europe that defends its values for all its citizens. the only answer europe can give to war and totalitarianism is to continue steadily along the path of the common european union of peoples and states, with conviction and acceptance of the diversity which is europe's strength and beauty. the current debate on the european constitution is a great opportunity to reaffirm these foundations, because for the first time in european history our values, our ideals, are enshrined in a constitution. europe is not simply a political construct. europe is a spiritual habitat. the response to the terrible war, whose end we are gratefully remembering today, therefore had to be a moral response: never again unfreedom leading to war, never again war leading to unfreedom! this is the sum total of the drive to build a new europe: a europe which rejects totalitarianism, rejects nationalist arrogance, rejects egalitarian hostility to man, a europe which rejects the hegemonic aspirations of individual states, a europe which is committed to the inherent dignity of each individual, to the balance of interests between social groups and peoples, a europe of respect and diversity, indeed strength through this diversity, a europe of democracy and law. the internal reconciliation of the peoples and states of europe has made great progress. we want and must complete this work of internal reconciliation, including with the people of russia and the people of the russian federation. in the new phase of our history, however, europe will also have to seek balance in the world and with the world around us more than ever before. the wars of europe became world wars. the european union must be a win-win for the world. we can be grateful that colleagues - and i thank in particular my colleague elmar brok - have written a resolution which expresses our values tomorrow. we are thinking at this hour of all the victims of the second world war, of all the suffering and destruction. we are reminded of the close link between peace and freedom and of the need to place our work at the service of people, including dialogue between cultures. wherever we succeed in this dialogue with the world, we will defend the values that carry us into the future. so this day of remembrance can give us a new mission, a mission to contribute to a better, more peaceful and free world. (applause from the centre)

the spirit of the constitution is that the former second pillar is to be integrated into the community method with a more intergovernmental method. this is the purpose of the debates in the convention and the intergovernmental conference, namely to integrate the former second pillar into a european union with legal personality, which should act from a single point of view both internally and externally. article 296 of the constitution states that the foreign service is established by a council decision after consulting parliament and obtaining the commission's consent. that's the point today. the commission has the power to determine the profile of this external service. we in parliament were concerned that the work in the council was much more advanced, that there were deadlocks and that there were already concrete ideas, whereas in the commission the approach was too hesitant and too reserved. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. what is the administrative and financial organisation of the service? they come to our market with prices that then destroy our agriculture. you talked about proactively moving towards service. mr mandelson, we cannot all cut each other's hair, but we must also produce something! in agriculture we need services through production. we are providing a great service to european society in the form of the cultural landscape, and for that the farmers must be paid on local terms. on the world market, you can buy professors, bankers and even commissioners cheaper than the products in the agricultural sector. so we have to talk about the terms, and that means balance and fair terms. it's not easy. it is easy to define the concept of 'free' in a quantitative way, but we must try to define it in a qualitative way! it was the right move to abolish export subsidies in an area which is one of the largest importers. but to say, let the world come to us and we will stop our production, that is just nonsense! we must have a qualified external protection system, where the conditions imposed on production here and on our farmers are also applied in these countries. and we must create the conditions, the prices and the levels so that these countries can develop their economies and not be pushed below the poverty line and the farmers here are ruined! mr mandelson, i hope that we can discuss this a little longer and more intensively with you in the committee on agriculture.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you for this opportunity to respond to this debate. it is important. it raises some very serious issues for us, and i am very glad this initiative has been taken. i am also very grateful to the distinguished chairman of the committee on international trade for making his points in such a balanced and moderate, but no less serious way. i agree that we have a great challenge on our hands to bring about the progressive integration of china to the global economy and to the international trading system. we also have a responsibility to those whom you represent, and to whom others of us are accountable and are answerable, to smooth these changes in the best way we possibly can. it is true that in one sense china is testing the limits of what is acceptable, as the honourable member said. another way of putting it, however, is that china is presenting a competitive challenge to us in europe to which we need to adjust. now many have. in some cases though that adjustment remains to be made and we have to assist people in doing so. my broad view is that china’s renaissance in recent years brings with it many implications for the european union and it is essential that we equip ourselves properly to deal with these challenges. i believe that china’s astonishing economic growth will be good, not only for china but also for europe and for the rest of the world. that makes it all the more important that we build the sort of dynamic relationship with china that is based on partnership, cooperation and respect, not just for each other, but for a rules-based multilateral economic system. it is against that backcloth that i want to address two sets of issues this morning: first of all, the appropriate response we need to make to textiles imports from china and, secondly, what we need to do to continue to push china on its wto implementation record and in particular its record of enforcement of intellectual property rights. i shall first address the issue of textiles. the level of textiles imports and the dramatic increase that we have seen since the beginning of this year, when textile quotas were finally removed, has become a very sensitive topic in many of our member states. there are many who have serious concerns and anxieties. it is clear why and i understand those anxieties. i am confident that our response is both appropriate and proportionate, but also legally defensible. we have to satisfy both those requirements, basing our response on facts and data. we need to act with a degree of caution, but also determination. the commission guidelines on the use of a safeguard mechanism were intended to equip us to respond effectively to any unreasonable surge in imports from china. as i am sure you know, the commission has now launched investigations into nine categories of chinese textile exports to the eu based on import statistics for the first quarter of this year. in all these categories, import volumes for chinese textiles have now risen above the ‘alert levels’ defined by the commission. i always said that i would act on the basis of the relevant data and i am doing so now. now that the alert mechanism has been activated, i have set up an experienced task force to conduct a full and rapid investigation into these named categories. it will reach its conclusions within a maximum of 60 days. this investigation will determine whether market disruption in europe and elsewhere really has occurred. we will also have to consider the actual damage to producer interests, set against the consumer benefits involved. if it proves necessary and justified, i will use the safeguard powers at our disposal. a number of other categories appear to give cause for concern, but after careful consideration i have decided that further analysis of the data is required. this is being undertaken. in addition, there have been requests for the application of the urgency procedure foreseen by the guidelines. this would mean going directly to formal consultations with china under the wto without an investigation, if there is evidence that irreparable damage will be caused to eu industry in the absence of such a course of action. my services are currently analysing these requests. in parallel, i have actively engaged with the chinese authorities to give them advance warning wherever possible, to urge them to provide concrete evidence that the measures they have put in place are having an effect, and to explore whether they cannot do more and indeed to urge them to do so. i have launched informal consultations with china in an attempt to find a sustainable solution for all parties. this was high on my agenda last week in paris when i met with the chinese trade minister bo xilai. my message to minister bo was that to avoid the eu having to take action, china needs to give a stronger response to curb its export growth in the short term. i believe that my message was received loud and clear. i have noted the statements made by the chinese prime minister wen jiabao yesterday in beijing and i would like to welcome the fact that china now understands the acute concerns of certain member states, as wen jiabao acknowledged yesterday in beijing, and that china prefers, as he said, a solution based on dialogue and cooperation. i also welcome the fact that china considers the need to resolve this issue as amongst china’s primary interests in relation to the eu. i noted with particular interest the statement by wen jiabao that, in addition to the measures already taken to curb textiles export growth, china will take even stronger measures in the near future. i welcome this, but i also believe that the effects need to be felt quickly if they are to stay our hand in any action that we might consider taking. it is imperative that china explain in detail, and quickly, the type of additional measures it intends to adopt and what consequences these will have on future trade flows. i am looking forward to receiving such information as a matter of great urgency. failing to receive such concrete information quickly would narrow the options available to the eu to resolve this issue and could leave me with no alternative other than to act under the wto. i have a team of officials in beijing this week. they are meeting chinese counterparts as we speak now, to follow up on my discussions with minister bo last week and on yesterday’s statements by prime minister wen jiabao. let me turn now to other matters concerning wto implementation. this is important because the wto agreement is the lynchpin for the development of our trade relations with china. china has made substantial progress in implementing its wto commitments, as set out in its accession agreement, but some issues still raise concerns. i am addressing these in both a bilateral and multilateral context. discussions have met with considerable success in a number of areas, in particular on coke, the construction and automobile sectors, and sanitary and phytosanitary measures. however, concerns still remain in the automobile sector, in services sectors such as banking, and in telecommunications. i raised these and pursued them when i was in beijing earlier this year and i will continue to do so. i accept that a particular area of concern is the need to ensure an adequate and efficient level of protection in china of intellectual property rights. china has shown willing, but the continuing difficulties encountered by european industry in terms of counterfeiting and piracy have made clear that more work is needed. i am addressing this issue on two fronts, using a combination of political pressure and cooperation, both bilaterally and on a multilateral level. i am determined to give practical answers to industry’s concerns. we took an important step forward when the chinese recently agreed to my proposal to set up an intellectual property working group. the intention here is to address problems in a systemic way and on a sectoral basis. it will include experts from business who know where the delivery problems in china’s laws exist. but ipr is a worldwide problem, and it therefore requires consideration on a global level. within the wto, the eu, as well as the us and japan, used the 2004 transitional review mechanism to challenge china on its implementation record of its obligations in respect of the agreement on trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights, otherwise known as trips. the answers given by china demonstrate its commitment to the fight against counterfeiting and piracy, but further efforts are obviously needed and i am committed to helping china make those further efforts. the eu has also suggested that the review mechanism could be usefully complemented by a multilateral discussion within the trips council, and i intend to follow this up. but i also believe that continuing to share our expertise by providing technical assistance on intellectual property is an important element of our work with china. we have recently concluded an ec-china agreement on customs cooperation. another example of assistance is eu financing of training on trademarks for judges. these are just two instances of the sort of cooperation that will help china build a sound and coherent enforcement system. finally, i would encourage european industry to make use of all available tools in the eu and in china to protect its own rights and put the system to the test. in conclusion, the level of cooperation and partnership that china and the eu are demonstrating in these areas are the building blocks for a dynamic and more effective relationship between us. nobody should underestimate the huge potential gains and benefits for us in europe of such a relationship growing and being soundly based. there are obviously going to be challenges ahead, and i will ensure that the eu responds in a timely and effective manner. but there will also be great opportunities for european industry and producers to supply into that rapidly expanding chinese market. if we can work together to ensure that a rules-based economic system is respected and strengthened in the dda, then the rapid economic growth in china will benefit the eu and the rest of the world. that is why in responding to the question originally put, i say again that we have to combine our short-term management of the problems that are thrown up by china’s expansion with a clear-sighted, longer-term perspective of the opportunities that china’s growth offers europe. and parliament is an expression of the culture of cooperation which respects the role of the respective institutions but seeks to deepen mutual understanding and cooperation, which is also reflected in the articles. this is the fourth agreement between the commission and parliament. i can say that agreement after agreement has gradually strengthened the role of this parliament as a chamber of citizens and, therefore, as a supervisory body of the european executive. we have made some progress on this agreement too. i would therefore like to thank the conference of presidents and in particular mrs wallström and others who have been involved in the establishment of the framework agreement. i would like to mention a few key points. the fourth framework agreement reflects precisely what we have discussed here. there are clear provisions on the political responsibility of the president and members of the commission in the event of conflicts of interest. without prejudice to the collegial nature of the commission, each member of the commission shall be responsible for acting within the scope of his or her competence. this is a very important principle, that all 25 members of the commission are individually responsible for what they do in their field. the president of the commission is responsible for the follow-up to conflicts of interest between commissioners and also for the decision to be taken. we also have clear rules on the procedure when a member of the commission resigns and is replaced by a new member. there have been long negotiations here. it is clear that a new member must also come before parliament, conduct the hearings and obtain a vote of confidence from the plenary before he can officially take up his duties. the second complex concerns cooperation in the legislative process and in budgetary decisions. i see that we have managed to get the commission and parliament to agree in advance on the annual legislative procedure and on the multiannual programming and that the commission does not publish any legislative or other major initiative before informing parliament. this is a very important point in parliament's participation in the major decisions taken by the european union! in this context, parliament is also equated with the council. we are kept fully informed of every legislative process at the same time as the council. it is also agreed that there will be a regular dialogue at the highest level every three months between the conference of presidents and the president of the commission or the vice-president responsible . i believe that this will also lead to more cooperation. the commission also undertook to provide information on the composition and work of the groups of experts at the request of the committee responsible. there are also several provisions concerning our position at international conferences. the commission will endeavour to keep parliament's delegations fully informed of the progress of these international conferences and, if possible, to involve them in the negotiating delegations. the commission also assists parliament in election observation. it systematically informs parliament of the progress of accession negotiations with candidate countries. we have codified the lamfalussy procedure. parliament would have liked more, because it applies only to securities, banks and insurance companies. we would have liked to have used this procedure in other areas. but that's probably not until the next stage. the commission is also proposing that the procedure for a framework agreement be made more transparent in the future and that the relevant bodies of parliament be involved a little earlier. but all in all, i recommend to the house that this agreement be adopted because it represents real progress, and i have already said that it is characterized by a culture of cooperation based on mutual respect, on the will to work constructively for the union's objectives. that is what the people and the citizens want from us!
president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs malmström, on this extremely comprehensive report covering all aspects of relations between the european union and russia. it goes without saying that these relations occupy a particularly important place in the external relations of the european union, a place which has become even more important since the enlargement of the eu. it is also true that much of this report was written before the summit. it will therefore be necessary to see how the analysis and presentation of this report should be supplemented in the light of the conclusions and discussions which took place at the 15th european union/russia summit in moscow on 10 may. at the summit, the european union and russia agreed on the terms of a strategic partnership which will allow cooperation to be strengthened in the four common areas: the economic area, the area of freedom, security and justice, the area of external security and, finally, the area of research, education and culture. the negotiation of the four roadmaps which identify cooperation in these four areas in a concrete way has obviously encountered difficulties, since it was intended to reorganise our relations as a whole by adopting several hundred operational points which now need to be implemented. however, we can be pleased with the result. by agreeing in moscow on an overall package of roadmaps for the four areas, russia and the european union have succeeded in taking a new step in their relations, namely the establishment of a genuine strategic partnership as decided at the st petersburg summit in may 2003. this is an undeniable success, which is not affected by the fact that the russian side mentions some difficulties in the transit of goods to kaliningrad. for president putin, the agreement on the four areas must allow, i quote, 'serious progress in the construction of a greater europe'. i believe that this is a goal we can share, provided that this great europe is based on values to which we ourselves are committed. as regards the economic area, russia renewed its agreement at the summit, which was given in 2004, to the gradual abolition of the rights of overflying siberia, which are no longer justified. negotiations on the exact terms of such a phase-out are due to be concluded in the near future and should therefore enter into force shortly. russia has called for greater cooperation in the energy sector, which is in our own interests. it presents itself as a reliable partner for the european union in this and other areas, and has committed itself to implementing the kyoto protocol, even as it threatens to withdraw if the regime is not reformed by 2012. these discussions show that the issue of global warming and the kyoto agreement, and especially what will come after the kyoto agreement, is of paramount importance and that we must therefore continue this aspect of the dialogue with the russians. russia's accession to the wto is also a prospect that must be developed rapidly, since it is a matter of once again fully integrating russia into the multilateral system, thereby subjecting it to international disciplines, in particular to trade disciplines. as regards the area of freedom, security and justice, one of the most important points in this area is certainly the one on the free movement of persons. even in the absence of concrete results on this issue at the summit, the european union continues to attach great importance to the speedy conclusion of negotiations with the russians with a view to the signing of an agreement providing for the facilitation, on the basis of strict reciprocity, of the conditions for granting short-stay visas, and also of a readmission agreement. the latter is essential for the union and there can be no visa facilitation without, at the same time, obtaining a readmission agreement. we know that the russians have expressed difficulties in this respect, but they no longer reject the conclusion of such an agreement, which they now link to the conclusion of similar agreements with their own neighbours. this is therefore a subject which must be developed continuously and in which dialogue with the russians must be actively pursued. i also welcome the signing by the russians on 18 may of the agreement on the delimitation of the borders with estonia. unfortunately, the signing of a similar agreement with latvia is still delayed and the russians must be encouraged to sign such an agreement. as regards the area of external security, we agreed with the russians at the summit that closer cooperation should make it possible to work together towards the peaceful settlement of the so-called frozen conflicts affecting our common neighbourhood, or rather, to use the wording which was finally adopted in the conclusions, 'the regions adjacent to russia and the european union'. in this context, i am thinking in particular of the transnistrian conflict in the republic of moldova. the adoption of the wording for the adjacent regions has enabled us to overcome the initial reluctance expressed by russia on this subject and i believe that both the european union and russia have much to gain from our cooperation in this region of the world where any development has direct repercussions on russia and on the union. it is also stated in the joint roadmap that all cooperation processes must be based on the sovereign decisions of the states and the text clearly recognises, and i think this is one of the most important points, that the european union and russia share the same common values. so it is these same common values which include respect for sovereign rights, but also respect for human rights and the principles of the rule of law that must guide the development of our relations with russia. let me take this opportunity to say a word about our common interests in the fight against terrorism: the fight against terrorism must be based on these values and respect the rule of law. the research, education and culture area is an important space where the russian and european peoples can meet and forge closer links, since we have a common cultural and historical heritage. in this important area, a number of initiatives need to be developed. one of them has already been decided: the opening of a european institute in moscow by 2006. i would like to conclude by stressing the importance of our overall relations with russia. we must build longterm relations of trust with this great country, which also holds the keys to the stability of our continent, based, i repeat, on democratic principles, on the values which must precisely characterize the construction of the great europe we want and which they themselves seem to want. in doing so, we cannot ignore that there is also a ruthless but constructive dialogue to be conducted on human rights issues, on issues involving freedom of the press, on other humanitarian issues that are arising in particular in regions such as chechnya. this dialogue has been initiated, particularly on human rights. it must be actively pursued as an integral part of our relations with russia, since it is in the european union's interest to have a reliable russian partner, to have a partner who contributes to the stability of our continent and who also shares the fundamental values that we want to defend on this continent. addition to our considerable humanitarian assistance. we have to create a new climate there and we also want to do a lot on the question of technical support. we want to bring people out of the northern caucasus, out of chechnya, so that they can also see a different environment. this is also very important for a future process designed to lead to reconciliation and to better social and economic conditions. of course all this should lead to free and fair elections. this should be the aim. we would also like to improve administrative and institutional structures. we have to continue our dialogue with the russian authorities on this point. we also agreed that human rights and international obligations must be respected as part of fighting terrorism in an effective and very resolute way. turning to external security, we agreed with the russian authorities that we both want an integrated europe without new dividing lines. even if the four common spaces include the notion of adjacent regions, president putin himself acknowledged that it is a common neighbourhood and we have to work within the common neighbourhood to make it a better, more stable neighbourhood for both of us. that means that we want to cooperate on the question of stability and prosperity in neighbouring countries such as ukraine, moldova and georgia, without forcing them to choose one camp. they should proceed with their internal reforms and find solutions for their very difficult problems. finally, let me underline the importance of our agreement on research, education and culture. those areas, even if they do not seem to be highlighted, are specific areas for people-to-people contacts. we want to promote more exchanges with regard to university studies and also want to work on mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the malmström report is a balancing act. it is clear to put it forward that the european union always gives priority to the countries that are members of the european union and that they are granted a special level of protection and support for historical, political and economic reasons. in this case, this applies in particular to poland and the baltic states. secondly, we must note that russia is undergoing a tremendous process of change, particularly with the dismantling of the soviet system, and that this has been successful in many areas, so that the supporters of the old soviet system no longer seem to have any real choice in russia today. thirdly, we must see that this can only work in the long term if it is based on democracy, the rule of law and human rights, and that there are criticisms to be made here. but this leads to the fourth point, which is that we must maintain a level of dialogue with russia. for this reason, we are developing a strategic partnership, as illustrated by the 'four common spaces', with a common energy policy designed to avoid unilateral dependence at our expense, a strategic partnership that is geared to the events of 2007 for which we are preparing together. the partnership and cooperation agreements will then expire, there will be elections in russia and russia's membership of the wto is also scheduled for 2007. the enlargement may be completed by then. we might even have a constitution. we must prepare ourselves sensibly for this year 2007, when all this may happen. that is why i think it is sensible, with all the necessary criticism, to attach importance to maintaining the ability to talk, in order to contribute to a sensible development of russia - member of the commission. mr president, the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing is a political priority for the european union. the commission adopted this proposal for a third directive on the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing less than a year ago! and today it is before this house. this testifies to the importance of this text. work has progressed fast because all the institutions of the european union have been fully dedicated to ensuring that the european union is equipped with state-of-the-art defences in the field. this directive builds on existing community texts and incorporates into community law the revised 40 recommendations of the financial action task force on money laundering and terrorist financing. the directive tightens the controls in the financial sector against money launderers and terrorist financers and strengthens cooperation between countries. not only will the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing benefit from this, but so will the integrity and stability of the financial sector. the eu is also setting an example for other countries in the world to follow and match. the third anti-money laundering directive will prohibit money laundering as well as terrorist financing. it is applicable to the financial sector as well as to lawyers, notaries, accountants, real estate agents and casinos, trust and company service providers as well as all providers of goods when payments are made in cash in excess of eur 15 000. these people need, firstly, to identify and verify the identity of their customer and of its beneficial owner and to monitor transactions with the customer, while taking into account a risk-based approach; secondly, to report suspicions on money laundering and terrorist financing to the national financial intelligence unit; and, thirdly, to take supporting measures, such as record keeping, training of personnel and the establishment of internal policies and procedures. the directive is completed with a section on supervision and offers the possibility to take implementing measures. with this updated system we have progressed enormously. i should like in particular to underline the following elements. the cooperation between the european parliament, the presidency and the commission on this directive has been extremely constructive. this shows not only the willingness to have a fast-track adoption at first reading, but also the priority that all of us give to combating money laundering and fighting terrorist financing. furthermore, i especially appreciated the fact that we have all shown a sincere desire to achieve a compromise on the main issues, i.e. the definition of the beneficial owner, the definition of and the application of enhanced due diligence in respect of politically exposed persons, the coverage of trusts and lawyers and last, but not least, comitology. in respect of comitology, i underline that in the actual situation the commission as a maximum is willing to accept a sunset clause. this clause provides for the suspension of the comitology procedure four years after the entry into force of the directive. in accordance with article 251 of the treaty, these measures may be renewed by parliament and the council on a proposal from the commission. i would like to thank parliament in advance for making a first reading agreement possible and in particular i would like to congratulate warmly mr nassauer, mr muscat and the shadow rapporteurs on the quality of their work and thank them for the extremely constructive spirit in which they have produced their report.
