vice-president of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i should like to take this opportunity first of all to express our sympathy and condolences to the families of the school children who were the victims of the serious road accident in the irish town of kentstown. this accident, in which five schoolchildren were killed and 46 injured, shows once again that we must do everything we can to mitigate the consequences of such accidents for the occupants. the proposals under discussion today are aimed at this. three of the proposals concern the safety of passengers in commercial vehicles, particularly buses. the fourth proposal concerns the safety of road users at particular risk in the event of a collision with vehicles equipped with bulldozers or bullbars. i would like to mention in this context that i have set up the cars 21 high-level group. the group is to present its recommendations on the future legal framework for the automotive sector by the end of the year. this will include an overview of the measures to be taken in the field of vehicle safety over the next ten years. as regards the three directives on safety belts, i thank mr costa and mr koch for their reports and for their efforts to get the three proposed directives adopted at second reading. the aim of all three directives is ultimately to make it compulsory for all cars other than passenger cars to be fitted with safety belts. you know that's been the case with passenger cars for several years now. this extension mainly concerns coaches. the aim is to prevent passengers from being thrown out of the bus in the event of an accident, which is the most serious consequence of accidents. this is only possible by installing safety belts and making it compulsory to wear them. the commission reiterates that the three directives must be adopted with all the greater urgency, since the fitting of seat belts in new vehicles must of course already be required before the mandatory use of seat belts can be introduced. the only disagreement on the seats is between the council and the committee on transport and tourism. if the safety belts are to be required on all seats, it will be necessary to ban side-facing seats in coaches, since the types of belts currently offered for this purpose do not provide optimum protection for the passenger. however, if the ban were to be imposed immediately, the market segment of the so-called conference buses would have been doomed to disappear. the proposed transitional period of five years will certainly allow industry to develop technical solutions better adapted to the different accident scenarios. the commission welcomes the fact that the two rapporteurs, mr costa and mr koch, have succeeded in reaching a compromise with the other institutions. the commission can accept the proposed amendments in their present form. i hope that this will enable the package to be adopted at second reading. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of the road is not compromised by the use of the road safety brake. i would like to thank the rapporteur in particular for having succeeded in achieving a broad consensus on this proposal at an early stage within the committee on transport and tourism. the commission has already submitted a communication to parliament on pedestrian protection. it included a voluntary commitment by european, japanese and korean car manufacturers to carry out a series of tests on new vehicles to make them more pedestrian-friendly and a ban on rigid frontal protection buckles. in its resolution on this voluntary commitment, parliament called for the control of the use of these frontal protection harnesses to be regulated by law. the commission has responded to this request by parliament in its proposal of october 2003 and i am pleased to note that the report of the committee on transport has reached the same conclusion. the commission can accept any amendments proposed by the committee on transport and tourism. i am therefore confident that this proposal can also be adopted at first reading.
the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i am here today on behalf of our colleague dr koch, who, as president of the european movement in thuringia, is chairing an international symposium on the constitutional treaty, and that is also an important matter. the first part of my contribution on this subject concerns three closely linked proposals for directives by the rapporteurs koch and costa. the commissioner has already explained that the issue is seats, seat belts and head restraints with their respective anchorages in vehicles. in the second part, i would like to address the subject of frontal protection bars or bull bars in cars for the shadow rapporteur, mr koch. this has to do with the protection of pedestrians, especially children, cyclists and wheelchair users. the first part is that we will take a major step towards improving road safety tomorrow by approving the koch report. we shall thus help to reduce red tape and also to safeguard jobs. because we know that a properly fastened seat belt can reduce the severity of injuries and save lives. it is therefore right to require that all seats in vehicles be fitted with safety belts. the requirement to be equipped with such a system, which has so far been limited to passenger cars, is extended to other categories of vehicles, in particular minibuses, certain buses and heavy and light lorries. the ban on the use of side-facing seats in cars, lorries and certain categories of buses is also welcome. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. however, these seats should only be permitted if they are fitted with appropriate safety belts and if they are grouped in the rear of the vehicle, preferably in a u-shape, around a table. this scheme should apply for at least five years. on the basis of the actual accident data then available and taking into account the further development of safety-belt systems, this regulation must then be extended, preferably in the context of a community type-approval for all vehicle categories. i am glad that, contrary to the initial view of the council and the commission, this is now seen by them as a sound basis for future authorizations. finally, the accident statistics we know, the studies and tests, do not give us any indication of an increased risk for passengers in side-facing seats in large conference buses. this is partly due to the different types of accidents and accident sequences for different vehicles. for cars and minibuses, the frontal impact is typical. this means heavy forward loads on the occupants, but also on the seats and the restraint systems. in the case of large bus accidents, the situation is quite different: they usually tip over. the purpose of the seat belts is not to absorb longitudinal forces but to keep the occupants in their seats in order to prevent them from being ejected from the vehicle. these requirements can be met by seats with side-facing seat belts as well, perhaps even better, than by seats with front- or rear-facing seat belts. the compromise reached, which the commission and the council have also indicated their support for, will help to reduce bureaucratic hurdles in the member states. this is because national exemptions for small series of buses are already possible today with bureaucratic effort. but this is contrary to the internal market strategy and even allows the authorization of side-facing seats without seat belts. the commission's decision will therefore in any case contribute to greater safety in road transport on the one hand and in the internal market on the other. we also decide on the viability of a typical european product in the tourism sector, the vip or conference bus. this will also secure jobs for manufacturers and bus companies and maintain or improve the comfort of travellers. the commission has already taken the necessary steps to ensure that the directive is adopted as soon as possible, and that the council and the commission agree on the matter. i would like to thank mr costa and the other shadow rapporteurs, and mrs hedkvist petersen for her negotiating skills as rapporteur on frontal protection harnesses for cars, which really do represent a great danger in accidents involving unprotected road users, especially in urban traffic. we're now making sure that new vehicles under 3.5 tons are banned with rigid frontal protection bars. the subsidiarity principle allows member states to subject existing vehicles to these rules and to authorise flexible frontal protection systems, but only in accordance with a uniformly prescribed test procedure. i think this is a good thing in terms of pedestrian protection, in terms of those who are really the most vulnerable in traffic, especially in our cities.

the next item is the report by mrs poli bortone, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, on nutrition and health claims made on foods (com (2003) 0424 c5-0329/2003 2003/0165 (cod)) (a6-0128/2005).
member of the commission. madam president, we all agree that we want an informed consumer in the european union; that we want the consumer to be able to decide for himself or herself and not to have a nanny state. it is something we all tend to agree on. however, in order for the consumer to achieve that, we need to provide the consumer with accurate, exact, correct, scientifically justified information. that is very important. we must not forget that in europe the consumer assumes and expects that any label that reaches him or her has been checked and approved by an authority. therefore, there is a responsibility here to do so. i would also like to remind you of something i mentioned earlier, that any vacuum that may be left in community legislation will be filled in by the member states and therefore will defeat the purpose of having this harmonised legislation and will mean a return to a fragmented set of rules and regulations that harm the industry, consumer confidence, cause problems for the internal market and of course do not achieve the level of protection that we would all like to have. that is why we presented this proposal. i would like to thank the committee for all the work it has done on such an important issue, the rapporteur, mrs poli bortone and of course the shadow rapporteurs. i would also like to thank mrs niebler and mr stubb, the draftsmen of the opinions of the two other committees, and the committees themselves, for the work they have done. the proposal says something very simple. it says that no one can make a voluntary claim without having the scientific justification for doing so. we must not forget that these are voluntary claims with the sole aim of profit, it is a marketing tool. therefore, in order to allow the use of this marketing tool for profit, we must make sure that it has the correct scientific justification and that it is substantiated scientifically. consumers, as i said earlier, have to be able to make their own decisions, but they must not be misled. they must not be convinced by products sold on unsubstantiated claims. the adoption of the proposal meets the purposes i would like it to. it protects the consumer; it advances health considerations; it helps the industry, competition and the internal market and it allows innovation. having a common set of rules in a unique legal environment also helps in the internal market and competitiveness. some claims that may have adverse effects will need to remain prohibited. it is also very important to maintain the link between claims and nutritional profiles. once again i have to remind you that these are voluntary claims and if they are going to be made, they have to based on a nutritional balance. if the nutritional balance is questionable then the use as a marketing tool of a specific characteristic of a foodstuff must not be allowed as it will eventually mislead the consumer. the nutritional profile is a key element of the proposal and therefore it should remain.
draft opinion of the consultative committee on industry, research and energy. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i would like to thank the rapporteur and all the shadow rapporteurs. what is the purpose of this regulation? it is a matter of regulating food advertising. the commission proposes to regulate everything: nutrition-related claims (such as fat content, high energy, low energy), health-related claims (such as 'a food strengthens the immune system', 'a food promotes concentration', etc.) and pure well-being claims (such as 'a food keeps fit, gives momentum, gives strength', etc.). the commission is proposing to ban all health claims and to require the approval of the european food safety authority for health claims. how this proposal for a regulation is to be compatible with the lisbon strategy is something that only the gods can really understand. the provisions, with the exception of the harmonisation of nutrition claims, are not to be justified. in all the discussions in the various committees it has been repeatedly stated that we in europe must do something about the obesity of many children. that is true, of course, but we cannot achieve that by banning advertising! if we want to do something about childhood obesity, we need to change our diet, we need to get our children to exercise more, and we need to reduce the amount of time they spend in front of the tv and computer. moreover, why should well-being and affectionate messages which express individual feelings and are easily recognizable as advertising be banned? i think the commission's approach is wrong. everything is forbidden unless it is allowed. that is the philosophy, and the commissioner has put it in words when he says that consumers expect every label to be checked by the authorities. excuse me, but this isn't just about labels, it's about advertising. i do not think that is a good approach and i am grateful that the committee on industry has also delivered an opinion, in particular on the deletion of articles 4 and 11. i hope that we will get the same result tomorrow when we vote: a modification of article 11 and the deletion of article 4.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals. we have been torturing ourselves for two years now with the commission's proposal on food advertising. the commission is clearly overstepping its bounds. it is not a consumer protection policy but a consumer abuse and disempowerment policy because the commission thinks that the european citizens are stupid, fat and greedy. the commission has therefore proposed that food be classified as good and bad by nutritional profiles, using a scientifically untenable method. and above all, on the simply wrong grounds that advertising alone is to blame for the increasing obesity of europeans. this is a strange thing, commissioner. i've been wondering all the time, what planet are you from? the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods are respected. of course advertising cannot lie! nobody wants to do that! but we don't need advertising censorship. we already have a law protecting the consumer from misleading advertising. and of course, advertising is the lifeblood of the food industry in this saturated food market. innovation in this sector is only possible if one product is different from another. it's the only way to successfully promote and market it. and innovation ultimately benefits the consumer, through ever better products. innovation is the key to business success and, with it, our jobs. do you have any idea how many jobs a law like this would destroy? a bureaucratic monster is to be created here. a cumbersome, time-consuming approval procedure for each individual advertisement from 25 member states to be submitted, of course, word for word in all twenty official languages! this would be the death knell for our smes. but they would be overwhelmed by the constantly new scientific evidence. why should we not be allowed to say more 'fruit is healthy'? because there might be a fruit that the commission finds too sweet? we're making a fool of ourselves. this is a matter of political disillusionment, of anti-europeanism! i ask you, commissioner, to withdraw this proposal at last! i would have told you so earlier, but you don't seem to like talking to these pesky parliamentarians. perhaps you should have come down from the glass tower of the berlaymont building to the lower floors of our offices and joined our committee. then you would know that we will do everything in our power tomorrow in plenary to put an end to this nonsense of nutritional profiles in article 4 and some other things.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the past. this is a good day for the european union, for policyholders, but also for insurance companies, because with the debate today and the vote tomorrow - which i assume will be unanimous - the much-maligned bureaucratic obstacles will be removed and european reinsurance will be strengthened in international competition. the supervision of primary insurance is regulated in numerous directives throughout europe: the european union has already put in place wide-ranging and necessary instruments to protect policyholders in the framework of the non-life and life insurance directives and the provisions on the solvency of insurance companies. the aim is to complete this body of rules by harmonizing the supervision of reinsurance. the directive, which was the subject of a major debate in the committee on economic and monetary affairs, is therefore an important element in the complementary approach to supervision in this important service sector. the reinsurance directive, which has now been successfully launched after more than three years of preparatory work, is largely based on the existing supervisory systems for primary insurance. in close cooperation with the council - as has already been said - the competent authorities of the member states and the representatives of the reinsurance industry, substantial differences between primary and reinsurance were also identified and taken into account in the draft directive. this includes, in particular, a uniform treatment of life and non-life reinsurance with regard to solvency margins, a prudential approach to capital investment and a clear time limit of 36 months after the entry into force of the directive for collateral which is still required by the supervisory authorities in each member state, the so-called collaterals. the harmonising but also liberalising regulation sought will further strengthen the competitive position of european reinsurance companies - this has already been said - and thus the european financial centre as a whole. at the same time, administrative barriers within the community are being removed. the implementation of the directive will eliminate the burden of national licensing within the eu. the supervisory authority of the home member state shall exercise the necessary supervision. the authorisation of a reinsurer is then valid for the whole of the eu. a major reorganization of the entire insurance industry is expected to be settled by corresponding applications or 'solvency ii' in the next year or two. i have submitted a proposal to ensure that this reinsurance directive does not prejudge the political debate on 'solvency' today. i should like to thank the rapporteur, mr peter skinner, for the good cooperation and we would like to see more time in the committees and more preparation for the next discussion of such an important resource.

to prepare for it. i would like to take this opportunity to answer mr florenz's question, who specifically raised the question of the threat of bioterrorism and the threat of nuclear terrorism. it is clear that this type of terrorism, which includes chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear terrorism, constitutes a threat to international peace and security. we know that terrorist networks have a persistent interest in these substances and weapons and that, if they were to acquire such weapons of mass destruction, they would be able to cause damage on an unprecedented scale and undermine the democratic foundations of our societies. that is why the european union should pay greater attention to the threat of biological, nuclear and chemical terrorism. you drew a parallel with the us legislation in this area. europe can certainly draw a great deal from what is being done in the united states, particularly in terms of training teams, building up vaccine stocks, research and development work on medical countermeasures, etc. similar initiatives have already been taken by the member states. the union institutions have also been involved in this type of activity. the union has, for example, early warning systems for all types of terrorist attacks, for which a central access point, called argus, will be set up within the commission. under the directive amending the directive establishing a community code relating to medicinal products for human use, member states are now entitled to allow the temporary distribution of authorised medicinal products in response to an attack resulting in the spread of pathogens, toxins, chemical agents or nuclear radiation. anti-cbrn training of medical staff is ongoing. information on civil protection capabilities and blood stocks shall be exchanged within civil protection mechanisms. other very extensive research is being carried out under the sixth research and development programme to better cope with such possible actions. the council's strategy against the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction is aimed at preventing terrorists from having access to such weapons, and it is regrettable that the new york conference was unable to agree on a common text, since one of the components of the non-proliferation conference was on the terrorist threat in these areas. as part of another directive, resulting from the declaration on the fight against terrorism adopted by the european council of 25 march 2004, the council and the commission adopted on 2 december 2004 the european union solidarity programme in the face of the consequences of terrorist threats and attacks, which revised the cbrn programme and extended it to all forms of terrorism. one of the basic principles of the eu strategy is that protection against the consequences of terrorist attacks is primarily the responsibility of the member states. however, the declaration on solidarity against terrorism adopted by the european council on 25 march 2004 confirms that the institutions of the european union and the member states are firmly committed to using all the instruments at their disposal to assist a member state on its territory, at the request of its political authorities. in this connection, i cannot refrain from referring to a provision of the constitution which strengthens the character of solidarity, particularly in the event of terrorist attacks. the cbrn programme and its successor, the solidarity programme, are multidisciplinary programmes involving political, technical, economic, diplomatic, military and legal means. it's hard enough, but, well... the european union's action against cbrn terrorism under the current solidarity programme is based on six strategic objectives, which i should like to mention briefly. threat analysis and assessment: several analyses of these threats have been undertaken by europol and the european union joint situation centre, sitcen. prevention and reduction of vulnerability: legislative measures have been taken to improve compliance with international biosecurity and biosafety standards. detection of cbrn-type attacks: the commission has taken steps to extend and coordinate community systems for detection, communication and information on chemical and biological threats to human, animal and plant health. finally, preparation to mitigate the consequences of possible attacks: the commission is assessing the civil protection, medical and pharmaceutical capabilities that member states could put at each other's disposal. it develops rules on the treatment of diseases linked to these substances. the council has also established a database of military assets and capabilities of interest to the protection of civilian populations against the effects of terrorist attacks, including cbrn-type attacks. as part of the reflection on the esdp dimension of the fight against terrorism, civil/military interoperability in the cbrn area is under consideration. the council is also working on an integrated crisis management regime. international cooperation is of course very important in this respect: it has broadly the same objectives as the solidarity programme, namely the sharing of epidemiological information on the cross-border spread of infectious diseases and cooperation on emergency plans, laboratory detection techniques, non-proliferation, mutual assistance and coordination of responses. the united states is involved in this work. another dialogue will be opened in due course. we believe that international cooperation, particularly with the americans but also with all other partners, is extremely important in this respect. i simply want to conclude on this, before the votes take place and my colleague, vice-president frattini, speaks: i believe that the european union is engaged in a comprehensive process of preparation for the fight against all forms of terrorism. the fight against terrorism - as i said at the beginning and as your reports have shown - must be a comprehensive approach. one theme must certainly be of particular concern to us: we must prevent terrorist groups from recruiting in our own societies. indeed, it is recruitment into our own societies, particularly among young people who are uprooted and poorly integrated into our societies, that constitutes the greatest terrorist question no 31 by mr alfredo antoniozzi (h-0384/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: promotion of the italian language in europe (eurydice 2005 report) and definition of the language regime within the community institutions the debate on the use of the eu's official languages within the institutions has not yet received a response to the proposal to draw up a new regime for the use of the official languages and a definition of working languages and their use. the subject of the debate should now be defined and the linguistic and cultural heritage of the eu member states should be better used. could the commission state how it intends to deal with the issue of official languages within the institutions and whether it intends to designate working languages (council regulation no 1/58 (article 1) refers only to official languages) and thus avoid leaving the decision on the use of one language instead of another to the discretion of senior officials (answer to question h-0159/05 - written reply of 8.3.2005) and thus avoid unfair discrimination? what proposals could the commission make to preserve italy's linguistic heritage following the publication of the eurydice report 'key figures for language teaching in europe', considering that eurydice is supported by the ec and that one should ask what the ec will propose based on the very negative data on the teaching of italian in europe contained in the report?
member of the commission. in reply to the honourable member, the commission has already pointed out several times, and in particular in its reply to oral question h-0159/05 by the honourable member, that, in accordance with council regulation no 1/58 (article 1) –the first one in the history of eu secondary legislation – all official languages are at the same time working languages and can therefore be used on the same legal terms and on the same basis within the institutions. so it is not correct to say that the current working languages within the european institutions have been reduced to three, namely english, french and german. as for internal procedures within the commission, the documents submitted to it are drafted in these three languages at least. it is a rule that has purely internal effects and aims to guarantee that the commission itself is in a position to understand documents of general interest. the commission has found no evidence of any discrimination against other working languages as a result of this rule, which was drawn up on the instructions of both the current and former presidents of the commission. moreover, it is normal that, for operational reasons, certain languages are used more than others by commission staff in their daily business. no senior management official has the power or the right to require his staff to use one working language rather than another. but sometimes it is the linguistic preferences or knowledge of commissioners themselves which may require the use of a particular language. it goes without saying that it is mandatory to maintain internal communication among the commission departments and inside the other institutions. all these practices are followed with due respect for the equality of languages as official and working languages. the commission reiterates that it has no intention whatsoever of introducing a specific system involving the privileged use of one or several languages in its services. on the other hand, if the work of its services goes beyond internal business and involves contacts with outsiders, the commission is committed to making use of as many official languages as possible, taking into account the limitations on available translation resources under the guidelines set out in its document 638/6. secondly, the commission actively promotes multilingualism within the european union, as indicated in its communication 'promoting language learning and linguistic diversity: an action plan 2004-2006'. under the socrates and leonardo da vinci programmes, specific actions and other actions for student and teacher exchanges can be used for the promotion of italian, as for all other community languages. thus, the lingua action under the socrates programme financed eight different projects to promote the italian language between 2000 and 2004.
member of the commission. in procedural terms, we use only some languages in the college, but at the official and working levels, all languages are equal. one of the changes or important phenomena, which one can see in the press conferences on wednesdays, is that there is the possibility of using all the official languages. with this attitude and with the promotion of language learning, with multilingualism as a policy, not just an administrative part of our daily work, we will achieve significant progress and improvement, within the limits of our possibilities. the situation for languages from the time of enlargement shows that the union is functioning – it did not collapse. all languages can be used by communicators within the union. speaking as commissioner for education, i must say that all our mobility programmes, our activities in the field of education, culture and vocational training strongly promote a language component. i am sure that, with that awareness and positive philosophy or policy we are on the right track.
member of the commission. i would like to support that idea. next month we want to introduce the communication on the new language competence indicator, which is now an important part of the growing question of competence and recognition of qualifications. we have agreed with member states to promote language learning as early as possible. in a broader context, the 1 + 2 formula is no longer a luxury, but a necessity for the younger generation and for all citizens, who need to learn not only their mother tongue, but also two other european languages, one of which should preferably be that of a neighbour. that is the policy and basic philosophy supported by the commission and, if this policy is promoted properly in member states, multilingualism and language competence will increase markedly in the future european union. i fully share the interest and support of the distinguished member of parliament.

question no 34 by mairead mcguinness (h-0386/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: charges for public service broadcasting in view of the importance of the media in today's world and the view that public service broadcasting is worth protecting, can the commission make a statement on how it sees the future of public service broadcasting and on the need for a clear and unambiguous interpretation of the question of how the charges are used by broadcasters and whether the use of public service broadcasting charges is uniform in the member states?
member of the commission. madam president, the importance of the public service of broadcasting and the competence of the member states to define, organise and provide for the mechanisms for financing this public service are guaranteed by article 86 (2) of the treaty and by the amsterdam protocol. as indicated in the 2001 commission communication on state aid, the role of private operators should not be overlooked as they contribute to pluralism, enrich the political and cultural debate and broaden the choice of programmes. the dual system which characterizes the european audiovisual landscape and which has beneficial effects on the media as a whole is thus very clearly recognised. as far as the public sector is concerned, it is now up to the member states to organise the financing of this sector. this financing may be entirely borne by public funds, in whatever form and, where appropriate, in the form of a fee, as envisaged by the honourable member. this financing may also be mixed and consist in part of revenues from the sale of advertising space. there is no objection to the choice of either of these formulae. however, the commission must ensure that the treaty rules are respected, in particular those on state aid, as interpreted by the 2001 communication. public funding must be used only to fulfil public service missions and must not exceed what is necessary in this respect: this is the rule of proportionality. the public service missions must be clearly and precisely defined and there must be a separation of accounts when public sector operators engage in commercial activities: this is the rule of transparency. it is therefore not for the commission to lay down other rules which would limit the member states' scope for manoeuvre in this highly cultural area.
member of the commission. madam president, i have not yet read the letter from the irish authorities. i suppose that this is a normal request made by the commission in relation to state aid, which is quite acceptable, for the public audiovisual sector. such state aid must be notified and there must be an exchange of questions and answers between the commission and the member state concerned. in the light of the member state's replies, the commission shall examine whether the situation in the member state is in conformity with the treaty, the amsterdam protocol and the 2001 commission communication. if yes, the green light is given; if not, there is a discussion between the member state and the commission. this is a normal procedure that happens regularly. there are usually no problems and the member states get the go-ahead fairly quickly. in a few cases, problems arose, particularly with the german authorities. however, as regards the public broadcasting sector, exchanges of information between the member states and the commission are not difficult.
question no 35 by mr manolis mavrommatis (h-0420/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: media programmethe worrying trend of concentration of media in individual countries is leading to the formation of monopolies and the dominance of a few television stations and their production companies. the media programme also covered television broadcasters and their production companies (which are neither independent nor small or medium-sized enterprises). how does this initiative affect the principle underlying the media programme of supporting independent producers and small and medium-sized enterprises? will the commission examine the impact of the programme on small and mediumsized enterprises, especially the independent companies supplying television productions, and the practical benefits of providing only a limited budget to finance television projects?
member of the commission. the honourable member raises the question of independent producers. it is clear that in the context of audiovisual production we need these independent producers. they are the ones who create the most important audiovisual works, and they do so in the cultural and linguistic diversity which is the real wealth of our continent. that is why the conditions for access to media grants are very clear: you must be an independent producer. it is not possible to receive a grant if you are a sub-organism of, for example, a television station. i would like to say that media+ sets out very clear obligations, to return to the producers. after a maximum of seven years, all systems will be reviewed to further support independent producers. so, in the context of the media review, we will be strengthening the measures to support this very important dimension of the european cultural industry.
question no 36 by mrs westlund (h-0436/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: public services and new directive on television broadcasting the commission is expected to present a proposal for a new directive on television broadcasting activities at the end of 2005, which is likely to include public service broadcasting. public service broadcasting is of great importance to the democratic, social and cultural interests of society. in order to enable public service media services to respond to these needs, community legislation needs to clarify that they can make use of any new technology and media form, such as internet and wap services, without being contrary to the rules of the internal market. does the commission share this view with regard to the right of public service providers to make use of any new technology and media? does the commission intend to introduce legislation with the new directive which only concerns audiovisual content and not media forms or technologies?
member of the commission. the commission presented last week its communication 'i 2010: an information society for growth and jobs'. the commission states that it will propose by the end of 2005 a revision of the 'television without frontiers' directive to modernise the regulation on audiovisual services, and that is what the honourable member is talking about. the minimum coordination provisions in this text strengthen the competitiveness of the european audiovisual industry. however, the directive does not contain any specific rights or obligations for public service broadcasters and there is no intention, at least for the time being, to introduce measures in the context of the review which would relate to the use of communication techniques and means by public service broadcasters. as in the case of the question to which i have already answered, i would like to recall that it is very important that member states have the responsibility to define the purpose of their public services and to determine how they are to be remunerated in order to be able to fulfil their mission, this area continuing to fall under the principle of subsidiarity in accordance with the 2001 commission communication on state aid and the rules of the treaty, including the amsterdam protocol. but in this communication we also say - and this is an important element - that the public service can include services which are not programmes in the traditional sense of the term: for example, online information services, in so far, of course, as they are intended to satisfy the same democratic, social and cultural needs as sui generis programmes.
member of the commission. madam president, i can only repeat what i have already said: the commission is the guardian of the treaties. it therefore relies on the articles of the treaties and the amsterdam protocol to allow exceptions in respect of state aid to public service broadcasting. it is therefore up to the states to define, first, the object and obligations of their public services and, secondly, how these obligations are remunerated by fees or advertising. the commission is merely checking whether what has been decided by the member states is being implemented in practice. so my colleague monti and i published in 2001 - in order to eliminate all questions that could arise about the interpretation of these articles of the treaty and the amsterdam protocol - a communication, which the european parliament is well aware of, which specifies all these rules: i can therefore reassure the honourable member, because both the commission and parliament are committed to the dual system and public broadcasters are absolutely protected, both by the treaties and by the rules that follow from them.

question no 38 by mr bernd posselt (h-0373/05) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: crossborder cultural promotionwhat role does the commission's promotion of cultural activities play in crossborder cooperation, for example between bavaria and the czech republic or austria and slovakia? what priorities does the commission envisage for the preservation of the common cultural heritage in border regions?
member of the commission. article 151 of the european community treaty, which is the base for our cultural cooperation, states that the community should encourage cultural cooperation between member states, including in the area of safeguarding cultural heritage and, if necessary, by supporting and supplementing their action in a certain number of areas. this objective is pursued by the culture 2000 framework programme in support of cultural cooperation in europe. implemented in order to encourage artistic and cultural cooperation in europe and to drive forward the creation of a common cultural area, the culture 2000 programme supports projects jointly produced and financed by at least three operators from at least three countries taking part in the programme. however, this programme is not specifically aimed at developing cross-border cultural cooperation. secondly, while the programme does not establish specific measures for the conservation of the common cultural heritage of border regions, it nevertheless contributes to disseminating know-how and promoting good practices in the field of conservation and preservation of this common cultural heritage. moreover, the european union also actively supports the conservation of europe’s cultural heritage through the structural funds and the sixth framework programme for research and technical development. thirdly, in the interreg iiia programmes, including those mentioned by mr posselt, culture is mainly promoted by supporting networks for creating or intensifying cross-border cultural contacts. under the entrepreneurship measures, many programmes also cover the promotion of cultural tourism. according to the guidance given in the commission communication of 28 april 2000, renovation and development of historic urban centres using a joint cross-border strategy, can also be promoted. this strategy, of course, excludes housing.

acting president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european council which will begin its work on 16 june will have to deliberate on two crucial issues for the future development establishing a constitution for europe was rejected by the french and dutch citizens, and signed in rome on 29 october 2004. the reasons for these negative votes are many and contradictory. many of us majority of french and dutch voters. i cannot help but recall, mr president, the massive vote by the european parliament on 12 january 2005 in favour of the draft european constitution. this vote was transparent, anchor its future in the common values we hold dear and, finally, regain the full confidence of its citizens. ten countries ratified the draft constitution, one of which - spain - by have to be faced. through these polls, concerns were expressed, aspirations and expectations, but also disappointments. unfortunately, european unification no longer appears to be the mobilizing project which for decades allowed our continent to be rebuilt in peace and prosperity before being reconciled by means of enlargement. has hope changed sides? would europe only inspire concern and in writing. agriculture is more than the production of food. the preservation of agriculture in all member states is therefore an important task for the european union. it strengthens economic and rural development and ensures a healthy natural and cultural landscape. financial support for farmers through the common agricultural policy must continue to be ensured. this must be reflected in the union's long-term financial planning. the forthcoming accession of bulgaria and romania in 2007 will aggravate the financial situation. the increase in the financial allocation for the agricultural policy to take account of this enlargement is not currently planned. the draft rather provides for a reduction or capping of the financial resources. accession would further reduce the funds available to farmers in the existing member states. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's agricultural policy is not disrupted by the introduction of new products. it is not the commission's job to make up the shortfall for its farmers. this does not mean renationalizing agricultural policy, but rather securing its financing in the long term. in order to maintain the benefits of the common agricultural policy, it may be necessary in the future for member states to contribute to the costs. it is unacceptable that the enlargement of the european union should be financed at the expense of farmers and that the agricultural budget should be used as a stone quarry for other policies.

president of the council. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i said this morning that one of the subjects on the agenda of the european council was the reform of the un, and in particular the summit in september this year, at which, we hope, this reform will be able to take place. the european union attaches great importance to this reform, as we have already had the opportunity to say and emphasize. we have repeatedly stated our support for the contents of the report by the secretary-general of the united nations, mr kofi annan, presented on 21 march, and for the preparatory reports on which it is based. these reports are in line with the general philosophy outlined in the european security strategy and offer promising pathways towards a stronger and more effective multilateralism. the european union supports the comprehensive concept of collective security proposed by the secretary-general, recognising that the threats to peace and security are not only war, international conflict, civil violence, organised crime, terrorism and weapons of mass destruction, but also poverty, underdevelopment, deadly epidemics and environmental degradation, including global warming issues. the european union expresses its agreement in principle with the package of proposals presented by the secretary-general, while maintaining an open approach. it intends to play a leading role in the process leading up to the september summit. the union considers that significant efforts will be required to achieve the best possible outcome at the summit covering a wide range of topics. it is crucial to maintain a good balance between the three main objectives outlined by the secretary-general, namely development, security and human rights. the challenge is therefore to achieve a certain critical mass of reforms in a coherent approach over time, while keeping open the possibility of further progress. in the european union we are used to these stepwise, transitional approaches. the european union fully endorses the secretary-general's analysis of the interdependence of the various areas concerned. it also emphasizes unequivocally that development is an end in itself and not just a means to security. the union is firmly committed to implementing the millennium declaration. it emphasises the link between the achievement of the millennium development goals and the implementation of the outcomes of un international conferences and summits in the economic, social, environmental and other fields. i will not repeat the objectives we set at the last general affairs council for an increase in development aid in the run-up to 2015. the union hopes that a number of issues of particular importance for the achievement of the millennium development goals will be duly taken into account in the conclusions of the summit. we also attach particular importance to the joint, united fight against aids. we want to think together about the link between environmental sustainability, security and poverty eradication. the european union strongly supports the idea of setting up a peacebuilding commission on the various security-related aspects. it is a priority for the union and it is essential that agreement is reached on this at the september summit. this proposal fills a gap. in the transition from a state of war to a state of sustainable peace, this peacebuilding commission could contribute to intensifying the planning activities carried out by the un for sustainable recovery, while strengthening the institutions guaranteeing the rule of law and good governance. at the same time, it could play a significant role in preventing new conflicts, which is often an important element in the consolidation of a lasting peace. this peace-building committee would be a permanent body, which could assist the security council and ecosoc depending on the phases of the conflict. the link with ecosoc is particularly important for the development dimension. the commission should also help ensure coherence between reconstruction and peacekeeping strategies. the union supports the overall strategy proposed by the secretary-general in his report and in his speech in madrid on the fight against terrorism. it is necessary to emphasize that terrorism is unacceptable in all circumstances, whatever the underlying factors invoked. the union recalls that the five pillars of the approach proposed by the secretary-general are consistent with the strategy developed by the union since the attacks of 11 september 2001 and reaffirmed in the wake of the tragic events in madrid. the european union also supports the recommendations presented by the secretary-general in the context of non-proliferation and disarmament, which are broadly in line with the approach of the european strategy against the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. since results can only be achieved through collective effort, the union is ready to take initiatives in this direction in a multilateral context and to address these issues in the context of its regular contacts and political dialogue in order to convince its partners to take these recommendations into account as well. the union considers that the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction constitutes the most serious and immediate threat to international peace and stability. the general safeguard agreements and additional protocols should now be the norm for verification in the nuclear field. the negotiations on a treaty to stop the production of fissile materials will also have to be concluded quickly. the union also intends to play an active part in the elaboration of binding international instruments to regulate the marking, tracing and illicit brokering of small arms and light weapons, all of which we have already had the opportunity to discuss in the context of the work of your parliament. the union reiterates its wish that the adoption of the principle of the responsibility to protect will become one of the major priorities of the summit. human rights violations, impunity and failure to respect the rule of law are among the main factors threatening peace and security and hindering the development process. the union supports the efforts of the secretary-general to adopt and implement the principle of responsibility for the protection of potential and actual victims of genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and other mass violations of human rights. finally, as regards the use of force, the union considers that the concept and criteria proposed by the secretary-general constitute a good basis from which all parties should be prepared to work. the proposed criteria are political rather than legal in nature and should reflect a broad international consensus, which would guide the members of the security council in their deliberations which may lead to the use of force. i would like to welcome the high priority given to human rights and the rule of law in the secretary-general's report. the union supports any proposal to strengthen democracy and to place human rights at the heart of the un system. we stress the need to strengthen the human rights system, in particular by integrating it into the whole of the activities of the united nations system, which would strengthen its capacity to respond permanently to human rights violations. we also support the call for the strengthening of the office of the un high commissioner for human rights and for sufficient financial resources to strengthen its capacity to carry out its mandate. the union thus agrees to the creation of a human rights council, a permanent body, in so far as it can help to increase the place of human rights in the un system. sixty years after the war and the creation of the united nations, the time has come to give a new impetus to multilateralism, to reform the united nations system, a system indispensable to world security, to the harmonious development of all nations and to the consolidation of peace. i think this is a chance we're being given. the european union must play an active role in this reform and i count on your parliament to support the council and the commission in this endeavour.

community. ownership must, however, be balanced by responsibility and the secretary-general's view that states seeking membership of the council should demonstrate a 'solid record of commitment to the highest human rights standards' is a welcome requirement, also in view of the obligations deriving from membership of the council. obviously the issue of reforming the security council is one of the high-profile elements of the current un reform debate. i note with interest the proposals made in the resolution for the establishment of an 'eu' seat. whilst security council reform is naturally an member of the commission. honourable members, thank you for giving me the opportunity to address parliament shortly before our yearly eu-us summit, which will take place in washington on 20 june. i wherever possible. that is the message our leaders will doubtless seek to convey at the upcoming june summit. president bush’s successful visit to brussels last february was a sign of the united states administration’s desire to reach out to europe and work together in partnership with the european union. it was an important signal that we have put the problems of approach that arose over iraq behind us and that we are ready to work together in a constructive manner as allies. the united states is increasingly adopting a more open attitude to the european union and listening more carefully to our concerns. even where there are differences between us, we are learning how best to talk through them. a good example is the recently launched european union-us strategic dialogue on east asia, a forum in which to discuss the security challenges in the region, including those related to the rise of china. coordination also continues on united nations reform, though much work still needs to be done. the eu-us summit on 20 june will focus on three global themes: promoting democratic governance and human rights around the world, increasing economic prosperity for our citizens and championing security and development. i would like to say a few words on each. promoting democracy and freedom is the essence of president bush’s foreign policy in his second term. european union foreign policy, which is firmly based on the principles of the united nations and the european security strategy, also aims to promote democracy, together with human rights and the rule of law. the promotion of democracy remains key in the wider middle east and in the mediterranean region, where transatlantic cooperation has increased substantially over the past 12 months. shortly after our summit in washington, we and the united states will co-host an international conference in brussels on iraq. this is an important signal of unified international support for the government and people in their difficult task of working towards stabilisation and reconstruction. in addition we have been in daily contact over lebanon’s election process, and together we will continue to support the lebanese people as they consolidate democracy. in israel and palestine, our cooperative approach within the quartet is also intensifying. on economic prosperity, the european union and the united states have the most integrated economies in the world and benefit from the largest trade and investment relationship. but we can do more, and we want to. to move this agenda forward, we have spent nine months consulting all stakeholders on the obstacles they encountered and distilled the result in the recently published commission communication, ‘a stronger eu-us partnership and a more open market for the 21st century’. the communication contains a set of pragmatic proposals for boosting eu-us trade and investment and thus promoting competitiveness, growth, and jobs on both sides of the atlantic. there are three basic strands to our proposals. first, regulating the transatlantic market, including areas such as services, investment, procurement and competition; second, promoting knowledge and innovation; and third, instituting smarter and safer borders for swifter trade and investment. in the field of regulatory cooperation, the idea is to find ways for regulators to engage with each other at an early stage to avoid unnecessary conflicts and costs, and to promote convergence. the second strand, on promoting knowledge and innovation, is crucial for generating economic growth and jobs. new technologies, in particular e-commerce, internet governance and mobile telecommunication services, generated considerable interest amongst the stakeholders consulted. the third strand of our package is striking the right balance between heightened security requirements and the continuation of open trade and passenger transport. our communication also addresses the overall structure and goals of transatlantic relations. the question we address is what the political profile of our relations should be 10 years after the signature of the 1995 new transatlantic agenda and fifteen years after the 1990 transatlantic declaration. in essence, we must make sure that the structure and the goals of transatlantic relations are adapted to today’s challenges. we would also like to see legislators – the european parliament and united states congress – build stronger ties. for this reason we suggest enhancing the transatlantic legislators’ dialogue and making it a fully-fledged transatlantic assembly. the commission stands ready to assist as necessary, but an initiative of this nature naturally has to come first and foremost from this house and from the united states congress. championing security and development is the third theme of the summit. as we continue to identify measures to enhance the security of our citizens against terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, it is worth remembering that such phenomena have claimed many more victims beyond our borders than within them. this reinforces our determination to work with the united states to spread the benefits of security in all its facets and to help release peoples everywhere from the daily tyranny of terrorism and violence. the european union and the united states should combine skills and experience in the field of conflict prevention and crisis response and bring to bear the full range of civilian and military tools at our disposal. we should consult routinely on current and potential crises. we should strengthen cooperation in post-conflict assistance and reconstruction. we should prepare, through joint training and exercises, and we should work together to improve international capacities to respond to crises and to prevent future crises from erupting. the european union is anxious to cooperate with the united states on crisis management, both civilian and military. we also recognise the need to tackle poverty, disease, corruption and instability, which terrorists seek to exploit and intensify. our common agenda should prioritise the millennium development goals. in conclusion, the commission welcomes the parliament’s motion for a resolution and, as i have indicated previously, we largely agree with it. we are taking an ambitious, forward-looking approach in developing our relations with the united states and are working actively in the areas mentioned in the draft resolution. we have a challenging agenda in front of us. we are looking forward to your support, and the support of united states congress, to accomplish it.

president of the council. on 7 march 2005, the council reaffirmed the european union's commitment to croatia's accession and adopted the framework for the negotiations for that country. the council also recalled the importance of full cooperation by all the western balkan countries with the international criminal tribunal for the former yugoslavia. this is a key requirement for their further rapprochement with the european union. as a result, after deliberation in the council and in the absence of common agreement, the opening of accession negotiations with croatia had to be postponed. in the meantime, a working group consisting of the presidency, the secretary-general/high representative, the commission and the next two presidencies has been set up. the task of the committee shall be to examine, in close contact with the court and croatia, the measures that croatia has taken and is still taking with a view to achieving full cooperation with the court. in this context, the working party met on 26 april 2005 with the court and the croatian party to examine the latest developments in cooperation between croatia and that institution. the group decided that the council conclusions of december and march remain valid and that the council would review the matter in due course, in the light of significant developments in the future in close cooperation with the court.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on 26 april i had the pleasure of presenting to you in committee the amendments to the two regulations underlying the stability and growth pact, which the college of commissioners had approved on 20 april. five weeks later, we are debating here in the european parliament's plenary session mr karas' reports on both regulations, which is yet another example of the good spirit of cooperation with which this parliament has approached this important issue. during these weeks, parliament, the council and the commission itself have worked to complete the legislative process of reforming the pact before the end of the luxembourg presidency. after this first stage of consideration of the commission's proposals here in the house, we are already closer to an agreement, which could materialize - and i hope, if possible, that it will materialize - before the end of this month. as i explained in my committee presentation, our proposal, following the mandate of the european council - which had in turn endorsed the report of the ecofin council in march - was limited to the amendments to the regulations which were strictly necessary to make them compatible with the council's agreement. however, during the council's discussions, several member states argued that certain provisions, such as the minimum annual fiscal adjustment of 0.5% of gross domestic product for countries in excessive deficit or needing to move towards a balanced position in the medium term, or the explicit enumeration of the other relevant factors, should be included in the wording of the regulations. these requests have prolonged for a few days the discussion on some points on which there was already agreement in the council. fortunately, that agreement has been maintained and i am informed that today the council working party has reached a final agreement on the matter. parliament, for its part, has expressed its concern in mr karas' reports about certain parameters affecting the credibility of multilateral budgetary surveillance, such as the quality of national fiscal statistics, debt monitoring and the reliability of macroeconomic forecasts. parliament too legitimately demands to be regularly informed about the excessive deficit procedures. i should like to say, ladies and gentlemen, that the commission shares the same concerns as parliament. many of these are, or can be, contained in some of the different components of the body of legal texts governing the coordination of economic policies in economic and monetary union. other concerns expressed in some of the amendments in mr karas' reports - i am referring more specifically to the monitoring of the debt and the regular reporting to parliament on the excessive deficit procedures - from the commission's point of view can be perfectly integrated into the pact's regulations. i said that to the eurogroup ministers on monday, and i even made some specific reference to how they might be collected. it is logically up to the council to take these suggestions into account and the council will formally express its opinion at the appropriate time - which i believe will be next monday. i hope that the cooperation we have enjoyed in recent weeks will continue until the end of the legislative procedure, so that we can have a renewed stability and growth pact as soon as possible, one which is adapted to the economic dynamics of the member states, both from a political and a legal point of view. the broad consensus with which we are implementing this reform is undoubtedly helping to strengthen the credibility of the pact and to demonstrate the unequivocal will to defend sound public finances as a necessary condition for sustained economic growth. just yesterday, here in strasbourg, the college of commissioners adopted a report recommending the opening of an excessive deficit procedure against one member state, italy. it is further proof of the validity of the stability and growth pact and a practical example of the spirit of the reform of the pact. it is also an indication that we must conclude the discussion on the rules for the operation of the pact as soon as possible and concentrate on the application of those rules and on the implementation of the principles and guidelines of the pact. finally, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, if there is one thing that has become clear in the recent negative votes in france and the netherlands on the draft european constitution, it is, in my view, the need to act and achieve concrete results that will lead to tangible benefits for the well-being of citizens, starting with employment and the consolidation of our social model. the european union must therefore take decisive action to boost our economies, create jobs and maintain our levels of social cohesion. the efforts of all the institutions - president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, for the last 15 years there has been talk of a statute for members of the european parliament and, as you know, many initiatives have been taken by your parliament and the council respectively to achieve such a statute. the status under discussion today was clarified during the belgian presidency in the second half of 2001, when parliament and the council were very close to reaching an agreement. at that time, the failure was linked to the reimbursement of actual costs and taxation. subsequently, no progress was made and it was during the italian presidency that mr rothley presented a new draft report which also had a good chance of succeeding. mr rothley had included in his report a solution which could reconcile the council and parliament. in particular, your parliament had committed itself to the reimbursement of members' actual expenses, which would come into force alongside the new statute. the rothley report was submitted to your committee on legal affairs on 21 january 2004. unfortunately, on 26 january the general affairs council failed to reach a political agreement, in particular because of the budgetary implications of the project. in november 2004, in his speech to the european council, president josep borrell, and you yourself, mr president, indicated that the european parliament was prepared to show flexibility on this matter in order to reach an agreement in the short term. he also stressed to the european council that parliament could not formally present a new proposal without the assurance that it would be accepted by the council and that informal consultations on the subject were therefore necessary. at the end of 2004, under the dutch presidency, such a consultation took place in the presence of the future luxembourg presidency and it was agreed to try to reach an agreement during the first half of 2005. on 12 january 2005, the president-in-office of the council, in his speech to the european parliament presenting the programme of the luxembourg presidency, confirmed the intention of the presidency to bring the negotiations on this dossier to a successful conclusion, in cooperation with the whole of parliament and its president. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after 26 years of electing the european parliament by direct universal suffrage, there is still no uniform status for members of the european parliament. that is why today and tomorrow, with the vote, could be decisive, since at last the council and the european parliament seem to be able to move forward with a decision. i particularly welcome, mr president, the efforts of the rapporteur and chairman of the committee on legal affairs, mr giuseppe gargani, and of the members of that vice-president of the commission. mr president, i sincerely welcome the efforts of the rapporteur mr gargani, parliament and the luxembourg presidency, in finding a solution agreeable to all parties on the members’ statute. the commission gave its opinion on the original proposal for a statute in june 2003. it was favourable and made two general observations. first, we pointed out that the provisions in the draft statute relating to the privileges and immunities of members and governed by primary law could not be amended in an act based on article 190 of the ec treaty. in this new draft these provisions have been removed. our second comment concerned the financial implications of the statute and these concerns have also been addressed. we have seemed very close to agreement before, only to have everyone’s hopes dashed at the last minute. i sincerely hope that this time the statute will finally be approved.
i am sorry, but i have to say that i am not in favour of the amendments. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the past. my group agrees that we need a statute for members of parliament. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. for this reason too there will be no uniform voting procedure in my group. we have always called for - and we have underlined this in our amendments to the rothley report - that the amount of travel expenses reimbursement should be equal to the actual travel expenses incurred, since transparency is the first principle. reimbursement in excess of the actual costs shall not be accepted. moreover, there is already the possibility of reimbursing travel expenses in excess, as is already the practice of german members of parliament in the context of their voluntary commitment. as regards the pension fund, we are divided on the level of the members' share in relation to the parliament's share. in any case, we support the basic principle that members of parliament should contribute to social security schemes like other citizens and should also contribute to the financing of the pension fund, even though we know that this is not a solidarity pension scheme but a pension fund. the same applies to the contribution to accident insurance. we should always bear in mind in our debate that parliamentary contributions are of course also necessary because we get our salary from the taxpayer. we are unanimous in our support of the principle of equal pay for equal work. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european parliament is able to exercise its right of initiative. the introduction of a uniform level of pay is therefore right. of course, the amount of the fine is debatable. and it goes without saying that members who receive a uniform salary must also be taxed in the same way, i.e. according to european tax law. if member states decide to add the difference between the european and national tax rates, they are entitled to do so, provided that double taxation is avoided.
the luxembourg presidency has succeeded in reaching agreement on the statute for members of the european parliament. the statute of members can remove many grey areas and inadequate regulations. i therefore believe that there is no point in refusing to accept this compromise again. european rules bring more transparency to citizens than 25 or 27 national rules and various compensation mechanisms, both permitted and not. i am aware that this compromise also has its obvious shortcomings. the pension scheme (article 14) remains a key problem. we must create a fund with a share of the members' own money. we have now lost our amendment no 1 to that. i am convinced, however, that the way to a solution below the level of the statute is still open and i will continue to advocate such a system, which must complement the statute. the members' statute finally opens the way for us to have an assistant statute. parliament must now bring this work to a successful conclusion as quickly as possible.
