proposals represent a chance for all three institutions of europe, parliament, the commission and the council, to stand united in the face of terrorism and organised crime and to send a message that we are determined to work together to achieve these things. i am proud of what has been achieved in this presidency. we have agreed a european union counter-terrorism strategy. we have taken steps to improve the exchange of information for law enforcement. we have adopted a strategy to address radicalisation and terrorist recruitment. we have established a european union programme to protect critical infrastructure against terrible attacks. we have established a peer evaluation of counter-terrorism practice and development. we have adopted a money-laundering directive. we have agreed proposals to enhance the sharing of information between law enforcement agencies and we have developed a european plan of action to tackle human trafficking. in that context, let me draw attention to the fact that we have also placed the issues of migration much higher up the european union agenda. this is a very substantial range of achievements. but i personally attach the greatest importance to the one we are debating today: the aim to achieve common standards for retention of telecommunications data. as mr frattini said, this has been a frank debate – with everybody ready to participate in discussion – but also a difficult debate, because the issues of principle and the technical issues have not been at all easy to resolve. my own commitment has been to listen as widely as possible to the views expressed within parliament and to discuss with my colleagues in the council how we can work together. to be candid, there was some scepticism in the council at the idea of going down the course of a first-reading deal and a process of this kind. people were not certain that it would be possible to get an agreement. that is why today is so important. to make the statement that the european parliament in particular, not just the council and commission, commits to proposals in this area seems to me very important. the tools we are talking about, the telecommunications data we are describing, are vital to investigate and detect terrorism and crime. it is essential, in my view, to provide a proportionate and balanced legal basis for the retention of data that would otherwise be erased or anonymised. variations in data retention practice mean that the ability of investigators and prosecutors to detect and prosecute criminals and terrorists to stop them causing harm, or to catch them after they have caused harm, is dependent on which communications service provider a suspect, a victim or witness has used or which member state they were in. that variation gives an open goal to our opponents in criminality, and it is that we are trying to close with this directive, which i hope we will adopt today. we have many examples, some of which i gave to the civil liberties committee in september 2005, where communications data has been used to trace the members of terrorist cells, to help identify murderers and free kidnap victims and to deal with those who organise very serious crime. the position of the council, supported by the commission, aims to find a compromise between parliament and the council, in particular, the need to balance law enforcement needs with individuals’ right to privacy by including specific rules on data protection. as amended, the directive would oblige member states to ensure the retention of data for the investigation, detection and prosecution of serious crime only. this was a call that came specifically from the european parliament. many told us that we had to ensure that this was limited to serious crime at community level. we have responded to that point in what is being put forward, which the council accepted. on periods of retention, the proposed period in the compromise, six to twenty-four months, represents a compromise between those in the council, who wanted a much longer maximum period – and there are some in the council who did not believe in principle that we should legislate on this basis at all – and those in the parliament, who would have been happier with a shorter retention period. i believe the compromise will enable law enforcement authorities to obtain the data they need without disproportionately infringing privacy rights. the presidency took account of concerns expressed by member states and industry and by some in parliament about costs, particularly those incurred by storing types of data such as unanswered calls. that is why the list of data in the directive has been restricted and why unconnected call data is outside the scope altogether. it is also one reason why i supported the commitment, given by the commission and council, to regularly review the effectiveness of the application of the directive together with the european parliament, the european data protection supervisor and representatives of industry. this is a fast-moving picture and it is important that all the institutions work together to keep us up to date on the best way to deal with it. as i mentioned, the council also took very seriously the concerns expressed in parliament about data protection and security. that is why the amendments include articles on data protection, data access and sanctions in the event of data abuse. i agree entirely with the representations made by the parliament that data must be kept safe and secure and can only be disclosed lawfully to people lawfully entitled to see it. there should not be overall access. i know this has been a difficult negotiation and the subject matter is technical and complex. i welcome, therefore, the requirement that the commission must fully evaluate the application of the directive and its impact on industry and consumers. our right to privacy, our right to property, our right to free speech and our right to life are all threatened by terrorists and criminals. i believe that, particularly in this democracy, democratic politicians have a duty and responsibility to protect these rights through the kinds of practical measures we are agreeing here. i hope we can say at the end of this debate that we have achieved that. i believe the commission’s proposal, as amended by the council and with the support of parliament, would secure an instrument which strikes a better balance between the need to retain data to protect our citizens and the need to protect and respect individuals’ privacy. we are embracing new technologies that offer great opportunities for learning, for doing business, for communicating. but those same technologies can be used and misused by those who do not respect the rights of others, and by their victims too. it is right, therefore, that we do all we can to deliver justice and to protect citizens. it is what they, our electors, demand of us and it is why we must vice-chairman of the commission . mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think it is fair to say that in the last few weeks there has been a debate and political action in this house which not only gives this parliament a stronger role in the fight against terrorism and organised crime but also strengthens the overall image of the three european institutions. in the course of the many speeches i have heard some people say that this directive is an undemocratic instrument, and some even spoke of stalin and hitler. this directive is a victory for democracy, it is an important and balanced instrument for the benefit of the citizens and, above all, for those who are involved, even at personal cost, in the fight against crime, i am referring to the investigating authorities, the police forces. i am not saying that we should not be concerned about the future of the community. we want to continue with 20 different legal systems, in which each member state does basically what it wants, or is it not better to converge, for the first time, on a european approach, on a directive, and start with harmonization? this is a directive, ladies and gentlemen, which is certainly based on the principles of necessity and proportionality. i have heard some questions, for example from mr reul and mr kudrycka, who have spoken about a case which the polish parliament is considering. i can say without any doubt that the retention of data for 15 years does not seem to follow the criteria of proportionality and necessity, although each member state has the duty to demonstrate why its request is proportionate and necessary, and frankly the case of 15 years seems to me to be a very limiting case. i would like to make two final remarks. i thank all those who have spoken, and in particular mr díaz de mera garcía consuegra and mr díez gonzález, who have wanted to remember the victims of crime and have wanted to stress how - and i fully agree with this - the fundamental freedoms of the individual must be guaranteed. however, ladies and gentlemen, if someone uses a mobile phone to set off a bomb, as has unfortunately happened, or to give instructions to a gang of paedophiles, is it right or not that the police and the judiciary, that is to say the legitimate institutions, should have the tools to prevent and combat such phenomena? i think it is right that this should happen and at the same time i think it is right, as we have written in the directive, that any abuse should be punished: more tools for police forces, more tools for the judiciary in our countries, which are democracies, and more checks to see if someone has abused. in conclusion, the european institutions have unfortunately been divided and are divided on important issues, but it is extremely comforting to see - and i hope that tomorrow's vote will confirm this - that on the issue of the security of citizens, the fight against terrorism and organised crime, the european institutions will not be divided, but will provide the capacity, all three together, to respond in extraordinary rapid terms to the demand of our fellow citizens.

the next item is the report by mr koterec, on behalf of the committee on regional development, on direct state aid as an instrument of regional development (2004/2255 (ini)) (a6-0364/2005).
member of the commission. madam president, the review of the regional aid rules is an integral part of the general reform of state aid policy, as was mentioned by the rapporteur. the overall objective is to adjust the state aid rules to the new approach to the structural funds for 2007-2013, and to give practical effect to the conclusions of the european council, which call for less and better targeted state aid. regional aid reform implies strict control of the more distortive aids by limiting the scope for investment aid for large firms to the regions most in need, in particular, as regards very large investment projects. the reform also allows member states a sufficient degree of flexibility to design aid matters to promote the realisation of the lisbon objectives and targets. that additional flexibility is just one of the elements which was introduced into the package as a result of consultation, including my discussions with the committee on regional development. our approach is coherent with the state aid action plan, which recognises the need to allow regional aid in order to promote cohesion and convergence but emphasises that this should be targeted on the regions most in need. let me reiterate the importance of the principle of concentration. if the aid is spread too thinly and too widely, it simply will not help the regions most in need. we also provide for limited additional coverage, which is put at the disposal of the member states concerned. naturally, we expect member states to target that aid on the areas most in need at national level and it is up to them to identify those areas. when i read the report, i feel bound to say that we are being asked to spread this form of aid too widely. the assumption seems to be that areas which are not eligible for regional aid are not eligible for any form of state aid. allow me to correct that impression: according to the latest state aid scoreboard, the type of aid we are talking about today – regional aid – makes up less than 20% of all state aid granted in the eu, excluding the agricultural, fisheries and transport sectors. those regions not eligible for regional aid will continue to receive other forms of support through the horizontal aid measures that are covered by the state aid action plan: aid for small and medium-sized enterprises, research and development, innovation, training, employment and risk capital. following a very extensive consultation process, i believe we are moving towards a global compromise that should meet the legitimate concerns of the vast majority of member states. no compromise is perfect and some limited adjustments to the text are always possible. however, i will study your proposals very carefully before putting a final package before the college next week for adoption. however, it will not be possible significantly to modify the overall balance that has been struck in the guidelines; otherwise we would risk upsetting the large majority of member states which welcome and support our text, and might call the whole exercise into question.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the support of enterprises by state aid is one of the factors influencing the decision of enterprises to invest in a given area and thus also contributing to economic growth and job creation in that area. it is understandable that these aids are mainly used in the most deprived areas of the european union, but they contribute - like the structural funds - to reducing regional disparities, which is why they should also be used as a priority in the convergence regions referred to in article 87 (3a). however, the same regime must also apply to regions subject to the statistical effect, as already called for in the third cohesion report on economic and social cohesion, until the end of the 2013 planning period. the obligation to maintain investments in the regions concerned must be at least i emphasise: at least five years after the end of the measure. seven years would have been better, five years is the minimum in this respect, to avoid any investment-hopping. this five-year period should be applied to both large companies and smes in order to avoid the use of state aid to encourage the relocation of jobs to another part of the eu and to finance large-scale redundancies and closures of establishments. indeed, if properly applied, monitored and analysed, such aid can be a valuable contribution to growth and job creation.
the socialist group will be voting in favour of the report. the commission is not prepared to accept this. i would like to take just two key words from this complex and very sensitive subject. the keyword of relocation is that nobody in this european union wants companies to move their premises just to get aid. but in each member state there have already been investments where the regions were happy to pay state aid supported by the european union. we need clear, transparent but fair and supportive rules. that is what the report calls for and i hope that the commission will contribute to that. the second point is the statistical effect regions. mr berend has already touched on this. i do not understand why commissioner hübner has always supported us in our decision, supported by a large majority, to treat the statistical impact regions as objective 1 regions for the whole period up to 2013, and then mrs kroes proposes a completely different idea and wants to split it in two. i hope that the commission will come to realise that parliament has good ideas from time to time and is therefore right to support the statistical impact regions.

discuss this matter with secretary of state rice last week in brussels. the united kingdom has expressed its satisfaction with the us statement. i understand some other european union colleagues have also made public comments upon the statement by secretary of state rice. the council welcomes the detailed statement by the us secretary of state, for all european countries share the determination of the united states to protect innocent citizens from the threat of terrorism, while operating within international law. let us be clear about the threat our people face from the modern terrorist. europe has faced terrorism for many years. i do not need to relate the names of the organisations and individuals concerned, but none of us have had to face the kind of threat we face – now and in the long term – from al-qa’ida and its supporters. modern terrorism means mass-casualty attacks. we have seen them in new york, washington, istanbul, madrid, and recently in london and in numerous other cities around the world. honourable members will recall that, just a few years ago, strasbourg was also the target of a thwarted attack. today we are exposed to fanatical suicide attacks on innocent civilians using modern techniques and technology previously confined to states but now available to individuals on the internet. that is a picture we face for the foreseeable future. our people need protecting against it; our governments have a clear responsibility to provide that protection. it is a responsibility that requires governments to make difficult decisions, take concrete action and explain and defend those decisions and that action. the european security strategy adopted in 2003 emphasised that transnational terrorism and the non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction pose a threat we cannot ignore. however, at the same time, in seeking responses to these new challenges, it is essential that the rule of law and the human rights of individuals are respected. the question of torture is a key element of this debate. torture is abhorrent. the prohibition against it is absolute. the british government – like all european governments – unreservedly condemns it. we never use it; we never instigate or condone it; we condemn it utterly, and we work hard with others to eradicate it. secretary of state rice’s statement of 5 december makes clear that the policy of the united states government is to comply with the un convention against torture, that the united states government complies with its constitution, its laws and its treaty obligations. she goes on to say that acts of physical or mental torture are expressly prohibited, that the united states government does not authorise or condone torture of detainees and that torture and conspiracy to commit torture are crimes under us law wherever they may occur in the world. the council welcomes this statement. it is right that the word of another sovereign government – expressed so clearly on such an important issue – is respected within a larger discussion on the balance between security and liberty. as secretary of state rice herself said on 5 september, that debate in and among democracies is natural and healthy. that must be right and this parliament can and has made a contribution to that debate. i understand that, in the light of the allegations, the secretary-general of the council of europe has requested from the member states of that international organisation an explanation of how they ensure the effective implementation of the provisions of the european convention on human rights. i am sure that member states will want to cooperate with the council of europe. informed exchanges on issues like this are important, including for the benefit of our people who look to their governments and institutions for a lead. i look forward to hearing your views and those of commissioner frattini on this important subject.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all the european commission feels it is its moral, institutional and political duty to ensure that the fundamental rights of every person are always respected and defended without any exceptions or derogations. torture and inhuman treatment are a denial of the values on which the european union was founded and which it is still based. secondly, i would like to reiterate the crucial and strategic importance of joint action and close cooperation between the european union and the united states of america in the fight international terrorism. as minister alexander has just said, i welcome the formal statement by the us secretary of state condoleezza rice that the united states of america does not tolerate, and rules of the rule of law, no accusation can be considered ascertained, and until the evidence is acquired i myself have a duty to respect the word and therefore also the denial that all the governments i have consulted so far and i say so far have provided. this does not exclude our common desire for truth, but it is clear, as i said to the libe committee the other night, that i cannot doubt, without proof to the contrary, the credibility of legitimate and democratic governments in the countries of the european union and the candidate countries. i cannot consider that there are any european countries which are 'accused', i say this in quotes and i say this in particular to our polish and romanian friends. there is a duty to ascertain whether abuses and torture have been committed throughout europe. we cannot point to this or that country as a target, as an accused, as a defendant. if torture or inhuman treatment has been carried out, we have a duty to verify this throughout the european union. some european countries, as you know, have launched national investigations. some governments have done so, for example the portuguese and polish governments, as have the judicial authorities of member states such as my own, italy, spain, germany and others. these judicial authorities are conducting investigations with the powers of the judiciary and it is clear of the council of europe. i also confirmed to mr davis the commission's strong support for the second parallel inquiry launched by the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe. mr marty, who is the rapporteur, deserves public appreciation for the work he is doing. as you probably know, the secretary-general will conclude his inquiry on 21 february 2006 and dr marty will present a first report on his inquiry to the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe by january 2006. i have asked, through commissioners barrot and ferrero-waldner, that eurocontrol's data on flight plans over european territory and all possible useful data collected by the european satellite tracking centre be made available to the council of europe for its investigation. there is currently no evidence to support the allegations, but we must continue - and i will continue - to work closely with the council of europe and this parliament to find the truth. it is not for me to say what instrument parliament will choose for this joint work, i will simply say that when we talk of inquiry, we need powers of inquiry, of questioning, of investigation and of inspection, and it is obviously for you to decide whether or not these powers are provided for, as the legal service of parliament seems to indicate. in any case, seeking the truth means for me not only identifying any abuses and then drawing the appropriate consequences, but also clearing the field of negative prejudices and suspicions that otherwise risk undermining our due international action to combat terrorism. in conclusion, therefore, if there is any doubt or evidence that abuses and torture have been committed in europe, we will certainly be weaker in the face of the terrorists and the anti-democratic propaganda of the terrorists. that's why we must know the truth, that's why we must do so as loyal friends and allies of the united states of america, but always as jealous guardians of our common values.

those involved in the process, and in particular the shadow rapporteurs from the various other groups. you have been willing to make many compromises, for which i would like to express my gratitude. i would also like to thank the commissioner responsible, who is here today, for his willingness to compromise on many details which were extremely important to us as a parliament, which made it much easier for members to accept the common position in a slightly modified form. i would like to mention five points which we consider to be of paramount importance. the aim of this directive, which is not readily understandable to every citizen - this must be seen in a self-critical way - was to establish a better distinction with other directives. there is a problem, namely the tractor directive. tractors were not previously covered by the machinery directive at the same time and are now subject to a parallel taxation: on the one hand the tractor directive and on the other the machinery directive. this is a difficult double burden for manufacturers, which we would like to see eliminated. and then, of course, there is the tractor seat directive, mr verheugen, which - as you will know from reading the newspapers in germany - is not only regarded as an absolute bureaucratic monster in germany. i am therefore very grateful to you for working together towards this goal - perhaps not quite as fast as we all wish - in order to arrive at a simple rule: the tractor directive only for tractors and the machinery directive only for all other machinery. we must now make sure that we achieve this goal as quickly as possible. i would naturally like to see the completion of the tractor directive, including all risks not yet covered, within the 18-month period required for the transposition of the machinery directive in the member states. i know that such wishes cannot always be fulfilled at once, but i would like to mention the objective, namely 18 months to reach the deadline for implementation. there are, of course, a number of points on which i would have liked to have gone further as rapporteur. this is the case, for example, with the exclusion of harmless machines, such as wristwatches. i have, however, withdrawn my request in the end because of the massive concerns, especially of the commission, about the resulting security gaps. however, parliament has made considerable progress in the area of the protection of trade secrets compared with the common position, and i believe that this also applies to the disposal of machinery. of course, we all know that sustainable production is of great importance for europe, also from the point of view of the lisbon strategy. it was certainly right, however, not to impose a kind of blanket liability on manufacturers, who really cannot foresee how the disposal of machinery will actually proceed and who in many places are small and mediumsized enterprises. i also believe that we must go a long way together on the issue of certification, particularly third party certification, because the situation we found in the common position on ce marking was by no means acceptable to us as members of parliament. we do not think it is enough for the council to find itself on the lowest common denominator, even though many meetings were needed to draw up this common position, and to find formulaic compromises which are then reflected in language which no human being, no citizen, no smes can understand. we are aware of the difficulties, for example in connection with translation. however, our aim must be to produce legal texts - and that is what you personally stand for, mr verheugen - that are understandable to every citizen. i am glad that we have taken a small step forward in the ce marking. i think we are not going far enough, but you have explicitly included the new approach to ce marking in your 2006 work programme, and i do not want to complain about it for long. i believe that this is the right opportunity to regulate ce marking in a broader and more coherent way across all sectors equally, which would be beneficial and which would mean better regulation in my view. however, in fixing this legislation we must think again carefully about the purpose of ce marking in the european union, what quality and safety standards we associate with it and who has the task of monitoring these standards, because i believe that we still have a process of clarification and discussion with the member states in the field of market surveillance. it is not possible for the european union to be responsible if problems arise while the member states do not fully comply with their responsibilities as regards the time in which supervision is to be exercised. overall, thank you very much. i believe that we have made some progress towards better regulation and de-bureaucratisation, but we still have some further to go. i hope that the commission will make further proposals, particularly in the field of tractors, to ensure that better regulation is pursued successfully.
the socialist group will be voting in favour of the report. the commission has already made a number of proposals. one and a half years of debate in the council is certainly a long time. but of course, it's nothing compared to machine running times. as someone who has worked in the mechanical engineering industry for 20 years, i know how important this directive is also for the predictability of legislation. after the initial scepticism of many users, i believe that all concerns have now been more or less allayed. we have received the first letters of approval, and this is important because we want to work with the user and not with the head. the directive is important not only for users but also for millions of consumers, because it contains legislation which is of great importance for the health and safety of consumers. this revision was necessary, among other things, because previous directives were not sufficient, but also to improve the necessary legal certainty, to define the scope more precisely and to ensure that the free movement of goods is guaranteed at a high level of safety and health protection for consumers. this is the main objective of european industrial policy. i would also like to thank you for the good cooperation with your colleagues and, above all, with the commission and the council. the social democrats, however, had to make some important contributions. we were also much closer to the council in most of the discussions. for example, we want the commission to develop guidelines to enable member states to increase their capacity to enable effective market surveillance to ensure the uniform application of the directive. the social democrats also felt that confidentiality and professional secrecy should not be allowed to affect the safety and health of individuals. we also wanted to make it easier for smes - and this has now happened - without any substantial loss and without any relevant financial burden. it was also important to us that the adaptation of this directive did not reduce the standards for disabled people in lifts. we have achieved all that. we were against the removal of agricultural and forestry tractors. we accept the commissioner's explanation. we would have preferred you to have given a date, namely 2008, but we are all still in parliament at that time and we will keep an eye on it. we did not want to take out the small appliances, mr schwab, because it is not just about wristwatches, but also about relatively dangerous fire extinguishers and similar small appliances. i think we have reached a good compromise. the social democrats will support him, and i would have liked to have praised the british once this week for an exceptional reason. we have also worked very well with the british presidency in this respect.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the importance of mechanical engineering in the european economy has just been pointed out. this is true throughout the european union, but certainly especially in my own country. it is therefore interesting to note that this directive was also drawn up at the request of industry. the industry has been working hard to get this directive under the heading 'a product, a regulation for the internal market'. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the quality of the products is not affected by the fact that they are not in conformity with the standards laid down by the european standards. in the light of this second reading, let me make the following remark with regard to the debate on the services directive. if we were to take this as a basis for our arguments in our discussions on the services directive, we would certainly be taking the debate forward there too. i should like to point out in this connection that european mechanical engineering is particularly dependent on the services directive, because, of course, not only products are sold, but also services with the machines. let me make a second political remark on this. we have noted in today's debate that the road to this directive was very long, five years. this has largely been the case in a european union of 15 member states. as we all know, we are now moving in a union of 25 states. in this context, and especially in the context of the return of regulation, it should be pointed out, also with regard to the economy and the relevant political bodies, that in the future it is likely that much longer distances will be needed to reach such regulation. here again, the principle is true: less is sometimes more. i would like to stress once again the positive impression that this directive has made on me.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i would also like to join in thanking mr schwab for the good work he has done, but at the same time i would also like to thank mrs weiler and mrs de vits, who have worked very hard on behalf of my group and have therefore also made sure that some progress has been made in cooperation with mr schwab. the keywords of health, safety and consumer protection have already been dropped. this is also what makes the quality features that, in products such as machinery, also mean the top position and that allow our product manufacturers to find a large market worldwide. that's a good thing. i can only agree with mrs weiler in this respect. legal certainty is the key here. legal certainty means that machine builders know exactly what they have to comply with, what regulations actually exist, and that they are not left in the dark. this also means that we can have a good market in this context. but legal certainty also means that we must avoid having several different directives apply to one product. legal certainty means that these steps are finally taken - particularly in the case of the tractor directives - and that a uniform regulation is adopted. it is not good for manufacturers to have to juggle between different regulations, and it is also very regrettable that we have not been able to get through with our proposal that this issue should finally be resolved by 2008 at the latest. this is a real mourning game. i remember that in the first reading, when we discussed this subject with the european commission and the council, it was said that we would have everything resolved in the next six months. that was a year and a half ago. the same answer was given when we discussed the subject this year: it will be settled in the next six months. so my request to all concerned is that you make sure that this problem is solved really quickly, because we should not leave the machine builders in the dark either.

in writing. the first lesson from the affair around the cia flights must be to close the us and nato military bases such as aviano in italy, ramstein in germany and kogalniceanu in romania in the eu and the future member states. after all, they are the infrastructure for the torture flights. eu interior commissioner franco frattini plays things down, wherever this is possible, and pushes the responsibility back to the member states. this is all the more dishonest, since the affair quite clearly also has an eu dimension. the eu, in the security political arena and precisely as far as the so-called struggle against terrorism is concerned, has agreed on a close cooperation with nato and the usa. agreements on secret service cooperation and on the unlimited transfer of information classified secret are part of the “berlin plus agreement”, which allows the eu to take military action using nato capacities. in february 2003, there was agreed directly with the usa a close cooperation in the transport of suspects. the scandalous behaviour in this sense is not only that of the us government, but the blame must also rest with the eu officials and the eu governments in the know.

a writer. the commission is not in early october, 28-year-old monk ngawang jangchub died in his cell at drepung monastery. his death is the result of an interrogation by the cadres of the so-called "patriotic education" campaign. critics of the regime are to be brought to their senses by means of drastic physical and psychological re-education measures. since 1996, more than 10 000 monks and nuns in tibet have been brainwashed - a flagrant violation of freedom of thought and religion. threats, arrests, torture are meant to get monastic residents to condemn the dalai lama in writing as an enemy of the state and separatist. on november 23, chinese security forces occupied the drepung monastery near the capital lhasa. liz lynn just pointed that out. they arrested five high-ranking clergymen. then 400 monks peacefully demonstrated for their release. police and special forces responded promptly. for days, the monastery was hermetically sealed off from the outside world. the chinese are not interested in the european parliament's human rights resolutions. the intervention of the commission, mr verheugen, and of the council is clearly not enough. or are they just footnotes in the much-heralded eu-china dialogue? i would remind you, on behalf of the epp-ed group, of our debate in october, in which we urgently called for the life-threatening conditions of detention of the highly respected lama tensin delek rinpoche to be improved so that he can be given a fair trial. manfred nowak, the united nations special rapporteur on torture, has just presented the results of his inspection of chinese prisons, labor camps and police stations. he confirms the torture. he confirms the mistreatment of prisoners and suspects. the chinese system of re-education through labor allows for people to be sent to a camp for up to three years without a court order. this is a clear violation of the personal integrity and dignity of every human being!
a writer. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the socio-political developments in russia are alarming. the deliberate closure of ngos by the new law, the ongoing repression of former yukos leaders mikhail khodorkovsky and platon lebedev and the war situation in chechnya are examples of gross human rights violations. khodorkovsky and lebedev are being held in siberian prison camps far from moscow, beyond the arctic circle, at -50 degrees celsius, in violation of russian law. lebedev is very ill. contacts with the families and lawyers are extremely difficult. they have no access to information. they don't get newspapers. their lawyers, yevgeny baro and yuri schmit, are now facing trial next week on charges of slander. these human rights abuses in the russian judiciary are being exacerbated by the increasing restriction of press freedom. we should take stock of these developments and call on the council and the commission to exert influence on russia to ensure that human rights are respected.
